Both provider operators declare this link, and subclasses, including mapped tasks, inherit it. A subclass that replaces operator_extra_links must keep SparkOnK8SOperatorLink() among its links. Otherwise, or for a listed operator that does not inherit from a provider operator, the tab reports that the task has no Spark application binding and does not read a record that the task pushed to XCom.

docs.title: Refresh and shared snapshots
docs.text:
By default, the tab refreshes every 10 seconds while the application is pending, running or in an unknown state. Once the application has succeeded or failed, live refresh ends and the tab says so; Refresh still loads the current state on demand. A driver log stream ends when the driver terminates and shows Stream ended; Reconnect requests the available logs again.

Viewers of the same task attempt share the application snapshot that the Spark API reads from Kubernetes for SPARK_ON_K8S_AIRFLOW_SNAPSHOT_TTL seconds, and concurrent requests share one lookup. Each request is still authorized by Airflow and resolves its own task binding before it can receive a shared snapshot, and different task attempts never share one. Kill and delete verify the driver's current application directly, then discard the shared snapshot. A failed lookup is not reused after it completes. Each Airflow API server process keeps its own bounded in-memory snapshots, so a deployment with several API server workers or replicas can still perform one lookup per process for each interval. History records, the History Server capability check and diagnostics are requested for each viewer.

docs.title: Automation and run identities
docs.text: These features describe the current source. For shell scripts and CI, use --output json instead of parsing human-readable progress messages.

docs.title: Submit and observe a run
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --namespace spark \
  --image registry.example.com/team/job:version \
  --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
  --name daily-report \
  --wait --timeout 900 --output json > result.json

The command writes one JSON document to stdout. Progress and driver logs go to stderr in JSON mode, so --logs --output json > result.json 2> driver.log keeps both streams separate. --logs waits for a terminal application state after the log stream ends; end-of-stream alone does not prove that a job succeeded.

A successful waiting submission has this shape:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "operation": "submit",
  "namespace": "spark",
  "error": null,
  "run": {
    "namespace": "spark",
    "app_id": "daily-report-20261107120000",
    "driver_pod": "daily-report-20261107120000-driver",
    "driver_uid": "5bdceeb0-7fa8-4f72-823b-80f26e6195c4"
  },
  "status": "Succeeded"
}

Without --wait or --logs, exit code 0 means the application resources were submitted, and status is null. It does not mean the workload succeeded. The receipt identifies the actual generated application ID and driver pod. It is retained in runtime error output if submission succeeded before waiting failed, timed out, or was interrupted. An error during resource creation can leave partial resources. The client records a confirmed driver UID immediately after receiving its creation response. Results include submission_phase (preparing, creating_resources, driver_created, resources_created) so a later owner-reference or Service failure can still return the known driver identity. If creation itself has an ambiguous transport result, no confirmed receipt is invented. Inspect the cluster before retrying. When the API server definitively rejects the driver Pod or a ConfigMap (a 4xx response other than 408), the client deletes only the Secret and ConfigMaps it created earlier in that submission, using their creation UIDs as preconditions. Server errors, timeouts and interruptions keep them because the driver may exist.

--timeout takes positive, finite seconds and requires a wait or log waiter on submission. It limits observation after submission, including a running job and a quiet log stream. It does not bound initial resource creation or an external Kubernetes credential plugin. The default is unlimited observation. The existing SPARK_ON_K8S_STARTUP_TIMEOUT remains a separate limit for a pending driver. Neither timeout nor interruption automatically kills or deletes the application. The deadline is checked before each status or log request and each poll sleep. A status returned by a request that started within the budget is reported: a final Succeeded or Failed read at the deadline exits 0 or 3, not 5. A timeout result has status: null.

To observe a previously submitted application:

spark-on-k8s app wait --namespace spark --app-id "$APP_ID" \
  --timeout 900 --output json
spark-on-k8s app status --namespace spark --app-id "$APP_ID" --output json
spark-on-k8s apps list --namespace spark --output json

A status or wait document contains schema_version, operation, namespace, app_id, status, and error. A list document contains the same common fields plus items, an array of { "app_id": "...", "namespace": "..." } objects; it does not contain app_id or status at the top level. On a list error, items is null. Listing does not make a status request for each application.

Runtime errors use error: { "code": "...", "message": "..." } with codes api_error, operation_error, not_found, timeout, or interrupted. A driver that disappears while it is watched is not_found (exit code 4) with status: null: its outcome is unknown, not finished. The SDK raises SparkAppDeletedError from wait_for_app in that case. JSON error messages exclude Kubernetes response bodies. Receipts do not contain submitted configuration or secrets. Driver logs remain application-controlled data and may contain sensitive information. Consumers should check schema_version, tolerate additional fields, and avoid depending on object-key order or human messages.

Some results also contain warnings, an array of { "code": "...", "message": "..." } advisories. connect check and connect server wait use the version_skew code when the Spark Connect client and server differ in major or minor version (see client and server versions). A warning never changes error or the exit code; text output prints it on stderr. Tolerate unknown warning codes, and test the array explicitly if a script must fail on one. CLI argument errors are reported by Click on stderr before execution and do not produce a JSON document. --help remains human-readable.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Submission accepted, successful query, or waiting workload succeeded 1 Operation, configuration, or Kubernetes API failure 2 Invalid CLI arguments or options 3 Waiting workload ended in Failed 4 Requested application or Kubernetes resource was not found 5 Observation, startup, or transport timeout 6 Waiting workload outcome is unknown; success was not established 130 User interruption

Workload outcome codes apply to app wait and app submit --wait / --logs. app status returns 0 when the query succeeds, even if the reported status is Failed. app logs remains a standalone streaming command; follow it with app wait when a script needs the workload result.

Shells configured with set -e stop on a failed workload. To retain and inspect failure output, explicitly capture the exit code:

exit_code=0
spark-on-k8s app wait -n spark --app-id "$APP_ID" --output json \
  > result.json || exit_code=$?
cat result.json
exit "$exit_code"

docs.title: Python run handles
docs.text:
Existing callers can continue using submit_app(...), which returns the driver pod name as a string. submit_run(...) accepts the same arguments and returns an immutable RunHandle with namespace, app_id, driver_pod, and driver_uid fields:

from spark_on_k8s.client import SparkOnK8S

client = SparkOnK8S()
run = client.submit_run(
    namespace="spark",
    image="registry.example.com/team/job:version",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    app_name="daily-report",
    app_waiter="no_wait",
)
print(run.to_dict())
client.app_manager.wait_for_app(
    namespace=run.namespace, pod_name=run.driver_pod, timeout=900,
)
status = client.app_manager.app_status(
    namespace=run.namespace, pod_name=run.driver_pod,
)

Python callers explicitly inspect the final status; the SDK does not convert it into a process exit code. Both submission methods update last_submitted_run and the existing last_submitted_app_id. A later attempt clears these properties before validation, so a failed submission cannot return a previous run's identity. Keep the returned handle when submitting multiple runs with one client. These per-client convenience properties are not intended for concurrent submissions.

For SDK submission with app_waiter="wait" or "log", the optional wait_timeout sets an observation budget after resource creation. Managers also accept timeout on wait_for_app and stream_logs; expiration raises TimeoutError. submit_run does not support dry runs. A handle contains no credentials, clients, or automatic reattachment behavior.

docs.title: Save identity before waiting
docs.text:
Add --receipt-file run.json to app submit, job submit, or sql submit. The parent directory must exist and the destination must be new. A private file (mode 0600) is published atomically after submission, before log streaming or waiting. A timeout, interruption, or observer crash does not remove it. Existing receipts are never overwritten. Stdout still contains a single final result.

spark-on-k8s job submit job.yaml --profile production \
  --receipt-file run.json --output json > result.json

The file contains schema_version: 1 and run with namespace, application ID, driver name and Kubernetes UID. Use its namespace and application ID with app wait to resume observation from another process using the same cluster. Receipts contain no credentials, kubeconfig or cluster endpoint. Select the correct cluster explicitly; a receipt is an identity, not authorization.

A known driver receipt is also saved when a later resource-creation step fails. If receipt persistence fails too, the original submission failure remains primary and receipt_error describes the storage failure. A receipt cannot recover an unknown submission response or make data writes idempotent. If local publication fails after submission, the command fails and its final JSON still contains the known run. Investigate that run before retrying.

docs.title: Cancel the recorded run
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s app cancel --receipt run.json --output json

Cancellation reads the current pod, verifies its UID, application label and driver role, then sends a Kubernetes UID precondition with the deletion request. A stale receipt cannot delete a replacement pod with the same name. Older receipts without a UID cannot use this command. accepted: true means the API accepted deletion; it does not establish that executors, volumes or finalizers have finished cleanup. --force requests zero grace period and still preserves the identity checks. No timeout automatically invokes cancellation. An unreadable or invalid receipt is a runtime failure (exit 1): the JSON result has run: null, an empty namespace and an operation_error. A receipt path that does not exist is a CLI usage error (exit 2) without a JSON document.

docs.title: Limit how long a driver can run
docs.text:
--timeout and wait_timeout only limit observation. To stop an application that runs too long, including one whose submitting process, CI runner or Airflow worker was killed, set a maximum driver lifetime in whole seconds:

spark-on-k8s app submit --namespace spark \
  --image registry.example.com/team/job:version \
  --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
  --max-runtime 7200 --wait --output json

The same setting is max_runtime in submit_app/submit_run, spec.max_runtime in job files, --max-runtime on sql submit and connect server create, ConnectServerConfig.max_runtime, compute.max_runtime for managed dbt and the Airflow operators' max_runtime argument. It is unset by default and has no environment-variable default. Values range from 1 to 2592000 seconds (30 days); offline plans show it.

The client sets the driver pod's spec.activeDeadlineSeconds; no process needs to keep running. Kubernetes counts the deadline from the pod's startTime, when the kubelet accepts the scheduled pod (image pulls count; time spent unschedulable does not, so keep startup_timeout for that). When it elapses, the kubelet stops the driver containers with the pod's termination grace period and marks the pod Failed with reason DeadlineExceeded. The driver is not restarted. Waiting commands report Failed (exit code 3), and app diagnose reports a deadline_exceeded finding. Unlike an observation timeout, this deliberately ends the application. It is a hard stop rather than a drain: interrupted work can leave partial output, as with any killed run. Choose a value well above the expected duration.

On that termination signal, Spark's driver shutdown normally deletes its executor pods (unless spark.kubernetes.executor.deleteOnTermination=false); an executor that loses its driver exits. The Failed driver pod itself remains, with its logs and the objects it owns: the driver Service, ConfigMaps, Secret and any retained executor pods. They request no further CPU or memory, but stay until the driver pod is deleted, after which Kubernetes garbage collection removes them. Delete the run with app cancel --receipt or app delete, or use apps prune below. With a driver pod template, max_runtime replaces the template's activeDeadlineSeconds; when unset, a template value is kept.

docs.title: Prune finished or orphaned drivers
docs.text:
apps prune finds drivers submitted by spark-on-k8s in one namespace. It only reports them unless you add --delete:

spark-on-k8s apps prune --namespace spark --older-than 86400 --output json
spark-on-k8s apps prune --namespace spark --older-than 86400 --delete --output json

A driver is selected only when it has the spark-role=driver and spark-app-id labels and the pod name that this client derives from that application ID. This covers drivers created by the SDK, CLI, remote API, Airflow operators, Connect server helper and dbt adapter. Pods from other launchers, or that merely copy the labels, are counted as unverified and never deleted. By default, only terminal (Succeeded or Failed) drivers are selected, including those stopped by max_runtime. --older-than SECONDS (default 0) sets a minimum age since pod creation, as shown by kubectl get pods, not since completion. --include-active also selects Pending, Running and Unknown drivers, and deleting them stops those applications; it requires a positive --older-than. Pods already being deleted are skipped.

With --delete, each selected driver is checked and deleted like app cancel: the current pod must still have the listed UID, application label and driver role, and the request carries a UID precondition with foreground propagation. Kubernetes then garbage-collects the executors, Services, ConfigMaps and Secret that the driver owns. An accepted request is not completed cleanup. Objects that were never owned by a driver, such as a Secret left by a submission interrupted before its driver existed, are not selected; the command does not list or read Secrets. It needs list, get and delete access to pods in the namespace. This is a one-time command, not a controller. Python callers can use the same steps through SparkAppManager.find_prunable_drivers(...) and delete_prunable_driver(...).

The JSON document adds dry_run, criteria (older_than, include_active), items and excluded to the common fields. Each item contains app_id, driver_pod, driver_uid, phase, the pod's reason (for example DeadlineExceeded) or null, created_at, age_seconds, action and error. action is would_delete without --delete, otherwise deletion_requested, absent (already gone), replaced (another pod now has that name; not deleted) or failed with an item error. excluded counts other matching pods as active, recent, deleting or unverified. If listing fails, items is null. If some deletions fail, the remaining requests are still sent and the command exits 1 with an operation_error; an interruption exits 130 and reports the requests made so far.

docs.title: Contract coverage and lifecycle ownership
docs.text:
Command family Structured success Structured runtime failures Completion meaning app submit/wait, job submit, sql submit --output json Versioned result after CLI parsing Inspect terminal status; detached submit means accepted app status, apps list, app cancel --output json Versioned result Query/deletion request succeeded, not data correctness apps prune --output json Versioned result with per-driver errors Selection only, or deletion requests accepted; not completed cleanup job validate --output json, per-profile results Versioned result; error repeats the first failing profile's error Offline validation only job plan --output json Load/build errors remain Click text Redacted preview, no reservation job assess-operator --output json Versioned result for unreadable input or draft write errors Offline field accounting; unsupported fields still exit 0 (migration) app diagnose, doctor --output json report Click text error, exit 1 (including a missing application) Observed evidence, not a health certification connect check, connect server --output json Versioned result Tiny query succeeded on existing server; server requests accepted; server list is a label-based observation remote plan/submit JSON by default Versioned result Request admitted or accepted, not workload completion legacy kill/delete/log commands Text Text Signal/deletion request or log observation

CLI usage errors still follow Click's text/exit-code contract. Do not assume every JSON-capable command serializes every failure.

docs.title: API error responses
docs.text:
Every JSON error from the REST API, including framework routing (404, 405) and request-validation (422) errors, uses the envelope of the remote /jobs/v1 contract:

{"schema_version": 1, "error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "Not Found"}}

Branch on the HTTP status and error.code; message is for people. Routes that know the cause return a specific code, such as history_not_configured, application_not_found or policy_denied. When Kubernetes refuses an application identifier for stop or delete, or a continue_from token for listing, the API returns 400 invalid_request and changed nothing. A remote upload whose client disconnects before the document arrives is recorded as 400 client_disconnected. Other errors use a code derived from the status: invalid_request (400, 422), unauthorized, forbidden, not_found, method_not_allowed, request_timeout, conflict, not_configured (412), body_too_large, invalid_content_type, too_many_requests, upstream_unavailable (502), unavailable (503) and upstream_timeout (504). An unexpected failure returns 500 with internal_error and a reference that also appears in the server log; its details are never returned. Kubernetes errors from the Spark UI proxy still render an HTML error page, and the Airflow task tab, which runs inside Airflow's web server, follows Airflow's own error format.

SparkJob is loaded by a client; it is not a Kubernetes custom resource or a reconciled controller. The caller submits and decides whether to observe or retry. Kubernetes runs the created workload after the client exits. Airflow owns scheduling and task retry policy when its operator is used. SDK/CLI observation timeouts retain the application; Airflow startup timeouts deliberately delete it, and an elapsed max_runtime deliberately stops its driver. A kill signal is a termination request, not evidence of a completed streaming drain or checkpoint.

Disable caching for workflow submission steps. Reusing a cached receipt does not establish that this workflow executed the data job. Observe the same run before starting downstream consumers; retrying observation and resubmitting are different actions. Use one active submission per SparkOnK8S instance: the compatibility last_submitted_* attributes are mutable and shared-instance concurrent submission is not supported. Persist the returned immutable run handle per operation.

docs.title: Chart deployment boundaries
docs.text: These controls describe the current source chart. Published charts, API images and Python packages have independent release histories; inspect the selected chart and image before upgrading. The chart is an API/console deployment with an optional Spark History Server. It does not deploy a Spark scheduler, create a cloud workload identity, or configure applications submitted through the SDK.

docs.title: Select the image explicitly
docs.text:
The API image uses image.digest when set. Otherwise it uses image.tag; an explicitly empty tag opts into that chart's appVersion fallback. A version tag is clearer than latest, but only a verified digest fixes the image contents.

The source chart requires an explicit compatible image tag or digest while its appVersion is unreleased. Release packaging sets a qualified application version, which becomes the default image tag. Building or rendering the local chart does not build an API image.

The API image contains the API, its locked dependencies and Python, but no pip, setuptools or wheel. To add packages in an image built FROM it, switch to USER root, run python -m ensurepip to restore the base image's pip, install your packages, then switch back with USER 10001:10001. That pip is the base image's older version, so remove or upgrade it in your image. Alternatively, install the packages in a separate build stage and copy the result.

The optional History Server has a separate image lifecycle. Enabling sparkHistory.enabled requires an explicit sparkHistory.image.tag or sparkHistory.image.digest; there is no implicit API-version or latest fallback. For both images, a digest takes precedence over a simultaneously set tag. Use repository without an embedded tag or digest, and put the complete sha256: plus 64 hexadecimal characters in digest.

No History Server image version is qualified by these chart-rendering checks. Validate your selected History image, event-log storage and Spark runtime together before deployment. An explicitly selected latest tag remains accepted for intentional development use; it does not make the deployment reproducible.

docs.title: Verify a published API image
docs.text:
The release workflow signs each API image it publishes with Sigstore cosign keyless signing, by digest. The signed digest is the multi-architecture image whose amd64 and arm64 images passed the workflow's checks; both registries receive those bytes without a rebuild, so ghcr.io/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s and docker.io/husseinawala/spark-on-k8s have the same digest. API images released before signing was added, including 0.12.1 and earlier, have no signature, and cosign verify reports that none was found.

Resolve the release tag once, then verify and deploy the digest it printed, not the tag. Use cosign 3; cosign 2.6 needs --new-bundle-format:

RELEASE_VERSION=X.Y.Z  # replace with the selected API release
docker buildx imagetools inspect "ghcr.io/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s:$RELEASE_VERSION"
# Set API_IMAGE_DIGEST to the sha256:... value of the Digest line printed above.
: "${API_IMAGE_DIGEST:?Set the digest printed for the release tag}"
cosign verify "ghcr.io/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s@$API_IMAGE_DIGEST" \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/$RELEASE_VERSION" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

Verification succeeds only for a signature made by this repository's release.yml running for that tag; a fork, another workflow, a branch run or a different release tag fails it. Each signature is recorded in Sigstore's public transparency log. Verify the Docker Hub copy with the same command and docker.io/husseinawala/spark-on-k8s@$API_IMAGE_DIGEST. Then pin the verified digest with --set-string image.digest="$API_IMAGE_DIGEST", as in the example below. A per-platform digest is not signed separately; deploy the multi-architecture digest.

The same index carries BuildKit SBOM and provenance attestations for each platform. They are listed by digest in the signed index, so retrieving them through the verified digest also authenticates them:

docker buildx imagetools inspect "ghcr.io/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s@$API_IMAGE_DIGEST" \
  --format '{{ json .Provenance }}'
docker buildx imagetools inspect "ghcr.io/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s@$API_IMAGE_DIGEST" \
  --format '{{ json .SBOM }}'

They describe the image contents and build inputs; they do not certify that the dependencies are free of vulnerabilities.

To enforce signatures at admission, configure a Sigstore-capable policy engine to require, for images from these repositories, the issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com and a certificate subject matching ^https://github\.com/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+((a|b|rc)[0-9]+)?$. Drop the optional group to refuse pre-releases. The signatures are Sigstore bundles attached as OCI referrers, the format cosign 3 writes; confirm that your engine version verifies that format, and exempt images released before signing.

docs.title: Start with scoped, externally managed access
docs.text:
The source includes chart/examples/production-values.yaml. It uses explicit analytics,batch namespaces, the preprovisioned spark-observer service account, external RBAC, a ClusterIP service, and illustrative resource reservations. Its REQUIRED_SHA256_DIGEST placeholder deliberately fails validation. Set a digest you have verified for the selected API image repository:

# Set API_IMAGE_DIGEST to the verified sha256:... digest; no sample image is implied.
: "${API_IMAGE_DIGEST:?Set the verified API image digest}"
helm lint ./chart -f chart/examples/production-values.yaml \
  --set-string image.digest="$API_IMAGE_DIGEST"
helm template spark-console ./chart --namespace spark-system \
  -f chart/examples/production-values.yaml \
  --set-string image.digest="$API_IMAGE_DIGEST" > rendered-console.yaml

Provision the release namespace and named service account before installation. The administrator must grant that account the needed access in the selected application namespaces. Review the rendered resources and adjust the example's namespaces, resource requests and limits for your deployment. The example does not establish availability, throughput or cloud-identity compatibility.

The default readOnly: true remains unchanged. With chart-managed RBAC, the default empty namespaces creates a Role and RoleBinding in the release namespace, and an explicit namespace string creates them in each listed namespace. namespaces: "*" instead creates a ClusterRole with the same rules and binds it cluster-wide; the chart does not bind the built-in view or edit roles. The chart passes the same scope to the API as SPARK_ON_K8S_API_NAMESPACES, so the API refuses other namespaces even where Service DNS would reach them. Neither the namespace scope nor hiding UI buttons provides user or tenant authorization; use the remote-submission security boundary.

docs.title: Decide who owns the account and permissions
docs.text:
rbac.create controls API roles and bindings independently of serviceAccount.create. Its default, null, follows serviceAccount.create to preserve existing rendering. The History Server has its own service-account setting; API RBAC settings do not grant History Server storage permissions.

API configuration Account created by Helm Roles/bindings created by Helm serviceAccount.create: true, rbac.create: null Yes Yes; legacy default serviceAccount.create: false, rbac.create: null No No; legacy external-account behavior serviceAccount.create: false, explicit serviceAccount.name, rbac.create: true No Yes, bound to that account in the release namespace serviceAccount.create: true, rbac.create: false Yes No serviceAccount.create: false, rbac.create: false No No; fully external ownership

The chart requires an explicit account name when creating RBAC for an external account. readOnly only changes chart-managed permissions; it cannot reduce permissions already granted externally.

docs.title: Review the chart-managed permissions
docs.text:
Chart-managed Roles and the cluster-wide ClusterRole render the same rules, all on core API resources in the served namespaces:

readOnly Rules Used for true get and list on pods, get on pods/log, list on events Application lists and details, driver logs, diagnostics, readiness and run history false Adds create and delete on pods, get and create on pods/exec, and create on services Stopping and deleting drivers, and remote submission

These are the only verbs the API calls: it never watches pods, the Spark UI proxy reaches Services by DNS, and a driver's Service is deleted with the driver through its owner reference. Grant more through externally managed RBAC if other tools use the API's service account.

Neither mode grants Secrets, ConfigMaps or any other resource. Remote submission creates only a driver Pod and its headless Service, so readOnly: false covers it; the API rejects jobs that would create Secrets or ConfigMaps. Spark drivers create executors with the job's own service account, not the API's; see cluster prerequisites for a baseline for that account.

With namespaces: "*", readOnly: false lets the API create, delete and exec into pods in every namespace, including system namespaces. Rendering fails unless rbac.allowClusterWideWrite: true acknowledges that grant; listing the namespaces the API manages keeps write access scoped instead. Read-only cluster-wide access and externally managed RBAC need no acknowledgement.

When changing ownership on an installed release, inspect the Helm diff first. Setting a create flag to false removes previously managed resources from the release; Helm can delete them during upgrade. Arrange the replacement permissions and deliberate resource-ownership transfer before that upgrade. Do not assume that changing the flag alone preserves the existing account or grants.

docs.title: Keep the four workload identities separate
docs.text:
Role Identity and metadata inputs Image and image-pull inputs API/console Chart serviceAccount.*, podLabels, podAnnotations; its Kubernetes credentials observe/manage applications Chart image.*, imagePullSecrets Spark driver Submission namespace, service_account, driver_labels, driver_annotations and driver template Submission image, image_pull_policy; driver template for supported pull-secret customization Spark executors Application executor template and Spark configuration for the chosen runtime; executor_labels and executor_annotations Application image/configuration and executor template; API chart pull secrets are not inherited History Server Chart sparkHistory.serviceAccount.*, sparkHistory.podLabels, sparkHistory.podAnnotations; independent event-storage identity sparkHistory.image.*; chart imagePullSecrets is applied to its pod too

These roles may share an account when that is intentional; they do not need to. The resolved submission service_account overrides a service account written inside the driver template. API chart account annotations and labels do not become application defaults. See driver templates for the supported merge rules and inspect the generated driver plan.

Cloud IAM bindings, storage credentials and admission policies remain owned by the cluster administrator. A successful doctor check establishes only its reported caller checks and account existence; it does not prove that a driver, executor or History Server can access your object store. Cloud-specific recipes and arbitrary-user container support are not qualified by this chart validation suite.

docs.title: Run the API as a non-root user
docs.text:
The API image runs as the dedicated user and group 10001. The chart's default podSecurityContext and securityContext match that identity and meet Pod Security restricted: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, runAsGroup and fsGroup 10001, fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch, the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile, no privilege escalation and all capabilities dropped. Override individual keys in your values file, or set a key to null to remove it; an image built with another user needs matching IDs. The History Server keeps its own security settings.

The API must be able to read files mounted from volumes, such as a remote-submission token or policy, or a kubeconfig selected with SPARK_ON_K8S_CONFIG_FILE. The chart sets SPARK_ON_K8S_IN_CLUSTER=true unless env sets SPARK_ON_K8S_IN_CLUSTER or SPARK_ON_K8S_CONFIG_FILE, so a selected kubeconfig is used instead of the pod's service account. Its home directory is /home/spark-on-k8s; /root is not readable. Keep service.port at 1024 or above, because some container runtimes do not let a non-root process bind lower ports. Mount a remote-submission Secret as a directory rather than with subPath, so a token rotation reaches running pods.

A run-history claim written by an earlier root API process holds root-owned files. On volume types that support fsGroup, such as most block-storage CSI drivers and local volumes, the kubelet makes them group-writable at the first non-root mount. Volume types that ignore fsGroup, such as hostPath-backed provisioners, keep them read-only: the API then exits with attempt to write a readonly database. Before upgrading such a claim, change ownership from the current root pod:

kubectl exec --namespace <release-namespace> deploy/<release-fullname> -- \
  chown -R 10001:10001 /var/lib/spark-on-k8s

If the upgraded API already exited, helm rollback to the root release and run the command there before upgrading again. To keep running as root instead, restore the previous identity and capabilities; the capabilities let root write files that a failed non-root start may have created. Such a pod does not meet Pod Security restricted:

podSecurityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: false
  runAsUser: 0
  runAsGroup: 0
securityContext:
  capabilities: null

readOnlyRootFilesystem is not a default because the Kubernetes client writes temporary files in some configurations, such as kubeconfig credentials embedded as data. To enable it, also mount a writable /tmp:

securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
volumeMounts:
  - name: tmp
    mountPath: /tmp

docs.title: Understand the scaling controls
docs.text:
Control What it scales Owner Chart replicaCount or autoscaling.* API/console replicas API deployment owner Application ExecutorInstances / Spark dynamic allocation Executors within one Spark application Application owner Kubernetes cluster/node-pool autoscaler Available worker nodes Cluster/cloud administrator

Increasing autoscaling.maxReplicas does not increase an application's executor ceiling or create nodes. The optional History Server has its own sparkHistory.replicaCount and autoscaling settings. CPU/memory HPA targets need appropriate container requests and the cluster's metrics support; setting a target to null or 0 disables that metric, and an enabled HPA requires at least one positive target.

The metadata recorder is separate from the Spark History Server. Enabling runHistory requires exactly one API replica, no API autoscaling, an existing writable persistent claim, and one to twenty explicit namespace entries. Unless namespaces is "*", every runHistory.namespaces entry must also be in the API scope: the release namespace by default, or the listed namespaces. Otherwise the API refuses to start, and with chart-managed RBAC rendering fails. The chart uses a Recreate rollout. It neither provisions the claim nor validates its filesystem locking behavior; use supported block/local storage, rehearse backups and allow for rollout downtime.

docs.title: Validate before installation
docs.text:
values.schema.json checks chart-owned types, image references, service ports, namespace forms, HPA bounds and recorder settings. Template guards cover cross-field comparisons, such as the cluster-wide write acknowledgement, and reserved volume names. Run both helm lint and helm template: lint can suppress template-level fail messages, while rendering rejects those cross-field conflicts. namespaces remains a comma-separated string; runHistory.namespaces is a YAML list. Kubernetes passthrough objects, such as affinity, resources and security contexts, remain open so normal cluster-specific fields are accepted.

Rendering checks do not validate cloud permissions, image availability, storage access or API server admission. Raw env overrides still take precedence over chart-generated environment settings and remain the operator's responsibility. An ingress.tls entry terminates TLS before the API, so browser log streams are rejected until env sets SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WEBSOCKET_ALLOWED_ORIGINS to the public https:// origins; see browser origins. To serve the API below an ingress path such as /platform/spark, have the ingress controller remove that prefix before forwarding and set SPARK_ON_K8S_API_ROOT_PATH to the same path in env; see mounted paths. To require single sign-on, keep the chart Ingress disabled and publish the console through the oauth2-proxy gateway recipe instead. Use the development guide for the Helm regression suite and release guidance for the artifact publication boundary.

docs.title: Add operational objects
docs.text: The settings in this section are disabled by default, apart from the History Server probes, which apply only when sparkHistory.enabled is set. A release upgraded with --reuse-values from a chart without these settings renders as before. Some invalid combinations fail only during rendering, so run helm template as well as helm lint.

docs.title: Restrict API traffic
docs.text:
networkPolicy.enabled adds a NetworkPolicy for the API pods. It admits traffic to the API port only from networkPolicy.ingress.from and from pods with this release's API labels: the API pods and the chart's helm test pod. With an empty list nothing else can connect, including an ingress controller, a gateway, Prometheus and clients of a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service. List every peer that needs the API:

networkPolicy:
  enabled: true
  ingress:
    from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
        podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus

The policy needs a network plugin that enforces NetworkPolicy; other plugins accept the object and enforce nothing. NetworkPolicy does not block traffic from a pod's own node, so kubelet probes keep working. Traffic through a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service can arrive with a node address rather than the client's, depending on externalTrafficPolicy and the plugin. A NetworkPolicy limits which peers can connect; it does not authenticate callers or replace remote mode or an authenticating gateway.

networkPolicy.egress.enabled also restricts the API's outbound connections to:

  • DNS on port 53 to networkPolicy.egress.dns.to: kube-dns pods in kube-system by default. An empty list allows port 53 to any destination, for example a node-local DNS cache;
  • the Kubernetes API server peers in networkPolicy.egress.kubernetesApi.to, on kubernetesApi.ports (443 and 6443 by default);
  • port 4040 on pods labeled spark-role=driver in the namespaces selected by namespaces, for the Spark UI proxy;
  • this release's API pods, so its helm test pod can connect, and the History Server pods on port 18080 when sparkHistory.enabled is set;
  • networkPolicy.egress.extraRules, for example a cluster selected by SPARK_ON_K8S_CONFIG_FILE.

The chart cannot discover API server addresses. Most plugins evaluate egress after a Service address is translated to its endpoints, so list the endpoint addresses of the default/kubernetes Service:

kubectl get endpointslices --namespace default \
  --selector kubernetes.io/service-name=kubernetes \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*].endpoints[*]}{.addresses[0]}{"\n"}{end}'

networkPolicy:
  egress:
    enabled: true
    kubernetesApi:
      to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 172.18.0.2/32

With an empty kubernetesApi.to, the chart's policy grants no API server access: the API stays unready unless another policy allows it, and the install notes warn about it. Plugins differ: some match the Service address before translation, and some do not match node or control-plane addresses with ipBlock at all and need their own policy resources for the API server. After enabling egress, check readiness, the Spark UI proxy and log streams. The driver namespace selector follows namespaces; an env override of SPARK_ON_K8S_API_NAMESPACES does not change it.

sparkHistory.networkPolicy.enabled adds an ingress-only NetworkPolicy for the History Server: the API pods and sparkHistory.networkPolicy.ingress.from can reach port 18080. History Server egress, such as to event-log storage, stays unrestricted.

docs.title: Keep replicas available during node drains
docs.text:
podDisruptionBudget.enabled adds a PodDisruptionBudget for the API pods, and sparkHistory.podDisruptionBudget.enabled one for the History Server pods. Set minAvailable or maxUnavailable to a pod count or a percentage such as "50%". Setting both is rejected; setting neither uses maxUnavailable: 1.

Rendering fails when a budget permits no voluntary disruption at the smallest replica count, which is replicaCount, or autoscaling.minReplicas with autoscaling enabled. Such a budget blocks kubectl drain, node pool upgrades and cluster autoscaler scale-down indefinitely. For example, minAvailable: 1 with one replica is rejected; Kubernetes rounds percentages up, so minAvailable: "60%" with two replicas is rejected too. Run at least two API replicas to keep the API available while a node drains. A single-replica API, as run history requires, can only use a budget that allows its pod to be evicted, so a budget adds no protection there.

docs.title: Scrape metrics with the Prometheus Operator
docs.text:
metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled adds a monitoring.coreos.com/v1 ServiceMonitor for the API's /metrics and requires metrics.enabled. Rendering fails if the cluster does not serve the ServiceMonitor API, rather than silently omitting the object and leaving monitoring unconfigured. helm template and client-side dry runs do not query a cluster, so pass the API explicitly:

helm template spark-console ./chart --namespace spark-system \
  --set metrics.enabled=true --set metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true \
  --set-string image.tag="$API_IMAGE_TAG" \
  --api-versions monitoring.coreos.com/v1/ServiceMonitor

Set metrics.serviceMonitor.labels to match your Prometheus serviceMonitorSelector, and interval or scrapeTimeout to override the Prometheus defaults. The API and History Server Services share the chart's selector labels, so the ServiceMonitor keeps only the API Service's targets by name. With networkPolicy.enabled, also list Prometheus in networkPolicy.ingress.from. Run-history metric values come from the run-history database, so every API worker reports the same values. The operation counters are kept by each worker instead, and each scrape reaches one worker: set workers: 1 before alerting on them.

With remote.enabled, /metrics requires the operator bearer token, and the ServiceMonitor authenticates with the remote.tokenKey entry of remote.existingSecret. The Prometheus Operator then copies that token into the configuration of every Prometheus instance that selects the ServiceMonitor. The token grants full operator access to the API, including submissions, logs, kill and delete: restrict access to that Prometheus configuration accordingly, or do not enable the ServiceMonitor in remote mode.

Prometheus sends that Secret entry as the bearer token byte for byte, while the API trims whitespace and accepts one token per line. The entry must therefore hold exactly one token with no trailing newline, or every scrape fails. During a token rotation the entry holds two tokens, so scrapes fail from step 1 until step 3 reaches the pods: expect a gap in these metrics and pause alerts on failed scrapes for that time.

docs.title: Set the API worker count
docs.text:
workers sets SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WORKERS, the number of API processes in each pod, from 1 to 64. The default null keeps the image default, which is 4 in the published image. An env entry with the same name takes precedence. Each worker is a separate process with its own memory, Kubernetes client and SPARK_ON_K8S_API_LIMIT_CONCURRENCY connection limit, so raise resources with the worker count. Run history keeps its single replica but supports several workers in that pod: a database lease elects one collector. In remote mode, each worker reads the token and policy files when it starts.

With more than one worker, spark-on-k8s api start exits with code 0 when a worker fails to start, for example on an unusable run-history volume or an invalid setting: uvicorn's process supervisor logs Child process [...] failed to start and stops without reporting the failure as an exit code. The chart's readiness probe on /ready keeps such a pod out of service, and Kubernetes restarts the container. Read that log line, or run with workers: 1 to get exit code 3, when diagnosing a pod that never becomes ready.

docs.title: Probe the History Server
docs.text:
With sparkHistory.enabled, the History Server container has readiness and liveness probes on its UI port, 18080, at /api/v1/version. Readiness keeps a starting server out of its Service. Liveness restarts a server that has stopped answering for about two minutes, after a one-minute initial delay. Adding the probes changes the pod template, so upgrading a release with the History Server enabled restarts its pods once.

Override individual probe fields under sparkHistory.readinessProbe and sparkHistory.livenessProbe, or set a probe to null to remove it. Helm merges your probe with the default, so set httpGet: null beside another handler such as tcpSocket. An authentication filter on the History Server UI must allow the probe path, or the probe must use tcpSocket.

docs.title: Enable remote submission
docs.text:
remote.enabled configures remote submission. The chart sets SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_ENABLED, SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_TOKEN_FILE and SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_POLICY_FILE, and mounts only the remote.tokenKey and remote.policyKey entries of remote.existingSecret read-only under remote.mountPath (/etc/spark-on-k8s/remote by default). The chart never creates this Secret and has no value for an inline token, so the token stays out of Helm values and release history. Create the Secret in the release namespace with your secret tooling, for example from a random token file and the policy:

kubectl create secret generic spark-api-remote --namespace spark-system \
  --from-file=token=./submission-token --from-file=policy.json=./submission-policy.json

remote:
  enabled: true
  existingSecret: spark-api-remote
namespaces: analytics
readOnly: false

Every route except /health and /ready then requires the bearer token, including the console; kubelet probes and the chart's helm test use those two public routes. Submissions create driver pods and Services, so with chart-managed RBAC set readOnly: false. Keep the policy's namespaces within namespaces: the API refuses to start with a policy namespace outside its scope. A missing Secret key also prevents the pod from starting. The Secret is mounted as a directory, so a token rotation or policy change reaches running pods after the kubelet's sync period; each worker then applies valid files without a restart. env entries for the same variables take precedence, and remote-submission is a reserved volume name. The token is one shared operator credential, not tenant isolation.

docs.title: Preparing the next chart release
docs.text:
The source chart marks appVersion as unreleased and requires an explicit compatible image.tag or image.digest. The release publisher sets the package's qualified application version; an empty image tag then selects that version. API 0.12.1 does not implement /ready and is not compatible with these probes. Do not publish this chart against that older API image. The helm-release workflow refuses an app_version below 0.13.0 or without a published ghcr.io/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s image, and a chart_version that the chart repository already lists. Run it only after the package release has published the API image, selecting that release tag in the workflow's ref selector so the chart source matches the qualified application.

When upgrading a release installed from published chart 0.3.0, pass your values file again, or use --reset-then-reuse-values (Helm 3.14 and later), instead of --reuse-values. --reuse-values replaces this chart's defaults with the old release's values, including its latest image tags, and omits new settings such as rbac, runHistory and metrics. The chart schema rejects such an upgrade with a missing properties error before rendering.

Shared RBAC resource names now include the release namespace identity. Existing installations can set rbac.legacyNames: true to retain their old names during an upgrade. New installations should use the default false, allowing identical release names in separate namespaces. To migrate existing installations, render and review both RBAC sets, ensure the new bindings exist before removing old bindings, and verify access under the service account. Switching the value in a normal Helm upgrade replaces the old resources; schedule that transition if a brief permissions interruption is unacceptable. Never reuse legacy names for two releases managing the same shared scope.

Releases with namespaces: "*" were bound to the built-in view or edit ClusterRole by a ClusterRoleBinding named after the release with a -view or -edit suffix. The chart now creates its own ClusterRole and a ClusterRoleBinding with the role's name and no suffix, whether or not rbac.legacyNames is set. Because a binding's roleRef cannot change, the binding takes a new name instead of being updated in place: the same helm upgrade creates the new role and binding and removes the old binding, so no manual deletion is needed. As with the name change above, schedule it if a brief permissions interruption is unacceptable. The API's account loses everything else those roles granted, such as reading ConfigMaps and, with edit, reading and writing Secrets in every namespace. If another workload shares that account and relies on such access, grant it separately before upgrading. A "*" release with readOnly: false must also set rbac.allowClusterWideWrite: true; without it, the upgrade fails before changing anything.

The default namespaces value changed from "*" to empty, which selects only the release namespace. A release that relied on the old default loses its cluster-wide binding on upgrade, and the API then refuses other namespaces. Set namespaces: "*" or list the namespaces before upgrading. With "*", the console opens the API's own namespace unless SPARK_ON_K8S_API_DEFAULT_NAMESPACE is set in env. If env sets SPARK_ON_K8S_API_DEFAULT_NAMESPACE to a namespace outside the new scope, the API refuses to start and helm upgrade --wait times out: include that namespace in namespaces, or change or remove the variable, in the same upgrade.

History configuration updates now roll its Deployment automatically. History affinity and tolerations are passed to the Pod. The rare long-name suffix collision is disambiguated; existing installations using those colliding names need a reviewed recreation because Deployment selectors are immutable.

docs.title: Build an ML image for Spark Connect
docs.text: A notebook connected to a Spark Connect server sends plans, not Python processes. Python UDFs, pandas UDFs and other Python code that Spark runs for a query execute in the server's driver and executor containers, using the packages installed in the server image. Packages in your notebook kernel are not copied there. This recipe extends the Apache Spark image with pinned Python libraries, then places the server on a private registry and an ML node pool with the typed server settings.

docs.title: Write a pinned requirements file
docs.text:
Pin every package, including transitive dependencies, so that a rebuild cannot pick up different code. Save this list as requirements-ml.txt. It has binary wheels for Python 3.10–3.13 on Linux x86_64 and arm64, and satisfies the pandas, PyArrow and NumPy minimums of PySpark 4.3 (2.2.0, 18.0.0 and 1.23.2). The image installs it with --no-deps, so an unlisted dependency would only appear later as an import error on the server. Change versions deliberately.

numpy==2.2.6
pandas==2.3.3
python-dateutil==2.9.0.post0
pytz==2025.2
six==1.17.0
tzdata==2025.2
pyarrow==21.0.0
scikit-learn==1.7.2
scipy==1.15.3
joblib==1.5.2
threadpoolctl==3.6.0

To check a changed list before building, resolve it for the image's Python version and platform without installing anything. The output must list exactly your pins, with nothing added:

uv pip compile requirements-ml.txt --python-version 3.12 \
  --python-platform x86_64-manylinux_2_28 --only-binary :all: --no-annotate

docs.title: Extend the Spark image
docs.text:
Use the Spark release and Python variant that your server runs, preferably by digest. The official images run as the spark user and contain Python 3 and pip in their -python3- variants. Save this Dockerfile beside the requirements file:

ARG SPARK_IMAGE=apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu
FROM ${SPARK_IMAGE}

USER root
COPY requirements-ml.txt /opt/spark-ml/requirements-ml.txt
# Install into a separate directory: newer Ubuntu releases protect the system Python
# (PEP 668). --no-deps and --only-binary install exactly the pinned wheels.
RUN python3 -m pip install --no-cache-dir --no-deps --only-binary=:all: \
      --target /opt/spark-ml/python --requirement /opt/spark-ml/requirements-ml.txt
# Spark adds the container's PYTHONPATH to its Python workers on the driver and executors.
ENV PYTHONPATH="/opt/spark-ml/python${PYTHONPATH:+:${PYTHONPATH}}"
USER spark

Build, check the libraries and the Connect server JAR, then push to your registry:

docker build --tag registry.example.com/data/spark-connect-ml:4.3.0 .
docker run --rm --entrypoint python3 registry.example.com/data/spark-connect-ml:4.3.0 \
  -c 'import sys, sklearn, pandas, pyarrow; print(sys.version, sklearn.__version__, pandas.__version__, pyarrow.__version__)'
docker run --rm --entrypoint ls registry.example.com/data/spark-connect-ml:4.3.0 \
  /opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar
docker push registry.example.com/data/spark-connect-ml:4.3.0

The same image runs the driver and executors, so every executor has the same libraries. GPU libraries such as CUDA builds of deep-learning frameworks also need CUDA user-space libraries compatible with your nodes' drivers; follow their vendors' instructions and pin them the same way.

docs.title: Match the client to the server
docs.text:
Two version pairs matter:

  • Spark. Install the pyspark-client matching the server's Spark major.minor version in your notebook environment. A mismatched client can pass readiness and fail later; readiness checks report a version_skew warning, as described in client and server versions. The Jupyter guide shows how to pin the client in an isolated kernel.
  • Python. A Python UDF is serialized by the notebook's Python and run by the image's Python. PySpark refuses to run it when their minor versions differ (PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH). Compare the sys.version printed above with your kernel's Python, and use the same minor version, or build the image from a base with your kernel's Python. DataFrame and SQL operations without Python UDFs do not depend on the image's Python version.

docs.title: Run on a private registry and a GPU node pool
docs.text:
An administrator creates the image pull Secret and installs the GPU device plugin, such as NVIDIA's, which advertises a resource like nvidia.com/gpu on GPU nodes. Clusters commonly label GPU nodes and taint them so that only pods tolerating the taint run there; use your cluster's actual label and taint.

spark-on-k8s connect server create \
  --image registry.example.com/data/spark-connect-ml:4.3.0 \
  --server-jar local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar \
  --namespace spark --service-account spark --name ml-notebook \
  --image-pull-secret private-registry \
  --executor-node-selector example.com/pool=gpu \
  --executor-toleration nvidia.com/gpu:NoSchedule \
  --receipt-file ml-server.json --output json

This places executors on the pool; it does not request GPUs. Spark requests them through its resource scheduling properties, which become Kubernetes container limits for executors when the vendor is set. To use one GPU per executor and per task, add these options to the command:

  --conf spark.executor.resource.gpu.amount=1 \
  --conf spark.executor.resource.gpu.vendor=nvidia.com \
  --conf spark.executor.resource.gpu.discoveryScript=/opt/spark-ml/getGpusResources.sh \
  --conf spark.task.resource.gpu.amount=1

Kubernetes does not tell Spark which devices it assigned, so the image must contain an executable discovery script, for example added with COPY --chmod=0755 getGpusResources.sh /opt/spark-ml/ before USER spark. The Spark distribution includes an example script at examples/src/main/scripts/getGpusResources.sh. See Spark's resource scheduling configuration and Kubernetes resource allocation for the requirements and for fractional task amounts. The server's driver Pod is created by this helper with CPU and memory from its resource settings only; do not set spark.driver.resource.*, which would not add device limits to that Pod.

Credentials for object storage or model registries belong in Kubernetes Secrets, referenced with --driver-env-from-secret and --executor-env-from-secret, as in Private images, credentials and node placement. For a runnable notebook that uses a pull Secret, a Secret-backed variable and a node selector, see the private server quickstart.

docs.title: Experimental managed dbt
docs.text:
Run dbt Core commands against temporary Spark compute on an existing Kubernetes cluster. The wrapper creates one server when dbt first opens a connection, shares it across dbt worker threads and across the commands of one invocation, and deletes its driver, executors and private Services when the invocation ends. Choose Thrift or Spark Connect in the profile; you do not create the server yourself.

Experimental, separately installed integration

This feature lives in integrations/dbt and is not part of a normal spark-on-k8s installation. Its profile and Python interfaces may change. The initial compatibility target is dbt Core 1.12.6, dbt-spark 1.11.0, Spark/client 4.3.0, PyHive 0.7.0, and Thrift 0.25.0. It is a Python dbt Core adapter, not a dbt Fusion, dbt Cloud or dbt v2 integration. SQL models, seeds and data tests are supported; Python models are explicitly rejected. dbt clone is explicitly rejected in this experiment.

docs.title: Prepare the platform
docs.text:
The platform owner supplies:

  • An existing namespace and driver service account with the permissions described in server setup. This integration does not create or delete the Kubernetes cluster, namespace or RBAC.
  • A compatible Spark image with the bundled Connect or HiveThriftServer2 JAR.
  • A shared warehouse reachable by the driver and executors and an external Hive metastore reachable by each new driver. The profile requires both. An embedded driver-local metastore would disappear when the driver is deleted. Driver-local warehouse paths, including file://, are rejected because this experiment does not mount persistent driver volumes. Supply a remote filesystem URI and its Spark connector; the integration fixture tests HDFS.
  • A trusted network for the private, plaintext server and catalog endpoints. The experiment uses Thrift auth: NONE; it is not a multi-tenant gateway.

For a local client, install kubectl and provide an explicit kubeconfig path and context. The wrapper opens a loopback-only tunnel to its driver, using an OS-assigned local port. If kubectl exits mid-run, statements on that tunnel fail and are not replayed; the next dbt connection gets a new tunnel after the driver UID and application identity are verified again. For a client already inside Kubernetes, set in_cluster: true and omit both kubeconfig fields; it connects to the private Service directly. The client's identity needs permission to create/read/delete its driver and Services, read the namespace/service account and observe executor pods, Services and ConfigMaps (including list permission for garbage-collection checks); local access also needs pod port-forward permission. spark-on-k8s-dbt check verifies these permissions without creating anything.

docs.title: Install from the repository
docs.text:
Until the experimental distribution is separately published, build both wheels from the same checkout. These commands use an isolated Python 3.12 environment:

# From the spark-on-k8s repository root:
uv build --wheel --out-dir dist/dbt-experiment
uv build --project integrations/dbt --wheel --out-dir dist/dbt-experiment
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv-dbt
uv pip install --python .venv-dbt/bin/python dist/dbt-experiment/*.whl
uv pip check --python .venv-dbt/bin/python

For reproducible development/testing, use the separate lockfile instead:

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT="$PWD/.venv-dbt" uv sync \
  --project integrations/dbt --locked --python 3.12 --group test

The integration declares PyHive and patched Thrift directly instead of selecting dbt-spark[pyhive], whose current extra caps Thrift below the patched releases. Do not add that extra to this environment: let the normal dependency resolver keep the transport compatible. Thrift's protocol size/recursion protections remain enabled; unusually large individual result fields can be rejected by those limits.

The package accepts Python 3.11–3.13. Kubernetes execution is tested with Python 3.12. The independent lockfile prevents dbt's dependencies from changing the normal SDK, API or Airflow environments.

docs.title: Configure a managed profile
docs.text:
Use this profile in your dbt project's profiles.yml, replacing the namespace, service account, kubeconfig, metastore and warehouse with your platform values:

analytics:
  target: connect
  outputs:
    connect:
      type: spark_on_k8s
      method: connect
      schema: analytics
      threads: 2
      compute:
        kube_config_file: /absolute/path/to/kubeconfig
        kube_context: my-context
        namespace: spark
        service_account: spark
        image: apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu
        server_jar: local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar
        startup_timeout: 180
        cleanup_timeout: 120
        driver_resources: {cpu: 1, memory: 1024, memory_overhead: 512}
        executor_resources: {cpu: 1, memory: 1024, memory_overhead: 512}
        executor_instances: {initial: 2}
        spark_conf:
          spark.sql.catalogImplementation: hive
          spark.sql.warehouse.dir: hdfs://namenode.data.svc:8020/warehouse
          spark.hadoop.hive.metastore.uris: thrift://metastore.data.svc:9083
          spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: '4'

Your dbt_project.yml must select profile: analytics. To use Thrift, change target and the output name to thrift, set method: thrift, and replace server_jar with:

server_jar: local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-hive-thriftserver_2.13-4.3.0.jar

The adapter selects the host and port. Do not supply host, port, SPARK_REMOTE or the upstream method: session workaround. Connect uses a separate explicit remote session for each dbt connection. Thrift uses PyHive's HiveServer2 protocol, not a JDBC client.

compute accepts app_name (default dbt-connect or dbt-thrift; set one per project or pipeline so its servers are recognizable), the explicit image, namespace, service account, resource, executor-allocation, package, node-selector and max_runtime fields of ConnectServerConfig, plus the cluster-selection fields above, startup_timeout, cleanup_timeout and poll_interval (positive seconds, at most 3600). max_runtime is unset by default; see receipts, failure and recovery. With method: connect, it also accepts the image pull Secret, Secret-backed environment and toleration fields and executor_node_selector, for example image_pull_secrets: [private-registry] or executor_env_from_secrets: {AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: "s3-credentials:access-key"}. method: thrift supports only driver_node_selector of these and rejects the others before contacting the cluster. Thrift fixes its managed port to 10000. Managed identity, ports and routing cannot be overridden through spark_conf. Put static Hive/catalog configuration in compute.spark_conf; server_side_parameters accepts runtime spark.sql.* settings; catalog, warehouse, Hive metastore and extension settings are excluded.

docs.title: Check a profile before running
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s-dbt check validates the selected output and its cluster access without creating a Spark server or any other Kubernetes resource, so configuration errors appear in seconds instead of after compute has been requested. It accepts dbt's profile-selection options with dbt's defaults and environment variables: --project-dir (DBT_PROJECT_DIR), --profiles-dir (DBT_PROFILES_DIR), --profile (DBT_PROFILE), --target/-t (DBT_TARGET) and --vars. With --profile, a dbt project is not required.

/path/to/spark-on-k8s/.venv-dbt/bin/spark-on-k8s-dbt check \
  --project-dir /path/to/analytics --profiles-dir /path/to/analytics --target connect

Each check reports pass, fail or skip; a failure includes a next step:

Check Verifies profile dbt renders and selects the output (including env_var() and --vars) and the adapter accepts its credentials, through the same code dbt uses. compute The adapter's compute validation, including the kubeconfig path and the Thrift server's managed settings. client_libraries The transport client imports: the Spark Connect client, or PyHive with its Thrift SASL and HiveServer2 modules. kubectl kubectl is on PATH for a local client. Skipped with in_cluster: true. kubernetes_config The selected kubeconfig and context, or the in-cluster configuration, loads. namespace The namespace exists, is not terminating, and the invoking identity can read it. service_account The driver service account exists. Its own permissions are not verified. permission.<verb>.<resource> A SelfSubjectAccessReview for each request the wrapper makes as the invoking identity.

The permission checks cover get on the namespace and driver service account; create, get, list and delete on Pods and Services; list on ConfigMaps for cleanup observation; and, for a local client, create on pods/portforward. The wrapper itself creates no Secrets or ConfigMaps; executor resources are created by the driver's service account. The API server evaluates access reviews without storing them. A review that cannot be performed fails rather than being assumed allowed. A missing namespace, rejected credentials or an unreachable API server skip the dependent checks. Kubernetes requests share a total --timeout (default 30 seconds).

--output json prints one versioned document on stdout; dbt's own warnings and other messages go to stderr. Every check ID appears once, in a fixed order:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "operation": "dbt_check",
  "status": "fail",
  "profile": "analytics",
  "target": "connect",
  "method": "connect",
  "namespace": "spark",
  "checks": [
    {"id": "profile", "status": "pass", "message": "...", "remediation": null},
    {"id": "permission.delete.pods", "status": "fail", "message": "Denied: delete pods in namespace spark.",
     "remediation": "Grant the invoking identity delete on pods in namespace spark."}
  ],
  "error": null
}

status is fail when any check fails. error is null unless the check was interrupted (interrupted) or stopped unexpectedly (operation_error). The command exits 0 when no check failed, 1 when any check failed, 2 for invalid options and 130 when interrupted.

A passing check is not a successful run

The check does not pull the image, schedule a driver, start Spark or contact the warehouse and metastore. Image pull failures, quotas, admission policies, node capacity, the driver service account's permissions, network policy and Spark configuration errors still surface only when spark-on-k8s-dbt run starts compute.

docs.title: Run dbt with automatic compute cleanup
docs.text:
Use the installed executable's absolute path if your current directory is a separate dbt project:

/path/to/spark-on-k8s/.venv-dbt/bin/spark-on-k8s-dbt run -- \
  build --project-dir /path/to/analytics --profiles-dir /path/to/analytics

Each wrapper invocation creates its own server. For example, seed, build, run-operation, test and docs generate can each use the same wrapper; to pay the server startup once for several of them, see Run several commands on one server:

/path/to/spark-on-k8s/.venv-dbt/bin/spark-on-k8s-dbt run -- \
  docs generate --project-dir /path/to/analytics --profiles-dir /path/to/analytics

The server survives dbt's intermediate connection cleanup, including the compilation phase of docs generate. It is removed only when the entire command finishes. Tables remain in the external warehouse/catalog for the next invocation. Commands that never open a database connection, such as parse and ls, do not provision compute. compile opens one to fill its relation cache unless you pass --no-populate-cache. Using plain dbt with this managed adapter reports that the wrapper is required; there is no unbounded background server hidden behind a connection-close hook.

While the server starts, and while it is deleted at the end, the wrapper writes short progress lines with the elapsed time to stderr:

Managed Spark +0s: requesting a Spark Connect server in namespace spark (startup timeout 180s)
Managed Spark +1s: driver pod dbt-connect-0f3c...-driver created
Managed Spark +1s: waiting for the driver pod to be scheduled (Unschedulable: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu.)
Managed Spark +12s: driver pod scheduled on worker-2; container driver is ContainerCreating
Managed Spark +40s: driver container running
Managed Spark +40s: opening a kubectl port-forward tunnel to the driver
Managed Spark +41s: waiting for the Spark Connect endpoint to answer a query
Managed Spark +55s: Spark Connect server ready (application dbt-connect-0f3c...)

A new phase prints immediately; an unchanged phase repeats at most every 30 seconds. Image pull errors point at compute.image, so you can interrupt instead of waiting for startup_timeout. The lines never go to stdout, so dbt's stdout, including --log-format json events, is unchanged; they are also not written to dbt's log file. They follow dbt's resolved console settings: --quiet (DBT_QUIET) or --log-level warn, error or none (DBT_LOG_LEVEL, or the project's flags) suppresses them. The receipt path is always printed.

Statements are not automatically replayed (query_retries must be 0). Spark SQL is not transactional: failure and cancellation can leave successfully written tables or rows. Review dbt's normal incremental/idempotency behavior before retrying. Connect supports cancellation but does not accept query_timeout in this initial version; Thrift retains dbt-spark's query timeout setting. Thrift serializes requests on each connection and limits acquisition of the request lock and individual blocking socket operations to 15 seconds. These transport limits do not cap the full SQL execution time: queries run asynchronously and the adapter polls for completion. A failed transport is closed rather than reused, and statements are not replayed. Connect buffers SQL results for dbt metadata/seed/materialization operations; it is not a streaming query-results interface.

docs.title: Run several commands on one server
docs.text:
Every invocation pays one server startup: scheduling the driver, pulling its image and starting Spark often take minutes. A job that runs seed, run and test, or build and then docs generate, pays it once when the commands share one invocation. Separate them with further --:

export DBT_PROJECT_DIR=/path/to/analytics DBT_PROFILES_DIR=/path/to/analytics
/path/to/spark-on-k8s/.venv-dbt/bin/spark-on-k8s-dbt run -- \
  deps -- seed --full-refresh -- build -- docs generate

Each group after a -- is passed to dbt exactly as written, as dbt <group> would receive it; the wrapper does not re-split or re-quote it. dbt reads DBT_PROJECT_DIR, DBT_PROFILES_DIR and DBT_TARGET, so shared options need not be repeated per command. Put wrapper options (--receipt-dir, --keep-going, --deadline) before the first dbt argument: everything after it belongs to dbt, and a standalone -- always starts the next command rather than being passed to dbt.

The commands run one after another in the wrapper's process:

Topic Behavior Server Created by the first command that opens a connection (deps does not), reused by every later command and deleted once, when the sequence ends, with the cleanup guarantees of a single command. Receipt One receipt covers the server for the whole sequence. Its dbt_exit_code is the sequence's exit code. Failure The sequence stops after the first command that fails. With --keep-going, the remaining commands still start. Exit code 130/143 when interrupted, even after an earlier failure. Otherwise the first failed command's code (1 or 2), also with --keep-going; then 5 when --deadline left a command unstarted; 0 when every command succeeded. A cleanup failure turns 0 into 2. Between commands The wrapper confirms that the same driver (by UID) is still running, and reopens an exited kubectl tunnel to it, before the next command starts. A failed startup, or a driver that stopped, is being deleted or was replaced, ends the sequence with exit 2 unless a command already failed. A sequence never creates a second server. Interruption Ctrl-C or SIGTERM during a command stops it as for a single command, and no later command starts. Between commands, nothing further starts. Compute is deleted in both cases. --deadline SECONDS No command starts once this many seconds have passed since the wrapper started. A running command is not interrupted or shortened: the deadline is not a cancellation. Owned compute is still deleted when the sequence ends. dbt semantics Each command is a separate dbt invocation: dbt parses the project again and applies its own --fail-fast, hooks, artifacts and result. Each command opens its own SQL sessions, so session settings and temporary views do not carry over.

Every command must select the same managed output. A command whose rendered profile selects a different method or compute mapping fails its first connection rather than creating another server; schema, threads and --vars that do not change compute may differ.

With several commands, the wrapper also reports each command's result and a final summary on stderr:

Managed dbt 1/4 (dbt deps) succeeded in 4s
Managed Spark +0s: requesting a Spark Connect server in namespace spark (startup timeout 180s)
...
Managed dbt 2/4 (dbt seed) succeeded in 71s
Managed dbt 3/4 (dbt build) failed with exit 1 after 240s
Managed Spark +0s: deleting managed Spark compute and observing its removal
Managed Spark +6s: managed Spark compute deleted
Managed dbt run finished with exit 1: 2 succeeded, 1 failed, 1 not run (stopped after a failed command; --keep-going runs the rest)

Commands are named by their leading words only; option values such as --vars are never echoed. Success lines follow dbt's console settings, as startup progress does. A failed or interrupted command, and the summary of a sequence that failed or left a command unstarted, are always printed. A single command prints none of these lines.

The server belongs to this one process for the duration of the sequence. It is not a shared or warm pool: other processes, including concurrent CI jobs, cannot attach to it.

docs.title: Receipts, failure and recovery
docs.text:
The wrapper prints the recovery receipt path to stderr. By default each invocation gets a unique directory under .spark-on-k8s/dbt/ in the working directory. Set --receipt-dir /new/private/directory before -- to choose it explicitly; the directory must not already exist. Add .spark-on-k8s/ to the project's .gitignore; every invocation, including one that starts no server, creates a directory there. Receipts have private file permissions and retain resource UIDs and cluster selection, not the original Spark configuration or its catalog credentials. Protect the dbt profile and normal dbt logs separately.

With --fail-fast, dbt cancels running statements and then still runs on-run-end hooks on the same compute. After Ctrl-C/SIGTERM the adapter opens no new connection. Normal success, dbt failures and a graceful Ctrl-C/SIGTERM all attempt cleanup. Exit codes are 0 for success, 1 for a dbt execution failure, 2 for invocation or cleanup errors, 5 when a sequence's --deadline left a command unstarted, and 130/143 for interruption. A cleanup failure preserves an already failing dbt exit code and records the separate cleanup failure. A successful command becomes nonzero if cleanup fails. Cleanup verifies the recorded namespace, driver and Service identities and observes disappearance before reporting success. It never deletes the warehouse or metastore.

A hard kill, machine loss, unavailable Kubernetes API, or ambiguous creation can leave compute running. If creation fails after the driver's UID is confirmed, the wrapper requests deletion of that driver by UID (its Services are owned by it) and records the outcome as creation_cleanup. The receipt stays incomplete because disappearance was not observed; confirm the driver is gone. After inspecting a complete receipt, retry safe cleanup:

/path/to/spark-on-k8s/.venv-dbt/bin/spark-on-k8s-dbt cleanup \
  --receipt /path/to/invocation/receipt.json

Deletion refuses changed identities and incomplete receipts. In those cases, inspect the recorded application and Kubernetes UIDs manually; do not delete by name alone or discard the receipt. No external orphan-reaper controller is installed. Avoid concurrent invocations targeting the same dbt output tables; separate process ownership protects compute, not conflicting SQL writes.

To bound what a hard kill can leave running, set compute.max_runtime (whole seconds) above the longest invocation you expect, including startup and on-run-end hooks. All commands of a sequence share one server, so the limit must cover the whole sequence. Kubernetes stops the server's driver that long after its pod starts, whether or not the wrapper survives; a command still running at that point fails like any lost compute. The stopped driver pod and its Services remain until cleanup or apps prune deletes them. See driver lifetime limits.

docs.title: Run in CI
docs.text: This recipe uses plain shell steps, so it fits GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or any runner that can reach the Kubernetes API. Install the wheels as in Install from the repository and put the environment's bin directory on PATH.

docs.title: Keep credentials out of the repository
docs.text:
