Commit a CI output that reads everything secret or job-specific from the environment, and let the CI system inject the values from its secret store:

analytics:
  target: ci
  outputs:
    ci:
      type: spark_on_k8s
      method: connect
      schema: "{{ env_var('DBT_CI_SCHEMA') }}"
      threads: 4
      compute:
        kube_config_file: "{{ env_var('SPARK_KUBECONFIG') }}"
        kube_context: "{{ env_var('SPARK_KUBE_CONTEXT') }}"
        namespace: spark-ci
        service_account: spark
        image: registry.example.com/analytics/spark-dbt:4.3.0
        server_jar: local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar
        startup_timeout: 600
        executor_instances: {initial: 2}
        spark_conf:
          spark.sql.catalogImplementation: hive
          spark.sql.warehouse.dir: hdfs://namenode.data.svc:8020/warehouse
          spark.hadoop.hive.metastore.uris: thrift://metastore.data.svc:9083

Write the kubeconfig secret to a private temporary file, or use your CI's file-type secret, and pass its path in SPARK_KUBECONFIG; never commit a kubeconfig, token or literal credential. Give CI an identity limited to the permissions that spark-on-k8s-dbt check verifies. For catalog or storage credentials in compute.spark_conf, read variables whose names start with DBT_ENV_SECRET, which dbt scrubs from its logs. Receipts never contain the compute configuration.

docs.title: Give each pull request its own schema
docs.text:
Derive the schema from the pull request number so concurrent pull requests never write the same tables:

export DBT_CI_SCHEMA="analytics_pr_${PR_NUMBER:?}"  # from your CI's pull request variable

dbt's default generate_schema_name prefixes custom schemas with the target schema (analytics_pr_123_marts), so models with +schema stay separate too. If your project overrides generate_schema_name, or a snapshot sets a fixed target_schema, check that the CI target still produces pull-request names. The wrapper never deletes warehouse or catalog data: drop a pull request's schemas when it closes, for example with a run-operation macro that refuses any schema without the analytics_pr_ prefix.

Different pull requests run separate invocations with separate servers and receipts. Each running job adds a driver and its executors to the namespace, so cap CI concurrency or the namespace quota: a driver that cannot be scheduled waits until startup_timeout. Two jobs for the same pull request write the same schema; let your CI cancel or serialize the older one (for example a GitHub Actions concurrency group with cancel-in-progress, or GitLab interruptible jobs).

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
# Step 1: fail in seconds on configuration or permission errors; creates nothing.
spark-on-k8s-dbt check

# Step 2: one server for the whole job. exec makes the wrapper the step's main
# process, so a cancellation signal sent only to that process reaches it.
exec spark-on-k8s-dbt run --receipt-dir "$JOB_TMP/dbt-receipt" --deadline 2400 -- \
  deps -- seed -- build -- docs generate

JOB_TMP is a private per-job directory, such as $RUNNER_TEMP on GitHub Actions; the receipt directory must not exist yet. Choose --deadline below the job timeout so that the last command and cleanup can finish: with a 60-minute limit, --deadline 2400 starts no command after 40 minutes.

CI systems usually signal a cancelled or timed-out job and kill it after a grace period that can be shorter than cleanup_timeout. Add a step that your CI runs even after failure or cancellation (for example if: always() on GitHub Actions) and keep the receipt as a job artifact. It contains resource identities and cluster selection, not credentials:

# Step 3: always run. Retry cleanup unless the receipt shows nothing to delete.
receipt="$JOB_TMP/dbt-receipt/receipt.json"
if [ -f "$receipt" ]; then
  stage=$(python -c 'import json, sys; print(json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))["stage"])' "$receipt")
  case "$stage" in
    cleaned | not_started | reserved) echo "No managed compute to delete ($stage)" ;;
    *) spark-on-k8s-dbt cleanup --receipt "$receipt" ;;
  esac
fi

reserved means the wrapper stopped before it requested any compute. cleanup refuses a receipt without a complete server identity: that step then fails, and the receipt tells you what to inspect manually. Nothing runs if the runner itself disappears before this step; compute then keeps running until you run cleanup with the preserved receipt, or until compute.max_runtime, if set, stops the driver. Set it above the job timeout.

docs.title: Size the managed server
docs.text:
compute sizes one Spark application: a driver that runs the Thrift or Connect server and plans every query, and executors that run the tasks. dbt's threads sets how many models run at once; each is a concurrent Spark query on the same executors. Resources and executor allocation come only from these fields; spark_conf cannot override them.

compute field Spark setting Kubernetes Pod driver_resources.cpu none Driver CPU request and limit driver_resources.memory (MiB) spark.driver.memory (JVM heap) Driver memory request and limit: memory + memory_overhead driver_resources.memory_overhead (MiB) none: headroom outside the heap Included in the driver memory above executor_resources.cpu spark.executor.cores: concurrent tasks per executor Executor CPU request, unless spark_conf sets a smaller spark.kubernetes.executor.request.cores executor_resources.memory (MiB) spark.executor.memory Executor memory request and limit: memory + memory_overhead executor_resources.memory_overhead (MiB) spark.executor.memoryOverhead Included in the executor memory above executor_instances.initial alone spark.executor.instances (2 when nothing is set) A fixed number of executor Pods executor_instances.min or max Dynamic allocation with shuffle tracking, starting from initial (at least min) Executors added while tasks queue and removed after 60 idle seconds by default, later while they hold shuffle data still in use

Each cpu and memory value applies to every executor; executors × cpu is the number of tasks that run at once across all models. More threads than that rarely helps, and Spark's default FIFO scheduling can let one large model's tasks delay smaller ones. Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions in compute.spark_conf to a small multiple of the total executor cores for small data; Spark's default of 200 creates many tiny tasks.

Memory overhead. A container that exceeds its Pod memory limit is killed by Kubernetes. For an executor, Spark retries the lost tasks elsewhere; for the driver, the server and the running dbt command fail. The heap is memory; everything else (JVM metadata, threads, network and shuffle buffers, native libraries) must fit in memory_overhead. Spark's own default rule is 10% of memory with a 384 MiB minimum, but spark-on-k8s always sets the overhead (512 MiB when omitted), so raise it yourself above about 5 GiB of memory. 0 is accepted and leaves no headroom. The driver also holds query plans and broadcast tables, and every result returned to dbt passes through it: large seeds and docs generate on big catalogs need driver memory, not more executors.

Startup time. These mostly decide how long startup_timeout must be:

  • Image size and pull policy. Spark images are large. The default image_pull_policy: IfNotPresent with an immutable tag or digest lets nodes reuse a cached image; Always contacts the registry on every start. Pre-pulling the image onto nodes removes the pull from startup. Executors pull it too, possibly on other nodes.
  • Node capacity and autoscaling. A driver that fits on no node stays Unschedulable (shown in the startup progress) until a node autoscaler adds a node, which can take minutes. A request larger than any node never schedules.
  • packages downloads Maven dependencies on every start; build them into the image instead.
  • Executors. Readiness does not wait for them, so the first queries may wait for executor Pods to be scheduled and their image pulled.

A sequence pays this once instead of once per command.

Starting points. The values below are illustrative starting points, not measurements or recommendations for your data. Adjust them from the Spark UI (task time, spill, garbage collection, skew) and from Pod memory usage. While a server runs, kubectl --namespace <namespace> port-forward pod/<driver pod> 4040 opens its UI; the driver Pod name is in the startup progress and the receipt.

Workload threads driver_resources executor_resources executor_instances spark.sql.shuffle.partitions Small: CI checks, sample data, models up to a few GB 2–4 {cpu: 1, memory: 2048, memory_overhead: 512} {cpu: 2, memory: 4096, memory_overhead: 512} {initial: 2} '8' Medium: models of tens of GB 4–8 {cpu: 2, memory: 8192, memory_overhead: 1024} {cpu: 4, memory: 16384, memory_overhead: 2048} {min: 2, initial: 2, max: 10} '64'

A fixed executor count starts every executor at once and suits short CI jobs. Dynamic allocation releases idle executors between models and commands, at the cost of waiting for new executors when work arrives. The integration tests run their small fixture with a 768 MiB driver and one 512 MiB executor on a single kind node; that shows the lifecycle works, not that those sizes perform.

docs.title: What the tests exercise
docs.text: The integration harness runs installed wheels on disposable Kubernetes with a shared HDFS warehouse and an external metastore fixture. It first runs spark-on-k8s-dbt check against each generated profile and requires every check to pass without creating compute. It checks both transports, parallel dbt workers, seeds/models/data tests, fresh compute across invocations, one driver shared by the commands of a sequence (including a command after a failure with --keep-going, and no further command after an interrupt), startup and cleanup progress, catalog persistence, documentation generation, failed SQL and graceful cancellation. Fixture storage is temporary and is not a production storage deployment recipe. The CI recipe and sizing values above are not exercised by these tests.

docs.title: Diagnose a Spark application
docs.text:
These commands are available from the current source tree. Check the documentation for your installed release before using them with a published package.

Diagnostics collect a bounded snapshot of driver and executor pod states and Kubernetes events. They explain observed image-pull failures, scheduling constraints, denied operations, OOM kills, crash loops, unavailable persistent volume claims and pods stopped by an elapsed max_runtime (deadline_exceeded). Each finding contains a stable code, severity, affected resource, evidence and a suggested next step. An unsuccessful exit code alone is not treated as proof of an OOM kill or another specific cause.

docs.title: Inspect an application
docs.text:
Use the application ID returned by submission:

spark-on-k8s app diagnose --namespace spark --app-id YOUR_APPLICATION_ID
spark-on-k8s app diagnose --namespace spark --app-id YOUR_APPLICATION_ID --output json

The SDK accepts either an application ID or an exact driver pod name:

from spark_on_k8s.client import SparkOnK8S

spark = SparkOnK8S()
report = spark.diagnose_app(namespace="spark", app_id="YOUR_APPLICATION_ID")
print(report.to_dict())

# Useful when the driver name was shortened with a hash or when inspecting an existing pod.
report = spark.diagnose_app(namespace="spark", pod_name="YOUR_DRIVER_POD")

The JSON report has schema_version: 1, namespace, app_id, driver_pod, findings, inspected_pods, inspected_events and incomplete. A report with no findings means that no specific problem was observed. It does not establish that the application is healthy. Events and previous container termination states may describe earlier attempts that have since recovered.

Collection reads at most 20 executors and 100 events per inspected pod by default. --pod-limit (1–50) and --event-limit (1–200) adjust those limits; the SDK accepts the same parameters and a positive timeout of at most 30 seconds (10 by default). Collection uses one executor page and one event page per inspected pod, without following pagination. A limit, denied read or timeout produces an incomplete report while retaining available evidence. A failed initial driver lookup produces an error.

Executor selection stays within the chosen namespace, uses Spark's application label, and verifies each executor's owner UID against the driver. Events must match the inspected pod UID, so events for a replaced pod with the same name are excluded. No logs, environment values, Secret contents or PVC contents are fetched. Event messages can still contain workload-specific information; share reports with the same care as Kubernetes events.

docs.title: Console and Airflow task tab
docs.text:
Open application Details in the standalone console to see the same findings. The JSON endpoint is:

GET /webserver/api/apps/{namespace}/pods/{driver_pod}/diagnostics

It returns { "application": { ... }, "diagnosis": { ... } }. The two objects come from the same inspected driver pod. Query parameters pod_limit and event_limit use the bounds above. The endpoint permits up to five seconds for the initial driver lookup, followed by the bounded collection budget.

The optional Airflow task tab uses the shared diagnostics panel. Its backend resolves the task's application and checks the driver ownership annotation against the authorized task before returning findings. It does not accept a browser-supplied namespace or application ID. Diagnostics are unavailable after the driver is deleted; the task's history link remains separate. When an application does not succeed, the Airflow operators also write these findings and the driver's last log lines to the task log before cleanup; see the failure postmortem. When the Spark API enables remote bearer authentication, the Airflow service URL must use a trusted gateway that authenticates the Airflow backend and injects that credential, or a separate restricted internal API. See remote submission deployment.

The API caller needs namespaced pod reads and list access to core events. Current source chart namespace Roles include this event permission. For an existing installation using an older chart or a custom service account, an administrator must review and add the permission before event collection can succeed. The page can still show pod evidence when event access is denied. API authentication and task authorization continue to apply; diagnostics do not grant additional access.

docs.title: Check cluster prerequisites
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s doctor --namespace spark --service-account spark
spark-on-k8s doctor --namespace spark --service-account spark --output json

doctor reads the named service account and submits non-persistent Kubernetes SelfSubjectAccessReview requests for the authenticated caller's application-management permissions. It does not impersonate the driver or apply resources. Service-account existence and the caller's access do not prove that the driver can create executors: driver_permissions_verified remains false. A denied or unavailable review is reported explicitly.

The caller checks cover pod creation, lookup, listing and deletion; driver log reads; service and ConfigMap creation; and event listing. They are targeted prerequisites, not an exhaustive validation of every optional workload feature. Cluster network reachability from the driver, image contents, admission policies and storage availability still require runtime evidence.

To prepare a namespace-scoped baseline driver role for administrator review, render manifests offline:

spark-on-k8s doctor --namespace spark --service-account spark --emit-rbac > driver-rbac.yaml

This command prints a Role and RoleBinding and never contacts Kubernetes. It does not create the namespace or service account and does not apply the manifests. The binding references the existing service account. The role allows Spark to manage pods, services and ConfigMaps within that namespace; collection deletion is limited to services and ConfigMaps for Spark cleanup. It grants no cluster-wide permissions, Secret access or pod exec access. Optional features such as dynamically created PVCs may need additional permissions that an administrator should review separately.

See the upstream Spark Kubernetes service-account guidance and Kubernetes RBAC guidance when adapting the baseline to your workload.

docs.title: Driver pod templates
docs.text:
Since 0.13.0, a Kubernetes Pod template for the driver is supported through the Python client, CLI and both Airflow operators. This feature does not require a Spark operator or a custom resource.

Use a template for settings such as pod/container security contexts, affinity, image pull secrets, sidecars, init containers and additional volumes. The client merges the template into the same driver pod it normally submits.

docs.title: Submit a template
docs.text:
Save this as driver.yaml. The application image still comes from the submission arguments, so the selected container does not need an image in the template.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    team: analytics
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 185
    fsGroup: 185
  containers:
    - name: driver
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities:
          drop: [ALL]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: scratch
          mountPath: /scratch
  volumes:
    - name: scratch
      emptyDir: {}

Select a user ID supported by your application image and ensure its working directories are writable. A template configures the driver only; use an executor template for executor pod settings.

from spark_on_k8s.client import SparkOnK8S

SparkOnK8S().submit_app(
    image="registry.example.com/team/spark-job:1.0",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    driver_pod_template="./driver.yaml",
    app_waiter="log",
)

spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --image registry.example.com/team/spark-job:1.0 \
  --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
  --namespace spark \
  --service-account spark \
  --driver-pod-template ./driver.yaml \
  --logs

driver_pod_template accepts YAML text, a local path string, a pathlib.Path, or a Python mapping. The CLI accepts YAML text or a local path. Files are read on the machine submitting the application; this option does not fetch remote URLs.

docs.title: Select the driver container
docs.text:
A template can contain additional containers. The client selects the container named driver, or the sole container if there is only one. Otherwise, specify driver_container_name="spark-main" or --driver-container-name spark-main. An explicit name must exist. An ambiguous or missing selection is an error.

The selected container becomes the first container in the submitted pod, retaining its name. Other containers keep their relative order and settings. Logs and kill operations target this selected container; the client also sets kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container for interactive kubectl use.

Ordinary sidecars must exit for the pod to finish. A sidecar that keeps running also keeps pod-based waiting and Airflow tasks running. Where supported by your cluster, Kubernetes native sidecars in initContainers with restartPolicy: Always provide a lifecycle that ends with the application containers. Sidecar lifecycle is controlled by Kubernetes, not by this client.

docs.title: Merge rules
docs.text:
The template is the starting point. Submission arguments and their resolved configuration defaults supply the generated fields below. In particular, omitting an argument does not make a template image, service account or CPU/memory setting override the client's configured default. Input mappings are not modified.

Field Result Pod name and namespace Generated application pod name and submission namespace. spark-app-id, spark-app-name, spark-role, spark-ui-proxy labels Managed application identity and proxy settings; template values are discarded. Other labels and annotations Template entries are retained; explicit driver entries override matching keys. Service account and restart policy Submission service account and Never; the deprecated serviceAccount alias is removed. activeDeadlineSeconds The submission's max_runtime when set; otherwise the template value, if any, is retained. Selected container image, image pull policy and arguments Generated from submission options and Spark configuration. Selected container command Removed, so the application image's Spark entrypoint runs the generated driver arguments. Selected container CPU and memory requests/limits Generated from driver_resources or configured defaults. Other resources, such as ephemeral storage or GPU limits, are retained. Environment variables Merged by name; generated values win, including spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.* properties and the managed SPARK_DRIVER_BIND_ADDRESS. See driver environment variables for precedence and validation. Environment sources (envFrom) Template sources first, then generated secret references; identical entries are not duplicated. Volumes, init containers Merged by name; an explicit matching entry replaces the entire template entry. Driver volume mounts Merged by mount path; an explicit matching entry replaces the entire template entry. Container ports Merged by name, or by port/protocol for unnamed entries; generated driver/UI ports win on matching keys. Node selector Merged by key, with explicit driver selectors winning. Host aliases Merged by IP, with explicit driver aliases winning. Tolerations Template entries followed by explicit driver entries, without exact duplicates. Other pod/container fields Preserved, including security contexts, affinity, image pull secrets and sidecar settings.

Lists with duplicate merge keys are rejected rather than resolved by position. Server-assigned metadata, owner references, generateName, and status are not accepted. Templates cannot supply annotations in the reserved spark-on-k8s.io/ namespace. Keep that namespace available for project-managed ownership metadata; use your own annotation prefix for application metadata.

Loading, container selection and merge validation finish before any Kubernetes Secret, ConfigMap, Pod or Service is created. This is not a complete Kubernetes schema validator: the API server still validates other fields and enforces cluster admission policies. Template settings do not bypass those policies.

docs.title: Airflow
docs.text:
Both SparkOnK8SOperator and SparkSqlOnK8SOperator accept the same template and container-selection arguments. These fields support Airflow templating and DAG serialization on Airflow 2.11 and Airflow 3.

from spark_on_k8s.airflow.operators import SparkOnK8SOperator

application = SparkOnK8SOperator(
    task_id="application",
    image="registry.example.com/team/spark-job:1.0",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    driver_pod_template={
        "apiVersion": "v1",
        "kind": "Pod",
        "metadata": {"labels": {"run-date": "{{ ds }}"}},
        "spec": {"containers": [{"name": "driver"}]},
    },
)

For a file path, Airflow renders the path string, then the SDK reads that file on the worker. File contents are not separately rendered by Airflow. Pass inline YAML or a mapping when the template contents themselves contain Jinja expressions. See the Airflow guide for connection and deployment setup.

docs.title: Application examples
docs.text: These examples describe the current source checkout. Run build and submission commands from the repository root, with namespace spark and service account spark configured as described in Getting Started. The example Dockerfiles default to the Apache Spark 3.5.9 image. To build them with Spark 4, set the image and matching Java dependency versions as described in Spark compatibility. For scheduled jobs, see the Airflow guide or the CronJob recipe. The ecosystem recipes also cover batch schedulers, OpenLineage and S3/MinIO storage.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
In this example, we use a small PySpark application that takes a parameter num_points to calculate the value of Pi: 

from __future__ import annotations

import random
import sys

from my_modules.pi import is_point_in_the_unit_circle
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Check if the number of arguments is correct
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("Usage: python script.py <num_points>")
        sys.exit(1)

    # Get the number of points from command-line arguments
    num_points = int(sys.argv[1])

    # Create a Spark session
    spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("Pi-Estimation").getOrCreate()

    # Generate random points within the unit square
    points = spark.sparkContext.parallelize(range(1, num_points + 1)).map(
        lambda _: (random.random(), random.random())
    )

    # Count points within the unit circle
    inside_circle = points.filter(is_point_in_the_unit_circle)

    # Estimate Pi
    pi_estimate = 4 * inside_circle.count() / num_points

    # Display the result
    print(f"Pi is approximately {pi_estimate}")

    # Stop the Spark session
    spark.stop()
and a Dockerfile to package the application with the spark image: 
ARG SPARK_IMAGE=apache/spark:3.5.9-scala2.12-java17-python3-ubuntu
FROM ${SPARK_IMAGE}

COPY my_modules /opt/spark/work-dir/my_modules
COPY job.py /opt/spark/work-dir/
ENV PYTHONPATH="${PYTHONPATH}:/opt/spark/work-dir"

Build the image from the repository root:

docker build -t pyspark-job examples/python

For a local cluster, load the image into one of the following cluster runtimes:

# Minikube
minikube image load pyspark-job
# Or kind
kind load docker-image pyspark-job

The supplied submission scripts use image_pull_policy="Never" (CLI: --image-pull-policy Never) for these preloaded images. For a remote cluster, replace the example registry below, push the tagged image, and update the script's image to that same name and its pull policy to IfNotPresent:

docker tag pyspark-job registry.example.com/team/pyspark-job:example
docker push registry.example.com/team/pyspark-job:example
Then, you can submit the job using the python client: 
from __future__ import annotations

import logging

from spark_on_k8s.client import ExecutorInstances, PodResources, SparkOnK8S

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    spark_client = SparkOnK8S()
    spark_client.submit_app(
        image="pyspark-job",
        app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
        app_arguments=["100000"],
        app_name="pyspark-job-example",
        namespace="spark",
        service_account="spark",
        app_waiter="log",
        # If you test this locally (minikube or kind) without pushing the image to a registry,
        # you need to set the image_pull_policy to Never.
        image_pull_policy="Never",
        ui_reverse_proxy=True,
        driver_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=512, memory_overhead=128),
        executor_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=512, memory_overhead=128),
        # Run with 5 executors
        executor_instances=ExecutorInstances(initial=5),
    )
or using the CLI: 
spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --image pyspark-job \
  --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
  --namespace spark \
  --name pyspark-job-example \
  --service-account spark \
  --image-pull-policy Never \
  --driver-cpu 1 \
  --driver-memory 512 \
  --driver-memory-overhead 128 \
  --executor-cpu 1 \
  --executor-memory 512 \
  --executor-memory-overhead 128 \
  --executor-initial-instances 5 \
  --ui-reverse-proxy \
  --logs \
  100000

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
This example is similar to the previous one, but it's implemented in java (with maven).

pom.xml: 

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>com.oss-tech.examples</groupId>
    <artifactId>java-job</artifactId>
    <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.source>11</maven.compiler.source>
        <maven.compiler.target>11</maven.compiler.target>
        <spark.version>3.5.9</spark.version>
        <scala.binary.version>2.12</scala.binary.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.apache.spark</groupId>
            <artifactId>spark-core_${scala.binary.version}</artifactId>
            <version>${spark.version}</version>
            <scope>provided</scope>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.apache.spark</groupId>
            <artifactId>spark-sql_${scala.binary.version}</artifactId>
            <version>${spark.version}</version>
            <scope>provided</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>
the job class (src/main/java/com/oss_tech/examples/TestJob.java): 
package com.oss_tech.examples;

import org.apache.spark.sql.SparkSession;
import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset;
import org.apache.spark.sql.Row;


public class TestJob {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    // Check if the correct number of arguments is provided
    if (args.length != 1) {
      System.err.println("Usage: PiEstimation <num_points>");
      System.exit(1);
    }

    // Initialize Spark session
    final SparkSession spark = SparkSession.builder()
        .appName("Spark Java example")
        .getOrCreate();

    // Get the number of points from command-line arguments
    final int numPoints = Integer.parseInt(args[0]);

    Dataset<Row> points = spark.range(1, numPoints + 1)
        .selectExpr("rand() as x", "rand() as y");

    // Count points within the unit circle
    long insideCircle = points.filter("x * x + y * y <= 1").count();

    // Estimate Pi
    double piEstimate = 4.0 * insideCircle / numPoints;

    // Display the result
    System.out.println("Pi is approximately " + piEstimate);
  }
}

Build the image from the repository root:

docker build -t java-spark-job examples/java

For a local cluster, load the image into one of the following cluster runtimes:

# Minikube
minikube image load java-spark-job
# Or kind
kind load docker-image java-spark-job

The supplied submission scripts use image_pull_policy="Never" (CLI: --image-pull-policy Never) for these preloaded images. For a remote cluster, replace the example registry below, push the tagged image, and update the script's image to that same name and its pull policy to IfNotPresent:

docker tag java-spark-job registry.example.com/team/java-spark-job:example
docker push registry.example.com/team/java-spark-job:example
Then, submit the job using the python client: 
from __future__ import annotations

import logging

from spark_on_k8s.client import ExecutorInstances, SparkOnK8S

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    spark_client = SparkOnK8S()
    spark_client.submit_app(
        image="java-spark-job",
        app_path="local:///java-job.jar",
        app_arguments=["100000"],
        app_name="spark-java-job-example",
        namespace="spark",
        service_account="spark",
        app_waiter="log",
        class_name="com.oss_tech.examples.TestJob",
        # If you test this locally (minikube or kind) without pushing the image to a registry,
        # you need to set the image_pull_policy to Never.
        image_pull_policy="Never",
        ui_reverse_proxy=True,
        # Run with dynamic allocation enabled, with minimum of 0 executors and maximum of 5 executors
        executor_instances=ExecutorInstances(min=0, max=5),
    )
or using the CLI: 
spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --image java-spark-job \
  --path local:///java-job.jar \
  --namespace spark \
  --name spark-java-job-example \
  --service-account spark \
  --image-pull-policy Never \
  --executor-min-instances 0 \
  --executor-max-instances 5 \
  --executor-initial-instances 5 \
  --ui-reverse-proxy \
  --logs \
  --class com.oss_tech.examples.TestJob \
  100000

docs.title: Driver configuration
docs.text:
This package manages Spark applications in Kubernetes by directly creating the driver pod and submitting the job in client mode. This approach bypasses some of Spark's built-in driver configuration mechanisms, causing certain settings to be ignored (e.g., spark.kubernetes.driver.podTemplateFile, spark.kubernetes.driver.label.[LabelName], ...).

To address this, the package provides internal implementations for some key driver configurations, ensuring greater control and flexibility when deploying Spark applications in Kubernetes.

docs.title: Driver service account
docs.text:
Instead of providing spark.kubernetes.authenticate.driver.serviceAccountName=<some-service-account>, you can use: 

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    service_account="<some-service-account>",
)

docs.title: Driver resources
docs.text:
Instead of providing spark.driver.memory, spark.driver.cores, spark.driver.memoryOverhead, you can use: 

from spark_on_k8s.client import PodResources

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=512, memory_overhead=128),
)

docs.title: Driver environment variables
docs.text:
The source version supports spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.NAME in spark_conf. The client copies these properties into the driver container's environment before creating the Pod. This also applies to the CLI and both Airflow operators, which use the same submission code. This requires 0.13.0 or newer.

For example, a launcher that loads a YAML property mapping into spark_conf can use:

spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.DATABASE_NAME: dbname
spark.executorEnv.DATABASE_NAME: executor_dbname

The driver receives DATABASE_NAME=dbname; Spark independently sets DATABASE_NAME=executor_dbname on executors. A driver-only property does not add an executor environment variable. With job files, put these properties under spec.spark_conf; with the CLI, pass them through --conf.

Names must be nonempty printable ASCII without =. Values may be strings, booleans, integers or finite floats; booleans become true/false, and an empty string remains empty. Null, structured values and NUL characters are rejected before Kubernetes writes. SPARK_DRIVER_BIND_ADDRESS is managed from the Pod IP and cannot be supplied through spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.

An explicit driver property replaces a matching driver template environment entry, including its valueFrom reference. Explicit environment entries also take precedence over matching envFrom Secret/ConfigMap keys, including secret_values and driver_env_vars_from_secrets. Sidecar and init-container environments are unchanged. Kubernetes retains its normal $(NAME) expansion behavior for environment values.

Use these properties for non-secret settings: they remain ordinary Spark configuration in the driver arguments and may appear in Spark diagnostics. Offline plan output redacts their values in both environment entries and configuration arguments, as it does for spark.executorEnv.* values; raw ApplicationPlan.resources retains the actual values for inspection. For credentials, use Kubernetes Secret references in the driver template or the Secret options below.

Use secret_values to create an application-owned Kubernetes Secret. Its keys become environment variables in both the driver and executors; executor delivery uses Spark's spark.kubernetes.executor.secretKeyRef configuration. To import existing Secrets into the driver only, use driver_env_vars_from_secrets. 

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    secret_values={"EnvironmentVariableName": "some-value"},
)

docs.title: Driver volume mounts
docs.text:
Pass Kubernetes volume and mount objects to volumes and driver_volume_mounts. The Secret secret1, ConfigMap configmap1 and persistent volume claim pvc in this example must already exist in the application's namespace. Replace the host and NFS paths with resources available in your cluster:

from kubernetes import client as k8s

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    volumes=[
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume1",
            host_path=k8s.V1HostPathVolumeSource(path="/mnt/volume1"),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume2",
            empty_dir=k8s.V1EmptyDirVolumeSource(medium="Memory", size_limit="1Gi"),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume3",
            secret=k8s.V1SecretVolumeSource(
                secret_name="secret1", items=[k8s.V1KeyToPath(key="key1", path="path1")]
            ),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume4",
            config_map=k8s.V1ConfigMapVolumeSource(
                name="configmap1", items=[k8s.V1KeyToPath(key="key1", path="path1")]
            ),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume5",
            projected=k8s.V1ProjectedVolumeSource(
                sources=[
                    k8s.V1VolumeProjection(
                        secret=k8s.V1SecretProjection(
                            name="secret1",
                            items=[k8s.V1KeyToPath(key="key1", path="secret/key1")],
                        )
                    ),
                    k8s.V1VolumeProjection(
                        config_map=k8s.V1ConfigMapProjection(
                            name="configmap1",
                            items=[k8s.V1KeyToPath(key="key1", path="config/key1")],
                        )
                    ),
                ]
            ),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume6",
            nfs=k8s.V1NFSVolumeSource(server="nfs-server", path="/mnt/volume6", read_only=True),
        ),
        k8s.V1Volume(
            name="volume7",
            persistent_volume_claim=k8s.V1PersistentVolumeClaimVolumeSource(
                claim_name="pvc", read_only=True
            ),
        ),
    ],
    driver_volume_mounts=[
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume1", mount_path="/mnt/volume1"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume2", mount_path="/mnt/volume2", sub_path="sub-path"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume3", mount_path="/mnt/volume3"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume4", mount_path="/mnt/volume4"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume5", mount_path="/mnt/volume5"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume6", mount_path="/mnt/volume6"),
        k8s.V1VolumeMount(name="volume7", mount_path="/mnt/volume7", read_only=True),
    ],
)

docs.title: Driver node selector
docs.text:
Instead of providing spark.kubernetes.driver.node.selector.[labelKey]=<labelValue>, you can use: 

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_node_selector={"labelKey": "labelValue"},
)

docs.title: Driver tolerations
docs.text:
Instead of configuring tolerations for the driver pod via a pod template file, you can use: 

from kubernetes import client as k8s

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_tolerations=[
        k8s.V1Toleration(
            key="key1",
            operator="Equal",
            value="value1",
            effect="NoSchedule",
        ),
        k8s.V1Toleration(
            key="key2",
            operator="Exists",
            effect="NoExecute",
        ),
    ],
)

docs.title: Driver init containers
docs.text:
Instead of adding init containers to the driver pod via a pod template file, you can use: 

from kubernetes import client as k8s

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_init_containers=[
        k8s.V1Container(
            name="init-container1",
            image="init-container1-image",
            command=["init-command1"],
            args=["init-arg1"],
        ),
        k8s.V1Container(
            name="init-container2",
            image="init-container2-image",
            command=["init-command2"],
            args=["init-arg2"],
        ),
    ],
)

docs.title: Driver host aliases
docs.text:
Instead of providing host aliases (entries added to pod's /etc/hosts file) for the driver pod via a pod template file, you can use: 

from kubernetes import client as k8s

spark_client.submit_app(
    ...,
    driver_host_aliases=[
        k8s.V1HostAlias(
            hostnames=["foo.local", "bar.local"],
            ip="127.0.0.1",
        )
    ],
)

docs.title: Executor pod template
docs.text:
The package provides an enhanced way to configure executor pod templates compared to Spark's built-in spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateFile configuration.

Instead of manually creating ConfigMaps and managing volume mounts, you can use the executor_pod_template parameter that accepts either:

  • Template content as a string (YAML)
  • Path to a local template file

The package automatically:

  1. Creates a ConfigMap with the template content
  2. Mounts it to the driver pod (so the driver can validate the template)
  3. Configures Spark to use the template for executor pods
  4. Sets the driver pod as the ConfigMap owner, so Kubernetes cleans up the ConfigMap when that pod is deleted

These submissions use the locally preloaded pyspark-job image and the spark namespace/service account prepared earlier. For a registry image, change the image name and use IfNotPresent as described in the Python example above.

Using template content as string: 

executor_template_yaml = """
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: executor
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "4Gi"
        cpu: "2"
      limits:
        memory: "4Gi"
        cpu: "2"
    env:
    - name: CUSTOM_ENV_VAR
      value: "custom-value"
  nodeSelector:
    node-type: "compute-optimized"
  tolerations:
  - key: "spark-executor"
    operator: "Equal"
    value: "true"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
"""

spark_client.submit_app(
    image="pyspark-job",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    image_pull_policy="Never",
    executor_pod_template=executor_template_yaml,
)

Using local template file: 

# Save your template to a file, e.g., executor-template.yaml
spark_client.submit_app(
    image="pyspark-job",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    image_pull_policy="Never",
    executor_pod_template="./executor-template.yaml",
)

Via CLI: 

# Using template file
spark-on-k8s app submit --image pyspark-job --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
    --namespace spark --service-account spark --image-pull-policy Never \
    --executor-template ./executor-template.yaml

# You can also set it via environment variable
export SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_TEMPLATE="./executor-template.yaml"
spark-on-k8s app submit --image pyspark-job --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/job.py \
    --namespace spark --service-account spark --image-pull-policy Never

Note: executor_pod_template and executor_pod_template_path are mutually exclusive. Use executor_pod_template_path (or --executor-pod-template-path in the CLI) for a template path already available to the Spark driver. Do not configure both options, including through environment defaults.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This guide describes the current source. Follow the installation guide to choose between a published release and a source checkout. Example file paths below are relative to the repository root.

docs.title: Before submitting
docs.text:
Install the core package using the installation guide, and use that same Python environment for these commands. Choose either the Python or CLI example below; they submit the same kind of application.

Have these inputs ready:

  • Kubernetes credentials for the intended cluster and namespace. By default the client loads your kubeconfig's current context. Use SPARK_ON_K8S_CONFIG_FILE and SPARK_ON_K8S_CONTEXT to select them explicitly, or SPARK_ON_K8S_IN_CLUSTER=true when running with an in-cluster service account.
  • A namespace and driver service account with the permissions described below. The submitting client's credentials and the driver's service account are separate.
  • A Spark application image accessible to every node that may run a driver or executor, with the application file and its dependencies included. A local:/// application path names a file inside that image, not on your laptop.
  • Data and storage access for both driver and executors.

The submitter does not need Spark or Java installed locally. The application image must have compatible Spark, Java and application runtimes; use the Spark compatibility guide when choosing it. If you do not yet have an image, follow the Python or Java examples first.

docs.title: Set up the Kubernetes namespace
docs.text:
The client creates the Spark driver pod. The driver uses its Kubernetes service account to create and manage executor pods. The following examples use namespace spark and service account spark; the submitting client also needs permission to create the application resources in that namespace.

If your administrator has already provided that namespace and service account, skip the setup helper and use their names in the submission examples.

The optional setup helper creates the namespace if needed, a service account named spark, and a ClusterRoleBinding to the built-in edit ClusterRole. This grants that service account edit access across all namespaces. It is broader than a namespace-scoped Spark driver role. On a shared cluster, ask the cluster administrator to provision a suitably scoped service account instead.

Running the helper requires credentials that can list namespaces, service accounts and ClusterRoleBindings, create missing resources, and bind the edit role. Use it only when that cluster-wide grant is intended. See the Kubernetes RBAC documentation for the difference between RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings.

With Python:

from spark_on_k8s.utils.setup_namespace import SparkOnK8SNamespaceSetup

namespace_setup = SparkOnK8SNamespaceSetup()
namespace_setup.setup_namespace(namespace="spark")

With the CLI:

spark-on-k8s namespace setup -n spark

docs.title: Python client
docs.text:
Replace the image and application path with an image accessible to your cluster and an application file included in that image. The values below are placeholders:

from spark_on_k8s.client import SparkOnK8S

client = SparkOnK8S()
driver_pod_name = client.submit_app(
    image="registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0",
    app_path="local:///opt/spark/work-dir/my-app.py",
    app_arguments=["arg1", "arg2"],
    app_name="my-app",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    app_waiter="log",
    image_pull_policy="IfNotPresent",
)

submit_app returns the driver pod name. The application ID is generated from the application name with a timestamp suffix and is available in the application list. The driver pod is usually named <application ID>-driver; an ID longer than 56 characters instead keeps a readable prefix followed by a hash of the full ID, so use the returned name or run receipt rather than deriving it. For a private registry, configure image-pull credentials for the pods in your cluster.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The CLI can submit applications and manage applications created by either the CLI or the Python client. Submit an application and stream its logs:

spark-on-k8s app submit \
  --image registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.0 \
  --path local:///opt/spark/work-dir/my-app.py \
  --namespace spark \
  --service-account spark \
  --name my-app \
  --image-pull-policy IfNotPresent \
  --logs --timeout 300 \
  param1 param2

The CLI example waits up to 300 seconds after submission and reports the final status. A timeout stops observation; it does not cancel the application. Confirm Succeeded and check the application's expected output before treating the run as successful. For JSON output, saved receipts and safe cancellation, follow Automation and run identities.

List applications to find their generated IDs:

spark-on-k8s apps list -n spark

To kill a running application, copy its actual ID from that output. The following ID is illustrative; my-app alone is the application name, not the generated ID:

APP_ID="my-app-20261107120000" # Replace with the ID from the application list
spark-on-k8s app kill -n spark --app-id "$APP_ID"

To have Kubernetes stop a run that outlives its expected duration, even after your terminal or CI job has gone, add --max-runtime SECONDS to app submit. Finished drivers and their Services, ConfigMaps and Secrets remain until deleted; spark-on-k8s apps prune -n spark --older-than 86400 lists them and deletes them only with --delete. See driver lifetime limits and pruning.

Check the help for further commands and options:

spark-on-k8s --help
spark-on-k8s app --help
spark-on-k8s apps --help

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
Install the api extra before starting the REST API and web UI. The API serves only its current namespace unless SPARK_ON_K8S_API_NAMESPACES names others; outside a cluster, that is the namespace of the kubeconfig context. For local access to the spark namespace:

export SPARK_ON_K8S_API_NAMESPACES=spark
spark-on-k8s api start \
    --host "127.0.0.1" \
    --port 8080 \
    --workers 4 \
    --log-level error \
    --limit-concurrency 100

List applications in the spark namespace:

curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/apps/list_apps/spark' \
  -H 'accept: application/json'

The console provides a searchable application list, status filters, namespace selection, application details, and confirmed stop/delete actions. It refreshes in the background without resetting your filters. The last successful fetch age and polling state help you recognize stale data. Counts and filters describe the applications loaded so far; use Load more when additional pages are available. Completed applications from the configured history server appear as archive entries without live-driver actions.

The driver-log view supports search, a configurable tail and frozen reading while new lines arrive. Its live buffer retains the most recent 10,000 lines. Download exports that buffered text; it is not a complete historical log archive. The excerpt preview lets you review and edit bounded text before copying or sharing it. Connection failures appear separately from log text, and a history-server outage leaves live applications available. JavaScript and CSS are packaged with the Python distribution; no CDN is needed.

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/webserver/apps?namespace=spark and use Open Spark UI for an application submitted with ui_reverse_proxy=True in Python or --ui-reverse-proxy in the CLI. Its direct URL is http://127.0.0.1:8080/webserver/ui/spark/APP_ID; replace APP_ID with the actual application ID. The API process must be able to reach the driver's service. When placing the console behind a gateway, configure the browser and proxy boundaries, including the public WebSocket origin when needed.

Use --host 0.0.0.0 to listen on all network interfaces when deploying behind an appropriate service or proxy. Client URLs should use the server's reachable host or address, not the wildcard bind address 0.0.0.0.

When a gateway serves the API below a path such as /platform/spark and removes that prefix before forwarding, pass --root-path /platform/spark or set SPARK_ON_K8S_API_ROOT_PATH=/platform/spark. See the mounted path guidance.

docs.title: Deploy the API with Helm
docs.text:
The chart deploys the API, its Service and RBAC resources. Ingress and the optional Spark History Server are controlled by chart values. The chart's env list sets environment variables for the API and its Kubernetes client.

The published chart is released independently from this source checkout. Inspect the selected published chart's values before deploying it; unreleased chart fixes and defaults described below may not be present:

helm repo add spark-on-k8s https://hussein.awala.fr/spark-on-k8s-chart
helm repo update
helm show values spark-on-k8s/spark-on-k8s
helm install spark-on-k8s-release spark-on-k8s/spark-on-k8s \
  --values examples/helm/values.yaml

To use the chart from this checkout, render it for review first, then install that local chart. Set API_IMAGE_TAG to a compatible, tested image from the current source; the old 0.12.1 API does not implement the readiness endpoint:

helm template spark-on-k8s-release ./chart --values examples/helm/values.yaml \
  --set-string image.tag="${API_IMAGE_TAG:?Set a qualified API image tag}"
helm install spark-on-k8s-release ./chart --values examples/helm/values.yaml \
  --set-string image.tag="$API_IMAGE_TAG"

Choose one chart source for a release. The commands above use example values from this checkout; adapt them to your cluster and selected chart version. The source chart defaults to readOnly: true, namespaces: "" (the release namespace), a ClusterIP Service on port 8000, and disabled ingress. Set namespaces to a comma-separated string such as "spark" or "spark,analytics" to serve those namespaces, or to "*" to serve every namespace through a chart-owned cluster role with the same permissions. The chart-created Kubernetes permissions follow the same value, and the API refuses requests, Spark UI proxy connections and log streams for other namespaces. Enable readOnly: false only if the API should be able to kill or delete applications; with "*", that also requires rbac.allowClusterWideWrite: true. The separate web UI button settings control visibility, not Kubernetes authorization. The API has no built-in user authentication; its namespace scope limits what it can reach, not who can use it. Expose the API through access-controlled networking or an authenticating proxy.

The source chart supplies in-cluster Kubernetes configuration and the API bind address and port. It requires an explicit API image tag or digest; a published chart defaults to its appVersion tag. Using a local chart does not build or install the Python source into an image. Set image.repository and image.tag to the API image version you intend to deploy, or use image.digest to select verified image contents; the digest takes precedence over the tag. This is independent of the Spark application image passed to submit_app. Follow Chart deployment boundaries for scoped access, image selection and existing-release upgrades.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Set environment variables before starting the CLI/API process or importing the Python client: configuration values are read at module import time. The table below lists defaults in the current source, before chart or caller overrides. unset means no environment default (None); {}, [] and an empty string are distinct empty defaults. Use lowercase true or false for boolean settings.

Most client defaults also apply to the CLI. The six node-selector, label and annotation variables marked CLI are CLI defaults; Python callers should pass the corresponding driver_* or executor_* dictionaries to submit_app. If all three executor-count variables are unset, applications use two executors with dynamic allocation disabled. The two executor-template settings are mutually exclusive, including when supplied through environment variables.

A value that cannot be parsed, such as SPARK_ON_K8S_DRIVER_CPU=two or an empty integer, stops the CLI with one error line naming the variable; the SDK, API and Airflow raise ConfigurationError (a ValueError) when the configuration is imported. JSON values are never echoed in these errors.

Environment variable Description Default SPARK_ON_K8S_DOCKER_IMAGE Spark driver and executor image; required unless passed explicitly unset SPARK_ON_K8S_APP_PATH Application file URI; required unless passed explicitly unset SPARK_ON_K8S_NAMESPACE Application namespace default SPARK_ON_K8S_SERVICE_ACCOUNT Driver service account spark SPARK_ON_K8S_APP_NAME Application name; generated when unset unset SPARK_ON_K8S_SPARK_CONF Spark properties as a JSON object {} SPARK_ON_K8S_CLASS_NAME Main class for a JVM application unset SPARK_ON_K8S_PACKAGES Maven coordinates separated by commas empty string SPARK_ON_K8S_APP_ARGUMENTS Application arguments as a JSON array of strings [] SPARK_ON_K8S_APP_WAITER Wait mode: no_wait, wait or log no_wait SPARK_ON_K8S_IMAGE_PULL_POLICY Pod image pull policy: Always, IfNotPresent or Never IfNotPresent SPARK_ON_K8S_UI_REVERSE_PROXY Configure the application for Spark UI reverse proxy access false SPARK_ON_K8S_DRIVER_CPU Driver CPU cores (integer) 1 SPARK_ON_K8S_DRIVER_MEMORY Driver memory in MiB (integer) 1024 SPARK_ON_K8S_DRIVER_MEMORY_OVERHEAD Driver memory overhead in MiB (integer) 512 SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_CPU Executor CPU cores (integer) 1 SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_MEMORY Executor memory in MiB (integer) 1024 SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_MEMORY_OVERHEAD Executor memory overhead in MiB (integer) 512 SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_MIN_INSTANCES Minimum executor count; enables dynamic allocation when set unset SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_MAX_INSTANCES Maximum executor count; enables dynamic allocation when set unset SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_INITIAL_INSTANCES Initial executor count; fixed count when minimum and maximum are unset unset SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_ALLOCATION_RATIO Dynamic allocation ratio (number) 1.0 SPARK_ON_K8S_SCHEDULER_BACKLOG_TIMEOUT Backlog duration before requesting executors 1s SPARK_ON_K8S_SUSTAINED_SCHEDULER_BACKLOG_TIMEOUT Backlog duration for subsequent executor requests value of SPARK_ON_K8S_SCHEDULER_BACKLOG_TIMEOUT SPARK_ON_K8S_SECRET_ENV_VAR Driver and executor environment values as a JSON object; stored in an application-owned Secret {} SPARK_ON_K8S_DRIVER_ENV_VARS_FROM_SECRET Existing Secret names separated by commas; import their keys as driver environment variables empty list SPARK_ON_K8S_STARTUP_TIMEOUT Driver startup timeout in seconds when waiting or streaming logs (integer); 0 disables it 0 SPARK_ON_K8S_CONFIG_FILE Kubeconfig file path unset SPARK_ON_K8S_CONTEXT Kubeconfig context unset SPARK_ON_K8S_CLIENT_CONFIG JSON object of synchronous kubernetes.client.Configuration constructor arguments unset SPARK_ON_K8S_ASYNC_CLIENT_CONFIG JSON object of kubernetes_asyncio.client.Configuration constructor arguments; requires the api or airflow extra unset SPARK_ON_K8S_IN_CLUSTER Load Kubernetes credentials from the running pod false SPARK_ON_K8S_SPARK_DRIVER_NODE_SELECTOR CLI driver node selector as a JSON object {} SPARK_ON_K8S_SPARK_EXECUTOR_NODE_SELECTOR CLI executor node selector as a JSON object {} SPARK_ON_K8S_SPARK_DRIVER_LABELS CLI driver labels as a JSON object {} SPARK_ON_K8S_SPARK_EXECUTOR_LABELS CLI executor labels as a JSON object {} SPARK_ON_K8S_SPARK_DRIVER_ANNOTATIONS CLI driver annotations as a JSON object {} SPARK_ON_K8S_SPARK_EXECUTOR_ANNOTATIONS CLI executor annotations as a JSON object {} SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_POD_TEMPLATE_PATH Executor template path already available to the driver unset SPARK_ON_K8S_EXECUTOR_TEMPLATE Executor template YAML or local file path; creates and mounts a ConfigMap unset SPARK_ON_K8S_API_NAMESPACES Namespaces the API serves: empty for its current namespace (the pod's, or the kubeconfig context's), * for every namespace, or a comma-separated list empty SPARK_ON_K8S_API_DEFAULT_NAMESPACE Namespace the API/web UI uses when a request names none; must be in the scope the first namespace in scope; with *, the current namespace SPARK_ON_K8S_API_HOST API bind address 127.0.0.1 SPARK_ON_K8S_API_PORT API listen port (integer) 8000 SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WORKERS API worker count (integer) 4 SPARK_ON_K8S_API_LOG_LEVEL API server log level info SPARK_ON_K8S_API_LIMIT_CONCURRENCY Maximum concurrent API connections/tasks (integer) 1000 SPARK_ON_K8S_API_ROOT_PATH Public path prefix, such as /platform/spark, that a gateway removes before forwarding to the API; --root-path default empty string SPARK_ON_K8S_API_SPARK_HISTORY_HOST Spark History Server host and port, optionally with an HTTP(S) scheme unset SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WEBSERVER_APPS_KILL_BUTTON Show the kill button in the applications page true SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WEBSERVER_APPS_DELETE_BUTTON Show the delete button in the applications page true SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WEBSERVER_APPS_REFRESH_INTERVAL Applications-page refresh interval in whole seconds; 0 or a negative value disables it 10

Boolean settings in this table accept true or false in any letter case; any other value is treated as false.

JSON settings use JSON syntax, including double-quoted keys and strings. Packages and existing Secret names use comma-separated strings instead of JSON arrays:

export SPARK_ON_K8S_SPARK_CONF='{"spark.sql.shuffle.partitions": "8"}'
export SPARK_ON_K8S_APP_ARGUMENTS='["--input", "s3a://example/input"]'
export SPARK_ON_K8S_DRIVER_ENV_VARS_FROM_SECRET='spark-storage,spark-catalog'
export SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WEBSERVER_APPS_REFRESH_INTERVAL='10'

The named Secrets must exist in the application's namespace. Refresh values such as 10s are invalid because the setting is parsed as an integer.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Choose the package release before following examples. develop documents the current main branch, which can include features that are not yet on PyPI. For a published package, choose its matching documentation in the version selector. The Python package, API container and Helm chart have separate release versions.

docs.title: Published releases
docs.text:
Use a virtual environment with a Python version accepted by your selected release. Check its metadata on PyPI. For example, create and activate an environment on macOS/Linux using that Python interpreter:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Then choose one of these installations:

python -m pip install spark-on-k8s # Python client, CLI and helpers
python -m pip install "spark-on-k8s[sql]" # Also submit SQL files without Airflow
python -m pip install "spark-on-k8s[api]" # Also install the REST API and web UI
python -m pip install "spark-on-k8s[airflow]" # Also install the Airflow integration

These commands install from PyPI. They do not install this development branch or the repository's example files. Availability of other extras and features depends on the selected release. For an existing Airflow deployment, follow the Airflow guide in the matching docs.

docs.title: Current source
docs.text:
The current source requires Python 3.11 or newer. The core client and API are tested on Python 3.11–3.15. Airflow 3.4 is tested on Python 3.11–3.14; the legacy Airflow 2.11.2 CI profile uses Python 3.12. Use Airflow 3 for new deployments. The airflow, airflow-ui and connect extras require Python below 3.15. Installing one of those extras on Python 3.15 does not provide its integration dependencies.

The submitting machine does not need Spark or Java. The application container supplies its own Spark, Java and, for Python jobs, Python runtime. Check the Spark compatibility guide when selecting that image. The optional Spark Connect client uses a reachable server. Server creation and lifecycle use the base package; query readiness and notebook sessions need the compatible client extra.

Clone the repository to obtain the source and example files:

git clone https://github.com/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s.git
cd spark-on-k8s

With uv, choose one row below. Each command uses the committed lockfile and creates .venv in the checkout. Python 3.12 is used here so every listed optional integration has a supported interpreter.

Functionality Installation command Python client, CLI and job files uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups SQL submission uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra sql REST API and web console uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra api Spark Connect companion uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra connect Airflow integration uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra airflow Airflow 3.4+ integration with its native task tab uv sync --python 3.12 --locked --no-default-groups --extra airflow-ui

Select multiple --extra options when needed, such as --extra api --extra sql. airflow-ui already includes the Airflow integration. A later uv sync selects a new profile and can remove unselected extras.

Run commands through that environment:

uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s --help

To use the bare spark-on-k8s and python commands in the other guides, activate .venv in your shell first. On macOS/Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

Alternatively, use pip in an activated virtual environment with a supported Python version. From the checkout, install . for core or select extras, for example:

python -m pip install ".[api,sql]"

This pip path resolves dependencies from the package metadata; it does not use uv.lock. Use the uv profile above when you need the checkout's locked environment.

docs.title: Check the environment and continue
docs.text:
Using the selected environment, confirm the installed package and CLI are visible:

python -c 'from importlib.metadata import version; print(version("spark-on-k8s"))'
spark-on-k8s --help

These checks do not contact Kubernetes.

Continue with Getting started to submit an existing application, or choose another route in Start here. Commands that reference examples/ run from the repository root. Contributor dependencies and the separate Airflow 2.11 environment are in Development and validation.

docs.title: Portable job files and offline plans
docs.text:
Use one versioned job definition from your laptop, CI, or an Airflow DAG. Job files need only the base package: no Airflow or API installation is required.

apiVersion: spark-on-k8s/v1
kind: SparkJob
metadata:
  name: daily-etl
spec:
  image: registry.example.com/team/spark-etl:1.0
  app_path: local:///opt/spark/jobs/etl.py
  namespace: spark
  service_account: spark
  executor_instances:
    initial: 2
  spark_conf:
    spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: 8
profiles:
  production:
    spec:
      namespace: production
      executor_instances:
        initial: 4
      spark_conf:
        spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: 32

spark-on-k8s job validate job.yaml --profile production
spark-on-k8s job plan job.yaml --profile production --output json
spark-on-k8s job submit job.yaml --profile production --output json

Coming from the Kubeflow Spark Operator? spark-on-k8s job assess-operator reports how each SparkApplication field translates and drafts a job file; see Migrate from the Spark Operator.

Validation and planning do not open a Kubernetes connection. Plans use the same resource builder as submission, with deterministic preview identifiers. They are illustrations, not reserved runs or manifests to apply with kubectl: owner references require the real driver pod UID and are attached during submission.

The display preview redacts Secret and ConfigMap contents, literal environment values, sensitive configuration keys, and application arguments. Review any custom metadata before sharing it; arbitrary user text can contain credentials in places no automatic redactor can identify. ApplicationPlan.resources is the raw in-memory representation and can contain secrets; use to_dict() for display.

docs.title: Profiles and settings
docs.text:
Profiles recursively merge objects and replace lists and scalar values. A selected profile is validated after merging. Unknown settings, duplicate YAML keys, aliases, invalid resource quantities, and incompatible executor allocation bounds are errors. Files are limited to 1 MiB. Resource memory and overhead are integer MiB; CPU values are positive whole cores. For dynamic allocation, an omitted initial count defaults to the minimum (or zero when only a maximum is given).

Settings under spec match the Python SDK names: image, app_path, namespace, service_account, class_name, packages, app_arguments, spark_conf, driver_resources, executor_resources, executor_instances, image_pull_policy, app_waiter, startup_timeout, max_runtime, ui_reverse_proxy, driver/executor node selectors, labels and annotations, driver_env_vars_from_secrets, and executor_pod_template or executor_pod_template_path, plus driver_pod_template and driver_container_name. Secrets are referenced by name; literal secret payloads are deliberately not a job-file field.

spec.spark_conf accepts spark.kubernetes.driverEnv.NAME for driver environment variables. See driver environment variables for conversion, precedence and Secret handling.

Job submission defaults to no_wait, namespace default, service account spark, two executors, and 1 CPU/1024 MiB memory/512 MiB overhead per pod. Job files do not inherit SPARK_ON_K8S_* submission defaults. Set spec.app_waiter: wait or log to wait, and optionally bound CLI waiting with --timeout SECONDS.

spec.max_runtime (whole seconds, at most 30 days) makes Kubernetes stop the driver that long after its pod starts, even if nothing is still watching the run; the plan shows it as the driver pod's activeDeadlineSeconds. A profile can set it to null to remove a base value. See driver lifetime limits for what Kubernetes does to the driver, executors and owned objects.

A driver or executor template may be a Pod mapping, inline YAML, or a .yaml/.yml filename. Local filenames resolve relative to the job file, not the current directory. executor_pod_template_path is a path visible to Spark, not a local file to upload. Application paths are also interpreted by Spark; local Python files are not bundled.

Choose cluster credentials explicitly when needed:

kubernetes:
  config_file: ./kubeconfig
  context: development

Or use kubernetes: {in_cluster: true} inside Kubernetes. The default uses the standard kubeconfig/current context. A custom kubeconfig filename resolves relative to the job file. Never commit kubeconfig credentials to source control.

docs.title: Python and Airflow
docs.text:
from spark_on_k8s.jobs import JobSpec

job = JobSpec.from_file("job.yaml", profile="production")
preview = job.plan().to_dict()
driver_pod = job.submit()

The same definition works with both supported Airflow versions:

from spark_on_k8s.airflow.operators import SparkOnK8SOperator
from spark_on_k8s.jobs import JobSpec

job = JobSpec.from_file("job.yaml", profile="production")
run = SparkOnK8SOperator(
    task_id="daily_etl",
    kubernetes_conn_id="spark_cluster",
    **job.to_operator_kwargs(),
)

For Airflow, use a job without a kubernetes section: the operator connection owns credentials. Set app_waiter to wait or log when downstream tasks depend on completion, and use the operator's existing deferrable option when appropriate.

docs.title: Validate every environment
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s job validate job.yaml --all-profiles --output json

This validates the base definition and every named profile, including relative pod-template files, without connecting to Kubernetes. The result lists each profile and returns a nonzero exit code if any fails. The JSON result has schema_version, operation: "job_validate", valid, a profiles list of {profile, valid, error} entries and a top-level error. Each failure is an object with code (invalid_job for an invalid definition, read_error for an unreadable job or template file) and message; the top-level error repeats the first failure and is null exactly when the exit code is zero. --profile and --all-profiles are mutually exclusive. Run this in your configuration CI; validating only a development profile does not validate production overrides.

docs.title: Review CPU and memory requests
docs.text:
Plans include a capacity summary derived from the generated driver requests and effective Spark configuration. It shows executor heap, explicit overhead, off-heap and PySpark allocations, executor counts and minimum/initial/maximum CPU and memory requests. Memory is reported in MiB and CPU in cores.

spark-on-k8s job plan job.yaml --profile production --output json \
  --max-cpu 12 --max-memory-mib 32768

Optional budgets fail when a requested maximum exceeds the limit or cannot be calculated. Executor templates, driver sidecars/init containers, invalid resource settings and unbounded dynamic allocation are called out instead of being silently estimated. The manifest remains the source for detailed review. Admission mutation, quota availability, scheduling placement, storage, GPUs and runtime-created resource profiles are outside this estimate. This is a request budget check, not a pricing estimate or an admission controller.

For promotion, select the cluster as well as the namespace:

profiles:
  production:
    kubernetes:
      context: production-cluster
    spec:
      namespace: analytics-production

The context name is a reference to externally managed credentials, not a secret payload. Namespace selection alone does not select a cluster. For Airflow, omit this Kubernetes section and use the reviewed Airflow connection instead.

docs.title: Jupyter notebooks on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Create a Spark Connect server from a local Jupyter notebook, run DataFrame and SQL queries on Kubernetes executors, reconnect after a planned kernel restart, and delete the recorded server. The notebook uses the existing server lifecycle SDK and independent Connect sessions; Jupyter runs on your machine.

Use the canonical example at examples/jupyter/spark_connect.ipynb with notebook_support.py beside it. A shorter private server quickstart in the same directory adds an image pull Secret, a Secret-backed credential and a node selector. You can also download the notebook bundle, notebook, quickstart, or helper. These downloads are built from the same source as the selected documentation version. The bundle contains both notebooks and the helper; it does not include credentials or an environment.

docs.title: Prepare the cluster and client
docs.text:
Server provisioning is available in the current source and may not be in your installed PyPI release. Follow current-source installation and use a checkout matching the documentation version. Run the following commands from that checkout's root. The example does not create a cluster, namespace, service account, catalog or storage.

  • An administrator must prepare an existing namespace and Spark driver service account with permission to create and manage executors. See the namespace setup guidance.
  • Your Kubernetes identity needs access to create, read and delete the driver and Services, inspect executor resources and logs, and use pod exec and port-forward. The example's startup helper uses exec to wait for the Spark listener before opening a tunnel.
  • Install uv, Git and kubectl locally. Use Python 3.12 for this example; the optional Connect client supports Python 3.11–3.14. Local Spark and Java are not required by the thin pyspark-client.
  • Choose a Spark 4 image available to the cluster, for its architecture, containing the exact Connect server JAR. The commands below select Spark 4.3.0; the integration workflow also selects 4.0.5. Use the client/server pair selected below and consult the compatibility guidance.

The server exposes plaintext gRPC through a private ClusterIP Service. The example opens a notebook-owned tunnel bound only to 127.0.0.1; it does not expose a public endpoint. Use a trusted development cluster. Server authentication, TLS, data authorization and network policy remain administrator responsibilities. Kubernetes access does not provide isolation between clients of a shared server.

docs.title: Start an isolated Jupyter kernel
docs.text:
On macOS or Linux, create a separate environment using the repository's locked notebook dependencies and Connect extra. The optional JupyterLab frontend is installed into that same environment; it is not needed by the automated notebook runner.

This notebook uses these client/server pairs:

Spark server Thin client 4.3.0 (default) pyspark-client==4.3.0 4.0.5 pyspark-client==4.0.5

A newer client API can require a newer server even when a simple query works. In validation, client 4.3.0 passed readiness and range queries against server 4.0.5, but createDataFrame from local rows failed because that server lacked spark.sql.session.localRelationSizeLimit. This specific failure is why the notebook checks matching versions; it does not establish that every operation across different versions is incompatible.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=.venv-notebook uv sync --python 3.12 --locked \
  --no-default-groups --group notebook --extra connect
uv pip install --python .venv-notebook/bin/python 'jupyterlab==4.6.6'
uv pip install --python .venv-notebook/bin/python --no-deps 'pyspark-client==4.3.0'
uv pip check --python .venv-notebook/bin/python
.venv-notebook/bin/python -c 'from importlib.metadata import version; client = version("pyspark-client"); assert client == "4.3.0", client; print("Connect client:", client)'

export IPYTHONDIR="$PWD/.venv-notebook/jupyter-state/ipython"
export JUPYTER_CONFIG_DIR="$PWD/.venv-notebook/jupyter-state/config"
export JUPYTER_DATA_DIR="$PWD/.venv-notebook/jupyter-state/data"
export JUPYTER_RUNTIME_DIR="$PWD/.venv-notebook/jupyter-state/runtime"
export JUPYTER_PATH="$PWD/.venv-notebook/share/jupyter"
mkdir -p "$IPYTHONDIR" "$JUPYTER_CONFIG_DIR" "$JUPYTER_DATA_DIR" "$JUPYTER_RUNTIME_DIR"
.venv-notebook/bin/python -m ipykernel install --prefix "$PWD/.venv-notebook" \
  --name spark-connect-notebook --display-name 'Spark Connect (Python 3.12)'

The kernel registration and notebook state stay in this environment instead of a user-wide kernel installation. Jupyter can still discover other configured kernels; select Spark Connect (Python 3.12) in the notebook. An existing Jupyter frontend can also use this kernel when configured with the same kernel search path. See the upstream kernel installation guide and Jupyter directory settings.

Do not install full pyspark alongside pyspark-client in this environment: both provide the pyspark Python import namespace. A later uv sync can restore the locked client version and remove the separately installed JupyterLab frontend. Both version choices explicitly select the client after the locked sync, matching the CI matrix even if a future lockfile selects a newer client. After resyncing, reapply the selected client version, reinstall the frontend, and check versions before launching a new kernel. Use the environment's executables directly so an implicit sync does not undo that choice. Normal source use is editable. CI installs the built wheel and checks the actual kernel interpreter and package location separately.

Set explicit cluster settings before launching Jupyter:

export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_KUBECONFIG=/absolute/path/to/kubeconfig
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_CONTEXT=your-kubernetes-context
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_NAMESPACE=your-prepared-namespace
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SERVICE_ACCOUNT=spark
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SPARK_VERSION=4.3.0
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_IMAGE=apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SERVER_JAR=local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_ARTIFACT_DIR="$PWD/downloads/jupyter-results"

To choose Spark 4.0.5 instead, override the thin client in this same isolated environment after the locked sync and before starting Jupyter:

uv pip install --python .venv-notebook/bin/python --no-deps 'pyspark-client==4.0.5'
uv pip check --python .venv-notebook/bin/python
.venv-notebook/bin/python -c 'from importlib.metadata import version; client = version("pyspark-client"); assert client == "4.0.5", client; print("Connect client:", client)'
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SPARK_VERSION=4.0.5
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_IMAGE=apache/spark:4.0.5-scala2.13-java17-python3-ubuntu
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SERVER_JAR=local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.0.5.jar

If changing an already running example, finish its server cleanup and stop its kernel first.
