Use a new artifact directory for the new run after confirming that cleanup; do not overwrite or discard the previous server receipt. Changing a Python package on disk does not replace a client already imported into a kernel.

Launch the notebook with the selected pair:

.venv-notebook/bin/jupyter lab examples/jupyter/spark_connect.ipynb

The helper reads these settings without changing your current Kubernetes context. When SPARK_NOTEBOOK_SERVER_JAR is unset, the helper derives local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-<version>.jar from the selected Spark version; override it for a different image layout. SPARK_NOTEBOOK_IMAGE_PULL_POLICY defaults to IfNotPresent; use Never only when the image is already loaded on the cluster's nodes. The notebook requests one small executor; adjust capacity for your workload rather than treating the example's resource settings as production sizing.

For the download, extract both files into a writable directory and open its spark_connect.ipynb using the same environment. Keep the helper beside the notebook. Keep the artifact directory until resource cleanup is confirmed; it contains the server receipt needed to reconnect or delete safely.

docs.title: Run, restart and reconnect
docs.text:
Run the numbered notebook sections in order:

  1. Sections 1–3: inspect the kernel and settings, create the server, save its receipt, and open the loopback tunnel. Query readiness performs a real action and verifies the remote application against the receipt. A Running pod alone is not query readiness.
  2. Section 4: run distributed DataFrame and SQL queries and display a bounded pandas result. The range sum is 49,995,000. The result table has books and games, each with quantity 3 and revenue 45.0. The notebook compares the reported executor hostnames with actual owned Kubernetes executor pods.
  3. Section 5: open an independent session, verify that temporary views and SQL settings do not leak into it, and recover from an intentionally invalid query.
  4. Section 6: close the client sessions and tunnel, save restart evidence and leave the server running. Use Kernel → Restart Kernel. Do not use Run All across this boundary.
  5. Section 7: resume in the new kernel. It restores the recorded server, establishes a new tunnel and session, and checks the same application and driver UID. The query returns the same sum. The previous session's temporary view is absent and must be recreated.
  6. Section 8: explicitly delete the server and wait for owned resources to disappear. The final notebook-result.json records status: passed, kernel_restart_verified: true, and owned_resources_remaining: [].

The creation cell refuses to create a second server when its receipt or pending creation guard exists. Do not delete these files to bypass the guard. Reconnect to the known server or complete its cleanup first. If receipt publication fails after creation, retain the full identity printed by the cell and the available server handle; resources can still exist.

The notebook's helper manages the tunnel separately from the SDK. Closing a session, tunnel or notebook does not delete the server. A readiness timeout also leaves the server running. Keep the receipt and inspect the existing resources before attempting another creation. For your own servers, ConnectServerConfig accepts an optional max_runtime in seconds so Kubernetes stops a forgotten server's driver; see the server guide.

docs.title: Private server quickstart
docs.text:
examples/jupyter/private_connect_quickstart.ipynb creates a server whose image is pulled with an image pull Secret, whose driver and executors receive a credential as the QUICKSTART_API_TOKEN variable from a Secret key, and whose pods run on selected nodes. It previews the server offline, waits for a real query, runs a small query, checks that the variable is set on the executors without returning its value, and deletes the server. It has no kernel-restart boundary. The settings are described in private images, credentials and node placement.

The notebook contains no credentials. An administrator creates the Secrets in the namespace first; the notebook only references them by name. For example, reading values from files rather than typing them into a shell:

kubectl --namespace "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_NAMESPACE" create secret generic private-registry \
  --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=./registry-config.json
kubectl --namespace "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_NAMESPACE" create secret generic notebook-credentials \
  --from-file=api-token=./api-token.txt

Use the same kernel and SPARK_NOTEBOOK_* cluster settings as the main example, with an image that the pull Secret can pull, then set the references and launch it:

export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_PULL_SECRET=private-registry
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_CREDENTIAL=notebook-credentials:api-token
export SPARK_NOTEBOOK_NODE_SELECTOR=kubernetes.io/os=linux  # Or your pool's KEY=VALUE label.
.venv-notebook/bin/jupyter lab examples/jupyter/private_connect_quickstart.ipynb

The default node selector matches every Linux node. Its receipt is quickstart-receipt.json in the artifact directory, separate from the main example's receipt; use it with connect server status and connect server delete if the notebook stops early. Every client of a server can read its environment variables through queries, so give the server only credentials that all of its users may hold. To install Python libraries on the server and run executors on GPU nodes, see Build an ML image for Spark Connect.

docs.title: Data and session boundaries
docs.text:
Where state lives What survives a notebook kernel restart Notebook variables and local Python objects Nothing in the old kernel; rerun imports and recreate variables Connect session temporary views and session settings A new session does not inherit them The Kubernetes driver and executor resources They continue until explicitly deleted or failed; the receipt identifies them Shared catalog and durable data Only what your separately configured catalog and storage preserve

Paths passed to Spark refer to the server/executor environment. Local notebook files, installed Python packages and credentials are not automatically copied to executor pods. Use shared storage reachable by both driver and executors, and install required connectors and worker dependencies in the appropriate image. Collect only bounded results with toPandas() or collect(): those results are transferred into the notebook process.

Spark Connect exposes DataFrame and SQL operations; classic SparkContext/RDD APIs are unavailable. The example proves these generated-data operations and notebook rendering, not every Python UDF, extension, storage connector or production catalog. See the upstream Spark Connect quickstart.

docs.title: Recover without notebook variables
docs.text:
The restart exercise deliberately closes sessions and the tunnel before restarting the kernel. It uses phase-one.json to prove that the kernel changed and the server did not. This is a planned restart test, not abrupt-crash recovery coverage.

If the kernel exits before that evidence file is written, server status and deletion still need only server-receipt.json and your cluster credentials. From the checkout, use the same environment and explicit cluster settings:

.venv-notebook/bin/spark-on-k8s connect server status \
  "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_ARTIFACT_DIR/server-receipt.json" \
  --kubeconfig "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_KUBECONFIG" --context "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_CONTEXT" --output json
.venv-notebook/bin/spark-on-k8s connect server delete \
  "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_ARTIFACT_DIR/server-receipt.json" \
  --kubeconfig "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_KUBECONFIG" --context "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_CONTEXT" --output json

Deletion requests cleanup; keep the receipt until the resources are observed absent. If you no longer know which artifact directory belongs to a server, for example after several forgotten notebooks, list the servers and their ages in the namespace, then follow finding forgotten servers to stop the ones nobody uses:

.venv-notebook/bin/spark-on-k8s connect server list --namespace "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_NAMESPACE" \
  --kubeconfig "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_KUBECONFIG" --context "$SPARK_NOTEBOOK_CONTEXT"

To continue work instead, use the receipt-only recovery instructions at the end of the notebook: restore ConnectServerHandle from the receipt's inner server mapping, open a new tunnel, verify readiness, and create a new session. That workflow does not require the planned-restart evidence file.

An abruptly terminated kernel can leave a tunnel process running. Inspect the example's tunnel process records and stop only the process you confirm belongs to that notebook; do not assume a recorded PID still identifies the same process. The SDK does not own tunnels. A failed driver also is not automatically replaced: inspect its recorded status and follow server recovery before creating a replacement with a new receipt.

Problem Next action Wrong kernel or import failure Select the registered kernel and check its printed interpreter and package versions Readiness warnings contains version_skew Install the client for the server's major.minor version from the client/server pairs, then restart the kernel Pending driver or listener timeout Inspect scheduling, image/JAR, service-account permissions and driver logs; retain the receipt Lost tunnel or readiness timeout Repair connectivity and retry readiness for the recorded server; do not create a duplicate Receipt or pending creation guard already exists Inspect the saved/partial identity and reconnect or finish cleanup; an uncertain response is not absence Same-name resource has a different UID Stop; inspect the ownership conflict instead of deleting by name

docs.title: Automated coverage
docs.text:
The Spark Connect Kubernetes workflow executes this exact notebook through a real IPython kernel, restarts that kernel at the marked boundary, and checks distributed execution, rendered table output, session separation, failure recovery and cleanup. It uses a built wheel on disposable kind clusters with matching client/server pairs 4.0.5/4.0.5 and 4.3.0/4.3.0. Its evidence includes the executed notebook and JSON results. The same workflow runs the private server quickstart against test Secrets it creates: it checks the executor pods' node selector, pull Secret and Secret reference, the variable's presence in executor tasks and cleanup, and that the random test value appears in no notebook output or saved evidence. The kind nodes already hold the image, so the pull Secret is referenced but never used for a pull.

This automation covers notebook kernel execution and output. It does not click through JupyterLab's browser UI, test arbitrary extensions, or simulate an abrupt kernel/driver crash. Follow development validation for the runner and workflow; a failed or unexecuted matrix row is not passing runtime evidence.

docs.title: Know which identity is acting
docs.text:
The local client uses its selected kubeconfig/context; the API submits with its own Kubernetes identity. Driver and executor service accounts govern workload access to Kubernetes and external storage. An Airflow connection selects the submitter identity and is separate from the task UI's service credentials. A gateway authenticates callers; it does not make a shared API service account act as each caller. Use separate API deployments and namespaces for separate trust boundaries. Do not treat namespace filtering as tenant authorization.

The convenience namespace setup helper currently creates a cluster-scoped binding to Kubernetes' edit role. Administrators should provision a namespace-scoped RoleBinding for production deployments instead. Neither the chart nor this library is a cloud IAM administrator. Prefer workload identity and external Secret references to literal credentials in job files.

docs.title: Diagnose evidence before changing resources
docs.text:
Record the cluster context, namespace, application ID and driver UID with your incident. Distinguish application fetch time, diagnostic collection time and Kubernetes event time. Refresh before acting on an old view. Retained history can say Running after an application disappears; it is not current health. Incomplete reads, missing events and empty logs do not prove health or justify resubmission. Compare current and previous container termination reasons, scheduler events and driver/executor logs before increasing resources.

Use namespace-scoped commands, substituting only identifiers from the receipt:

kubectl --context CONTEXT -n NAMESPACE get pod DRIVER -o wide
kubectl --context CONTEXT -n NAMESPACE describe pod DRIVER
kubectl --context CONTEXT -n NAMESPACE logs DRIVER -c driver
kubectl --context CONTEXT -n NAMESPACE get events --field-selector involvedObject.uid=DRIVER_UID

Do not replay data writes, delete shared PVCs or repair streaming checkpoints based only on a pod failure. Keep images, job definitions and external data recovery procedures independently versioned.

docs.title: Bound and clean up abandoned runs
docs.text: A killed client, CI runner or worker cannot stop what it submitted. For runs with a known upper duration, set max_runtime so Kubernetes stops the driver itself. Finished drivers keep their logs, Services, ConfigMaps and Secrets until deleted. Review spark-on-k8s apps prune --namespace NAMESPACE --older-than SECONDS before adding --delete: deleting a driver also removes its logs and owned objects, so collect the evidence above first. Active drivers are only selected with --include-active.

docs.title: Back up optional history consistently
docs.text:
The SQLite history store is an operational index, not a job queue or durable source of submission truth. Restrict database and backup access because labels and operational metadata may be sensitive. A live database may use WAL files; copying only the .sqlite3 file while it is being written is not a safe backup. Use SQLite's online backup API (or stop all writers before a filesystem copy):

import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

source = Path("/var/lib/spark-on-k8s/runs.sqlite3").resolve()
backup = Path("/secure-backups/runs.sqlite3").resolve()
with sqlite3.connect(source.as_uri() + "?mode=ro", uri=True) as original:
    with sqlite3.connect(backup) as target:
        original.backup(target)
        assert target.execute("PRAGMA integrity_check").fetchone() == ("ok",)

Choose a new protected destination and test restoration with the exact package version in a disposable deployment. Confirm records and retention settings, then verify live Kubernetes state separately. There is no automatic migration, restore endpoint or claim of multi-writer/high-availability database support.

docs.title: Qualify an additional integration
docs.text:
Cloud identity, table formats, accelerators and new orchestrators need a named owner and a reproducible acceptance test before joining the supported matrix. Pin image and connector versions. Prove work runs in executors, verify actual output and a controlled failure, and exercise interruption/restart semantics. For storage, check namespace, mount ownership and persistence across driver replacement. For streaming/lakehouse jobs, distinguish pod recovery from checkpoint correctness, table commits, ordering and replay guarantees.

Prefer a small recipe using the existing SDK and receipts over another control plane; see the ecosystem recipes. The Spark Operator assessor reports unsupported source fields; it does not silently translate unknown Spark Operator semantics. OpenLineage reports and Airflow run correlation are optional evidence, not proof that every data write committed. Deployment examples do not establish arbitrary multi-cloud or multi-tenant isolation guarantees.

docs.title: Audit events and metrics
docs.text:
The API writes one structured audit event for each remote plan or submit, kill and delete request, and for each request refused by bearer authentication or the namespace scope. An event identifies a request: its route, target, outcome and the address it came from. It does not identify a person. The API has no user identity, and the shared operator bearer is the same for every caller. Run history is a polled metadata index and is not an audit trail either.

Every HTTP response carries an X-Request-ID header with a new random ID generated by the server. The API ignores an X-Request-ID sent by the client. To correlate with gateway logs, have the gateway log the upstream response header.

docs.title: Configure the audit log
docs.text:
Variable Default Meaning SPARK_ON_K8S_AUDIT_LOG_ENABLED true Write audit events to the spark_on_k8s.audit logger; true or false. SPARK_ON_K8S_AUDIT_IDENTITY_HEADER empty A request header that a trusted gateway sets, such as X-Auth-Request-User, recorded as unverified_identity.

The log is enabled by default, because an event has to be recorded before you need it. Events are written only for the audited operations and for refusals, so each refusal adds one line next to the access-log line the server already writes for it. Invalid values prevent startup. Credential headers such as Authorization and Cookie cannot be used as the identity header.

spark-on-k8s api start writes each event to stdout as one JSON object per line. Each worker process writes its own events. Unlike the server's other logs, these lines do not depend on --log-level. If the deployment already configures logging handlers for spark_on_k8s.audit or its parent loggers, for example when another server embeds the application, the API sends the events to those handlers instead.

docs.title: Event schema
docs.text:
Events have audit_version: 1. A compatible version can add fields. A change to or removal of an existing field increments the version.

Field Value time UTC time, to the millisecond, when the request finished. event job.plan, job.submit, app.kill, app.delete, or access for a refused request to any other route. outcome succeeded, denied, rejected, failed or unknown; see below. code ok, or the error.code from the response's error body. status The HTTP status. A refused WebSocket handshake is recorded as 403. request_id The value of the X-Request-ID response header. method The HTTP method, or WEBSOCKET. route The route template, such as /app/{namespace}/{app_id}, never the raw path or query string. Authentication happens before routing, so a request it refuses has a null route unless it targets an audited operation. client The client address that the ASGI server reports; see the limits below. unverified_identity The configured gateway header, if the request has exactly one; otherwise null. namespace, app_id, driver_pod, driver_uid The target, when known; otherwise null.

Outcomes describe what the API did, not what the Spark application did:

  • succeeded: the API completed the request. A submission created the driver resources and a kill sent the termination signal. Neither means the Spark work succeeded.
  • denied: HTTP 401 or 403. The request was refused by authentication, the namespace scope or the submission policy, or Kubernetes RBAC refused the API's service account (code forbidden).
  • rejected: another 4xx response, such as invalid_job, application_not_found, application_state, invalid_request for an identifier Kubernetes refused, or client_disconnected for an upload the client abandoned. The API changed nothing.
  • failed: a server error during a plan, which creates nothing.
  • unknown: a server or Kubernetes failure during a submit, kill or delete. The resources may have been created, signalled or deleted anyway. An uncertain result does not mean nothing happened: inspect the recorded run before retrying.

After a submission is admitted, its event records the generated namespace, app_id and driver_pod, even if Kubernetes fails afterwards. It records driver_uid once the driver pod exists. For denied or invalid documents, these fields are null. A plan records only its namespace, because the identity in a plan is illustrative and no run exists. Kill and delete events record the target from the request path. access events record the refused namespace and any application identifiers in the path.

{"audit_version":1,"time":"2026-11-09T10:15:02.418Z","event":"job.submit","outcome":"succeeded","code":"ok","status":201,"request_id":"6f1c2a9e0b5d4e7f8a3b2c1d0e9f8a7b","method":"POST","route":"/jobs/v1/submit","client":"10.42.0.17","unverified_identity":"alice@example.com","namespace":"analytics","app_id":"report-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef","driver_pod":"report-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef-driver","driver_uid":"5bdceeb0-7fa8-4f72-823b-80f26e6195c4"}
{"audit_version":1,"time":"2026-11-09T10:16:40.007Z","event":"app.kill","outcome":"unknown","code":"internal_error","status":500,"request_id":"0d8e4f1a2b3c4d5e6f708192a3b4c5d6","method":"PATCH","route":"/app/{namespace}/{app_id}","client":"10.42.0.17","unverified_identity":null,"namespace":"analytics","app_id":"report-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef","driver_pod":null,"driver_uid":null}
{"audit_version":1,"time":"2026-11-09T10:17:11.250Z","event":"access","outcome":"denied","code":"namespace_forbidden","status":403,"request_id":"9a8b7c6d5e4f40312a1b0c9d8e7f6a5b","method":"GET","route":"/webserver/ui/{path:path}","client":"10.42.0.17","unverified_identity":null,"namespace":"kube-system","app_id":null,"driver_pod":null,"driver_uid":null}
{"audit_version":1,"time":"2026-11-09T10:18:30.912Z","event":"access","outcome":"denied","code":"unauthorized","status":401,"request_id":"47c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8e9f0a1b2c3d4e5","method":"GET","route":null,"client":"10.42.0.9","unverified_identity":null,"namespace":null,"app_id":null,"driver_pod":null,"driver_uid":null}

Events never include these values: authorization or cookie headers, bearer tokens, query strings, request or response bodies, job documents (including arguments, images and Spark configuration), Kubernetes response bodies, or exception text. Names in the target fields come from the workload or the request and can themselves be sensitive. Restrict access to these logs as you would for other API logs.

docs.title: Limits of the audit log
docs.text:
• Logs are the only transport. Collecting the logs, sending them off the node, retaining them, controlling access and protecting their integrity are the job of your log pipeline. Events are written as each request finishes. They can be lost if the process stops or the node fails before collection. The log is not tamper-evident and is not a durable audit store. A failure to write the log does not fail the request.
  • The client address is the network peer. client is the address the ASGI server reports. Behind a gateway or ingress, this is usually the gateway's address. The server reports another address only when its trusted-proxy setting accepts X-Forwarded-For from that peer. Uvicorn, which spark-on-k8s api start runs, accepts these headers only from the addresses in FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS (default 127.0.0.1). Keep that list limited to your gateways.
  • The gateway identity is not verified. The API records the configured header but does not authenticate it. The value is meaningful only if the gateway authenticates users, removes any copy of the header sent by the client, and the backend cannot be reached except through the gateway. If the header appears more than once, the API records null. Every bearer holder has the same permissions: the recorded identity helps attribute a request, but does not authorize it.
  • Kubernetes sees the API. Kubernetes audit logs record the API's service account as the actor. To find the matching API event, compare the time, namespace and application ID.
  • WebSocket handshakes and responses that the ASGI server writes itself, such as its concurrency-limit 503, do not carry X-Request-ID.

docs.title: Operation metrics
docs.text:
When metrics are enabled (SPARK_ON_K8S_METRICS_ENABLED=true), /metrics also serves these counters:

  • spark_on_k8s_api_audit_events_total{event,outcome,code}: increases by one for each audit event, including when the audit log is disabled.
  • spark_on_k8s_api_kubernetes_errors_total{status_class}: counts Kubernetes API error responses (4xx, 5xx, or other for a response without a usable status) received while serving kill, delete, submit, console, log-stream and application list requests. Readiness probes are not counted. The run-history collector reports its own spark_on_k8s_collection_failures_total. Connection failures and timeouts that return no Kubernetes response are not counted here. They appear as failed or unknown outcomes.

Label values come only from the fixed event and outcome names and the API's own error codes. Labels never contain a namespace, application ID, route or client. A namespace label would have no bound with the * scope, and refused namespaces are chosen by the caller, so any value in a request could create a new series. Use the audit log for per-namespace detail. A series appears after its first event.

The counters are kept in the memory of each worker process and reset when that worker restarts. The API image runs four workers by default (SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WORKERS). Each scrape reaches one of them, so successive samples can come from different workers, and rate() can mistake the differences for counter resets. If you alert on these counters, run one worker per pod (SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WORKERS=1). Alternatively, count the audit lines in your log pipeline, which receives the events of every worker. For example, with one worker:

sum by (code) (increase(spark_on_k8s_api_audit_events_total{outcome="denied"}[10m]))
increase(spark_on_k8s_api_audit_events_total{event="job.submit",outcome="unknown"}[15m]) > 0
increase(spark_on_k8s_api_kubernetes_errors_total{status_class="5xx"}[5m]) > 0

docs.title: Authorization review matrix
docs.text:
Surface Authenticator / authorizer Effective cluster identity Actor attribution Local SDK/CLI Kubernetes credentials and RBAC Selected local or in-cluster identity Kubernetes audit configuration Standalone internal API External network/gateway controls API service account No built-in end-user principal Remote-enabled API and metrics Shared operator bearer and admission policy API service account Shared operator, not a tenant identity Airflow task tab Airflow session, task permissions, ownership checks Configured Spark API service identity Airflow task binding; separate API has its own controls Airflow DAG execution Airflow Kubernetes connection and cluster RBAC Worker/triggerer connection identity Task execution and Kubernetes audit configuration

Disabling Airflow tab writes only disables browser mutations; it does not prevent DAG tasks from submitting workloads. Gateway TLS alone does not establish all these boundaries. See browser and gateway checks for prefixes, static assets, HTTP, WebSockets and direct-backend isolation.

Recovery restores recorded observations through the backup point, then collection resumes from currently visible pods. It cannot reconstruct deleted pods or intermediate statuses during an outage. Readiness indicates current service health, not historical completeness. Diagnostics classify infrastructure evidence, not workload efficiency; neither a successful pod nor an empty finding list means a Spark job is tuned.

docs.title: Ecosystem recipes
docs.text:
These recipes combine job files with common Kubernetes and Spark ecosystem tools. They reuse existing SparkJob settings and well-established Kubernetes or Spark configuration; nothing here adds a controller or a new integration package. They are configuration starting points, not part of the tested support matrix: this project's CI does not run a CronJob, a batch scheduler, an OpenLineage backend or an object store. Pin versions, run the recipe in a staging namespace and check the actual output before relying on it. See support boundaries for what the project owns.

Never write credentials into job files, ConfigMaps or spark_conf: Spark properties appear in driver arguments and the Spark UI. Use Kubernetes Secrets or workload identity as shown below.

docs.title: Schedule with a Kubernetes CronJob
docs.text: Use this when a schedule does not justify an Airflow deployment, for example to replace a ScheduledSparkApplication. A CronJob starts a small submitter pod that runs spark-on-k8s job submit, waits for the application and exits with the automation exit code. For dependencies between jobs, backfills or retries with history, prefer the Airflow integration.

docs.title: Submitter image and identity
docs.text:
Any image with the spark-on-k8s package works; the submitter does not need Spark or Java. Pin the version you validated and publish the image by digest:

FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir "spark-on-k8s==VERSION"
USER 10001
ENTRYPOINT ["spark-on-k8s"]

The submitter's service account is separate from the driver's service account (spec.service_account in the job file), which creates executors. Grant the submitter only what submission and waiting use, in the job's namespace:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: spark-submitter
  namespace: reporting
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: spark-submitter
  namespace: reporting
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["create", "get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["services"]
    verbs: ["create"]
  # ConfigMaps hold pod templates and are owned by the driver after creation.
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    verbs: ["create", "patch", "delete"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: spark-submitter
  namespace: reporting
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: spark-submitter
    namespace: reporting
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: spark-submitter

These rules follow the API calls the client makes for a job file without secret_values; confirm them with your cluster's audit logs. Add delete on pods only if the same identity also runs app delete for cleanup.

docs.title: Job file and CronJob
docs.text:
Make the submission wait so that the CronJob's concurrency policy applies to Spark runs, and select in-cluster credentials with a profile:

apiVersion: spark-on-k8s/v1
kind: SparkJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-report
spec:
  image: registry.example.com/team/report:1.0
  app_path: local:///opt/spark/work-dir/report.py
  namespace: reporting
  service_account: spark
  app_waiter: wait
  startup_timeout: 600
profiles:
  in-cluster:
    kubernetes:
      in_cluster: true

kubectl -n reporting create configmap nightly-report-job --from-file=job.yaml

Put pod-template files referenced by the job into the same ConfigMap so that relative paths still resolve next to job.yaml.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-report
  namespace: reporting
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  timeZone: Europe/Paris
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 600
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 5
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 0
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: spark-submitter
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: submit
              image: registry.example.com/platform/spark-on-k8s-cli@sha256:DIGEST
              args:
                - job
                - submit
                - /jobs/job.yaml
                - --profile
                - in-cluster
                - --output
                - json
                - --receipt-file
                - /receipts/$(POD_NAME).json
              env:
                - name: POD_NAME
                  valueFrom:
                    fieldRef:
                      fieldPath: metadata.name
              volumeMounts:
                - name: job
                  mountPath: /jobs
                  readOnly: true
                - name: receipts
                  mountPath: /receipts
          volumes:
            - name: job
              configMap:
                name: nightly-report-job
            - name: receipts
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: spark-receipts

The receipt is written before waiting starts, to a new file named after the submitter pod, so a crashed or deleted submitter still leaves the run's namespace, application ID and driver UID. Use a volume the container user can write; the JSON result on stdout (kept in the pod log while Kubernetes retains the Job) carries the same identity. Resume observation or cancel from any machine with access to the cluster:

spark-on-k8s app wait --namespace reporting --app-id "$APP_ID" --output json
spark-on-k8s app cancel --receipt nightly-report-29000000-abcde.json --output json

docs.title: Failure and concurrency semantics
docs.text:
• A receipt is not data success. Exit code 0 with app_waiter: wait means the application reached Succeeded; your application still owns output correctness. Exit 3 means it failed; 5 and 6 mean observation timed out or the outcome is unknown, and the application may still be running.
  • Retries resubmit. Kubernetes retries a failed Job pod by starting a new pod, which submits a new application. backoffLimit: 0 avoids duplicate runs after an ambiguous failure. To retry only confirmed Spark failures, add a pod failure policy that fails the Job for every exit code except 3, and raise backoffLimit. Make outputs idempotent before allowing any retry.
  • Timeouts do not cancel. --timeout, Job activeDeadlineSeconds and pod deletion stop the submitter only. The driver pod is not owned by the Job, so the application keeps running and a later schedule can overlap it despite concurrencyPolicy: Forbid. Cancel explicitly with app cancel --receipt.
  • Forbid covers waiting submitters. With app_waiter: no_wait, the submitter exits after submission and concurrencyPolicy no longer limits Spark runs. Replace deletes the waiting submitter, not the running application.
  • Schedules are best effort. Kubernetes can occasionally start a scheduled Job twice or skip one, for example after controller downtime past startingDeadlineSeconds. Design the job to tolerate a repeated or missed run.
  • History limits apply to submitters. CronJob history limits delete Job and submitter pods, not Spark drivers. Remove finished drivers with spark-on-k8s app delete; executors and client-created objects are owned by the driver pod.

docs.title: Run under a batch scheduler
docs.text:
Batch schedulers such as Volcano, Apache YuniKorn and Kueue queue pods by reading pod fields, labels and annotations. spark-on-k8s creates the driver pod directly, and the running driver creates executor pods through Spark. Both pods must therefore carry the scheduler's settings: the driver through driver_pod_template (or the driver label and annotation maps), executors through executor_pod_template (or the executor maps).

apiVersion: spark-on-k8s/v1
kind: SparkJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-features
spec:
  image: registry.example.com/ml/features:3.2
  app_path: local:///opt/app/build_features.py
  namespace: ml
  startup_timeout: 1800
  driver_pod_template:
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    spec:
      schedulerName: SCHEDULER_NAME
      priorityClassName: batch-low
      containers:
        - name: driver
  executor_pod_template:
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    spec:
      schedulerName: SCHEDULER_NAME
      priorityClassName: batch-low
      containers:
        - name: executor
  driver_labels: {}       # the queue or group labels your scheduler documents
  executor_labels: {}
  driver_annotations: {}  # the queue or group annotations your scheduler documents
  executor_annotations: {}

schedulerName and priorityClassName are standard Kubernetes Pod fields. spark.kubernetes.executor.scheduler.name in spark_conf is an alternative for executors; Spark's driver-side scheduler settings do not apply because the client creates the driver pod. Scheduler names, queue and group label or annotation keys, and whether a scheduler needs a separate group object are scheduler-specific: check your scheduler's documentation for the version you run. Kueue, for example, does not select pods by schedulerName; check how your Kueue version admits plain pods.

Consider these properties of direct submission when designing queues:

  • Executors do not exist when the driver is admitted. They are created later, in batches, and dynamic allocation can add or remove them during the run. Gang scheduling that expects every member up front does not see the executors when it admits the driver; check how your scheduler handles members created later.
  • Spark's built-in Volcano integration creates its pod group while spark-submit creates the driver in cluster mode. That step does not run here. Do not enable Spark's Volcano feature steps unless you have verified that the pod group they reference exists.
  • A queued driver stays Pending. startup_timeout bounds that wait for an observing CLI or SDK caller without deleting the application; the Airflow operator's startup timeout deletes it. Choose a value larger than expected queue time.
  • job plan --output json reports driver and executor CPU and memory requests, which helps size queue quotas. It does not predict admission or placement.

docs.title: Emit lineage with OpenLineage
docs.text:
The OpenLineage Spark integration is a Spark listener that sends run and dataset events from the driver. Configure it through packages and spark_conf, for example in a profile so that uninstrumented runs remain unchanged:

profiles:
  lineage:
    spec:
      packages:
        - io.openlineage:openlineage-spark_2.13:VERSION
      spark_conf:
        spark.extraListeners: io.openlineage.spark.agent.OpenLineageSparkListener
        spark.openlineage.transport.type: http
        spark.openlineage.transport.url: http://marquez.lineage.svc:5000
        spark.openlineage.namespace: analytics

spark-on-k8s job submit job.yaml --profile lineage --output json
  • Choose the artifact matching your image's Scala version (_2.12 or _2.13) and a release that supports your Spark version; check the OpenLineage documentation. A profile replaces the base packages list, so repeat any base packages in it.
  • packages downloads from Maven repositories when the driver starts. For reproducible or offline clusters, bake the jar into the image and add it with spark.jars: local:///..., as the lakehouse starter does with Iceberg.
  • The driver needs network access to the endpoint. Do not put API keys in spark_conf; use the credential options your OpenLineage version documents together with a Kubernetes Secret.
  • Lineage events are optional evidence of what Spark reported reading and writing. They are not proof that a write committed, and spark-on-k8s run history is not lineage.

docs.title: Read and write S3 or MinIO
docs.text:
Spark reads s3a:// paths through Hadoop's S3A connector from the hadoop-aws module. Most Spark images do not include it. Use the hadoop-aws version that matches the Hadoop client bundled with your image (check the hadoop-client-* jars under /opt/spark/jars); it brings the matching AWS SDK bundle.

apiVersion: spark-on-k8s/v1
kind: SparkJob
metadata:
  name: orders-to-minio
spec:
  image: registry.example.com/team/orders:2.1.0
  app_path: local:///opt/spark/work-dir/orders.py
  app_arguments: ["--output", "s3a://warehouse/orders/"]
  namespace: spark
  service_account: spark
  packages:
    - org.apache.hadoop:hadoop-aws:HADOOP_VERSION
  driver_env_vars_from_secrets:
    - minio-credentials
  spark_conf:
    spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.endpoint: https://minio.storage.svc:9000
    spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.path.style.access: "true"
    spark.kubernetes.executor.secretKeyRef.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: minio-credentials:AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
    spark.kubernetes.executor.secretKeyRef.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: minio-credentials:AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY

The Secret minio-credentials must exist in the job's namespace with the keys AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; create it with your secret management tooling rather than literal values in shell history. driver_env_vars_from_secrets exposes every key of the Secret to the driver, and the secretKeyRef properties expose the two keys to each executor. S3A's default credential chain reads these standard environment variables. Both driver and executors read and write data, so both need the credentials.

For AWS S3 with workload identity (for example EKS IAM roles for service accounts), omit the Secret and endpoint settings. Annotate the driver service account as your platform documents, and set the S3A credential provider for the Hadoop version in your image:

spec:
  service_account: spark-s3
  spark_conf:
    # Hadoop 3.4 (AWS SDK v2); Hadoop 3.3 uses com.amazonaws.auth.WebIdentityTokenCredentialsProvider.
    spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.aws.credentials.provider: software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.WebIdentityTokenFileCredentialsProvider

Executors use the driver's service account unless spark.kubernetes.authenticate.executor.serviceAccountName selects another, so the identity applies to both. Check the Hadoop S3A documentation for your version before changing committers, encryption or endpoint settings.

If the image's user has no home directory, set spark.jars.ivy to a writable path such as /tmp/.ivy2 so that packages can be resolved, or bake the jars into the image. job plan redacts sensitive configuration keys and Secret values, but it cannot detect credentials written under unrecognized names.

docs.title: Remote job submission
docs.text:
Remote submission lets an automation runner send an approved SparkJob to the API without loading a local kubeconfig. It is disabled by default. Enabling it also requires bearer authentication for the existing API, dashboard, static assets, proxies and WebSockets. Only the GET/HEAD liveness (/health) and readiness (/ready) probes remain public.

This is an operator API, not a multi-tenant authorization system. Its bearer token grants access to the existing read and management routes as well as admitted submissions. The submission policy restricts new jobs; it does not restrict an authenticated operator's existing list, logs, kill or delete permissions. Use a separate deployment and Kubernetes service account for each trust boundary.

docs.title: Configure the server
docs.text:
Install the api extra and configure the server's Kubernetes credentials as usual. Requests cannot supply a kubeconfig, context, client configuration or cluster endpoint. Create a random token, store it in a restricted file or Kubernetes Secret, and mount a policy file. Do not commit either deployment credentials or tokens to source control.

export SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_ENABLED=true
export SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_TOKEN_FILE=/run/secrets/submission-token
export SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_POLICY_FILE=/etc/spark-on-k8s/submission-policy.json
spark-on-k8s api start

The token must contain at least 32 printable ASCII characters without spaces; use a cryptographically random value such as one generated by secrets.token_urlsafe(32). During a rotation, the token file may contain two tokens on separate lines, and either is accepted. They are equivalent operator credentials, not separate identities. Missing or malformed configuration prevents startup.

Each API worker checks the token and policy files for changes at most once every SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_RELOAD_INTERVAL seconds (default 10, at most 3600), when it handles a request. 0 reads the files only at startup. Changes are detected by file identity, size and modification time, which covers in-place edits, atomic renames and the symlink swap Kubernetes uses to update Secret and ConfigMap volumes. A change applies only when both files are valid and the policy's namespaces are within SPARK_ON_K8S_API_NAMESPACES; the worker logs a warning when it applies one. Otherwise it keeps its last valid token and policy and logs an error once for that change, without token values: a token you removed remains accepted until a valid change is loaded, so check the logs after each change. SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_ENABLED, the file paths and the reload interval are read only at startup. With the Helm chart, set the remote values instead; see chart remote submission.

Terminate TLS at a trusted reverse proxy or gateway. Do not expose the backend's plain HTTP port outside that trusted boundary. For browser access, the gateway must authenticate the browser, protect write requests against CSRF, and inject Authorization: Bearer <server-token> on every HTTP and WebSocket request. Ordinary browser WebSockets cannot attach a custom authorization header themselves. The application does not accept query-string tokens or bearer cookies and does not place a token in the dashboard bootstrap. The gateway must remove client-supplied identity headers before injecting its own and keep the backend unreachable directly. With or without remote mode, the Spark UI and History Server proxies forward only content-negotiation, content-type, range and conditional-cache request headers. Bearer tokens, cookies, gateway identity headers and other credentials are not sent to application services. Log WebSockets use the server's Kubernetes client and do not forward browser authorization headers to pods. Standalone mode with remote submission disabled does not require bearer authentication. See browser and gateway security boundaries.

The Airflow task UI also makes server-to-server console requests. It does not have a bearer-token configuration option. When the Spark API uses remote mode, set SPARK_ON_K8S_AIRFLOW_SERVICE_URL to an administrator-controlled gateway that authenticates the Airflow service and injects the operator credential, or use a separate internal API deployment with remote mode disabled and access restricted to trusted services. Browser gateway injection alone does not authenticate the Airflow backend's requests. Never put the operator token in browser configuration, task arguments or the service URL.

Apply least-privilege Kubernetes RBAC, Pod Security admission, namespace ResourceQuotas and network policy independently of this feature. Approved code and images must be trusted: this API does not sandbox the application's code or prevent that code from using its service account. Set ingress request/concurrency limits for the capacity of the server and cluster.

docs.title: Admission policy
docs.text:
This example uses an illustrative image digest; replace it with an image you own and have reviewed. Application code must already be present inside that image. Prefer immutable digests, because an exact mutable tag can point to different code later.

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "namespaces": {"analytics": ["spark-worker"]},
  "applications": [
    {
      "image": "registry.example.com/data/report@sha256:1111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111",
      "app_path": "local:///opt/jobs/report.py",
      "class_name": null,
      "arguments": [[], ["2026-11-07"]]
    }
  ],
  "limits": {
    "driver_cpu": 2,
    "driver_memory_mb": 2048,
    "executor_cpu": 2,
    "executor_memory_mb": 2048,
    "executors": 4
  },
  "spark_conf": {"spark.sql.shuffle.partitions": [8, 16]}
}

Namespaces and service accounts are exact pairs. Each application entry binds an exact image, local application path, optional Java class and approved argument lists. Omitting arguments permits only an empty list. Arguments are not arbitrary free-form input: an approved wrapper could otherwise use them to execute unapproved code. Without the optional placement keys, an approved application may run with every approved namespace and service-account pair.

Memory ceilings include memory overhead. Driver and executor limits apply per process; the executor count also bounds dynamic allocation, which must declare an explicit maximum. The ordinary portable job defaults still apply: one CPU, 1024 MB plus 512 MB overhead per process, and two executors. A policy below those defaults requires explicit smaller job values.

Remote jobs may set spec.max_runtime (seconds), which makes Kubernetes stop the driver that long after its pod starts; it can only shorten a run. To bound runs whose remote client is lost or never stops them, an administrator can add the optional "max_runtime": 86400 to limits. Every remote job must then set spec.max_runtime no greater than that limit, or it is rejected; it is never filled in silently. Policies without this key keep their current behavior. See driver lifetime limits.

Remote requests reject pod templates, packages, secret imports, custom labels/annotations, node selectors, profiles, Kubernetes credentials and all other unsupported fields, except a policy's required labels. Only these Spark tuning keys can appear in the administrator's explicit value allowlist:

  • spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
  • spark.default.parallelism
  • spark.sql.adaptive.enabled
  • spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled
  • spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold
  • spark.sql.broadcastTimeout
  • spark.sql.session.timeZone

Values must match the policy, including their JSON types. Kubernetes settings, classpaths, plugins, environment variables, remote files, resource overrides and arbitrary Spark keys cannot be enabled through that allowlist. The API validates the generated pod before writing resources, and uses only the server-configured client for both planning and submission.

docs.title: Restrict where an application runs
docs.text:
The optional application keys namespaces and service_accounts and the optional top-level labels extend schema_version: 1. Policies without them are admitted exactly as before. An API version that does not support these keys refuses to start with a policy that uses them, instead of ignoring the restriction.

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "namespaces": {
    "analytics": ["spark-worker"],
    "finance": ["spark-worker", "spark-finance"]
  },
  "applications": [
    {
      "image": "registry.example.com/data/report@sha256:1111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111",
      "app_path": "local:///opt/jobs/report.py",
      "namespaces": ["analytics"]
    },
    {
      "image": "registry.example.com/finance/ledger@sha256:2222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222",
      "app_path": "local:///opt/jobs/ledger.py",
      "namespaces": ["finance"],
      "service_accounts": ["spark-finance"]
    }
  ],
  "limits": {
    "driver_cpu": 2,
    "driver_memory_mb": 2048,
    "executor_cpu": 2,
    "executor_memory_mb": 2048,
    "executors": 4
  },
  "labels": {
    "required": {
      "cost-center": {"values": ["cc-1001", "cc-1002"]},
      "example.com/team": {"pattern": "[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,30}"}
    },
    "fixed": {"submitted-via": "remote-api"}
  }
}

A job's namespace and service account must still be an approved pair. When the matched application entry lists namespaces or service_accounts, the job must also use one of the listed values, so the report above can run only as analytics/spark-worker and the ledger only as finance/spark-finance. Several entries may approve the same code with different placements; a job is admitted when any matching entry allows its pair. Otherwise it is denied with policy_denied and the message The application is not approved for this namespace and service-account pair. Every listed namespace must be a policy namespace, and every listed service account must be approved for one of the entry's namespaces, or the policy is rejected.

Placement restricts which approved code can run with which Kubernetes identity. It does not identify the caller: every bearer can still submit every approved application to its approved placements.

docs.title: Require cost-attribution labels
docs.text:
labels.required names the driver labels every remote job must set in spec.driver_labels:

spec:
  driver_labels:
    cost-center: cc-1001
    example.com/team: data-eng

A rule lists exact values, or a pattern (a Python regular expression that must match the whole value), or is empty ({}) to accept any value. Values must be nonempty Kubernetes label values. Jobs can set only the required labels: other driver labels, executor labels and annotations remain rejected, and a policy without required rejects driver_labels as before. The server adds the labels.fixed labels to every remote job; jobs cannot set them. Admitted and fixed labels are applied to the driver pod and, through spark.kubernetes.executor.label.*, to its executors, so cost tools can attribute both.

The policy cannot require or fix reserved labels: unprefixed keys beginning with spark- (such as spark-role and spark-app-id), and keys under the spark-on-k8s.io/ prefix, used by the Spark Connect and Airflow integrations, or under kubernetes.io/ and k8s.io/ and their subdomains. A remote job can therefore never set or replace the labels that identify and own its driver. Labels support cost attribution; they are not an authorization or tenant boundary.

docs.title: Submit from the CLI
docs.text:
The remote CLI needs only the core package and a YAML or JSON job file. It does not require the api extra, Airflow, or local Kubernetes credentials. The job's namespace, service account, image, path, class, arguments and resources must pass the server policy.

export SPARK_ON_K8S_API_URL=https://spark.example.com/team
export SPARK_ON_K8S_API_TOKEN_FILE=/run/secrets/spark-api-token
spark-on-k8s remote plan report.yaml
spark-on-k8s remote submit report.yaml --timeout 30

--api-url and --token-file override those variables. SPARK_ON_K8S_API_TOKEN is an alternative to a token file; prefer the file in shared environments. Tokens are never accepted as a command line argument. HTTPS certificate verification is mandatory. Plain HTTP is accepted only for loopback development. Redirects are refused so credentials cannot be forwarded to another location, and environment HTTP proxies are not used by this client.

Output defaults to one versioned JSON object on stdout. --output text prints a redacted plan or the submitted driver pod name. A successful submission returns HTTP 201 and this shape:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "operation": "submit",
  "run": {
    "namespace": "analytics",
    "app_id": "report-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
    "driver_pod": "report-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef-driver",
    "driver_uid": "5bdceeb0-7fa8-4f72-823b-80f26e6195c4"
  },
  "status": null,
  "error": null
}

The readable name prefix is shortened when necessary to leave room for the random run identity and Kubernetes driver suffix. Each request creates a distinct run; a plan does not reserve its preview identity. Submission returns after resource creation and does not wait for Spark to finish.

The CLI uses the automation exit codes: 0 for an accepted operation, 1 for a remote/API/transport failure, 2 for invalid local input, 4 for a missing/disabled remote route, 5 for a request timeout and 130 for interruption. Errors have schema_version, operation and error: {code, message}; command-line parsing errors still use Click's normal stderr output.

docs.title: HTTP contract and retry safety
docs.text:
Send the SparkJob document directly as JSON to POST /jobs/v1/plan or POST /jobs/v1/submit, with the bearer header. Both use the same admission rules. Plans return HTTP 200 with {schema_version: 1, operation: "plan", plan: {...}, error: null} and redact application arguments. Requests are limited to 1 MiB, and receiving the body has a 15-second deadline.

The remote CLI bounds responses to 4 MiB and applies a 30-second HTTP deadline by default, configurable up to 300 seconds. Stalled response headers or bodies are interrupted. Hostname resolution also depends on the operating system's resolver timeout. This timeout does not cancel a server operation or stop a Spark job.

Requests are never retried automatically. A timeout, disconnect or Kubernetes failure can occur after some or all resources were created. Inspect existing runs before retrying to avoid duplicates; partial resources may require operator cleanup. The CLI also reports invalid_response with this warning when a submission receives a success or 5xx status whose body is not a valid result: the server or a gateway may have accepted the job. Idempotency-Key is explicitly rejected until a durable, shared idempotency implementation is available. In-memory deduplication would not be reliable across API workers or replicas.

Authentication failures return 401, admission denials 403, disabled routes 404, unsupported idempotency or invalid JSON 400, a client that disconnects before its body arrives 400 client_disconnected (recorded only: the client is gone), bodies not received within the deadline 408, oversized bodies 413, unsupported content types 415, and invalid job schemas 422. Kubernetes conflicts return 409; other Kubernetes failures return 502, and unexpected server failures 500. Errors contain a stable code and a human-readable message, never the Kubernetes response body. Every response carries an X-Request-ID header. The API's audit events record each plan and submission with that ID, its outcome and, once admitted, the generated run identity.

Admission limits apply to each submitted job. They do not reserve shared capacity or account for concurrent accepted jobs. Enforce aggregate resources with Kubernetes ResourceQuota or your external admission system. A policy rejection, a quota rejection and a scheduler wait are different outcomes.

Namespace allowlists constrain the shared operator deployment. Every bearer holder retains management access within that deployment's exposed surface; the allowlist does not establish individual user or tenant identity. Use separate trust boundaries where independent authorization is required.

docs.title: Rotate the token
docs.text:
A rotation keeps a short overlap in which the current and the new token are both accepted:

  1. Add the new token as a second line of the server's token file.
  2. When every API pod has the updated file, switch every client to the new token: CLI token files, automation secrets and any gateway that injects the bearer header.
  3. Replace the server's token file with the new token alone. Once that update reaches every pod, the old token receives 401.

With the Helm chart's remote values, the chart mounts the Secret's token and policy keys as a directory under remote.mountPath (/etc/spark-on-k8s/remote by default), so Secret updates reach running pods. If you configure remote mode through the generic env, volumes and volumeMounts values instead, also mount the Secret as a directory. Do not mount these files with subPath: such mounts never receive Secret updates, so every step would need a pod restart. Rotate with files in a private directory, so tokens never appear in command lines. Recreating the Secret replaces both keys, so copy the deployed policy first:

umask 077
namespace=spark-system
secret=spark-api-remote
kubectl get secret "$secret" --namespace "$namespace" --output jsonpath='{.data.token}' \
  | base64 --decode > current-token
kubectl get secret "$secret" --namespace "$namespace" --output jsonpath='{.data.policy\.json}' \
  | base64 --decode > policy.json
# No trailing newline: the chart's ServiceMonitor sends the token file byte for byte.
python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32), end="")' > next-token

# Step 1: accept both tokens. Blank lines are ignored; the newline must separate the tokens.
{ cat current-token; echo; cat next-token; } > overlap-token
kubectl create secret generic "$secret" --namespace "$namespace" \
  --from-file=token=overlap-token --from-file=policy.json=policy.json \
  --dry-run=client --output yaml | kubectl apply --filename -

The kubelet projects Secret updates into running pods after its sync period, typically within a minute or two. Before step 2, confirm that each API pod sees the new file by comparing a checksum rather than printing tokens; for example, run kubectl exec --namespace "$namespace" <api-pod> -- sha256sum /etc/spark-on-k8s/remote/token for every pod and compare it with the checksum of overlap-token. A worker checks the files at the first request it handles once SPARK_ON_K8S_SUBMISSION_RELOAD_INTERVAL seconds have passed since its previous check, and logs the number of accepted tokens when it applies the change. An error in the log means that worker still uses the previous token and policy.

# Step 3, after every client uses the new token: accept only the new token.
kubectl create secret generic "$secret" --namespace "$namespace" \
  --from-file=token=next-token --from-file=policy.json=policy.json \
  --dry-run=client --output yaml | kubectl apply --filename -

With the chart's ServiceMonitor, metric scrapes fail from step 1 until step 3 reaches the pods, because Prometheus cannot send a two-line token. Store the new token in your secret manager and delete the local files afterwards. Policy changes reach the API the same way. To revoke a compromised token without waiting for the kubelet, update the Secret and restart the API pods; restarted workers read the current files at startup and refuse to start if they are invalid.

docs.title: Run history, readiness and metrics
docs.text:
The optional run recorder keeps a small operational history after Kubernetes driver pods disappear. It is separate from Spark History Server: it stores metadata, not Spark event logs, stages, executors' logs or replayable job definitions. The console's Recorded runs page lists recorded runs and filters them by namespace, last observed status and presence. It is read-only and does not offer kill, delete or replay controls for retained records.

History is disabled by default. When disabled, the application creates no database or background collector, and /runs/v1 and /webserver/runs return 404.

docs.title: Enable persistent metadata
docs.text:
Provision a writable directory on a local or block-backed persistent filesystem, then configure the API:

export SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_ENABLED=true
export SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_PATH=/var/lib/spark-on-k8s/runs.sqlite3
export SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_NAMESPACES=analytics,batch
spark-on-k8s api start

The published API image runs as user and group 10001 and provides /var/lib/spark-on-k8s owned by them. A volume mounted there must be writable by that user or group.

The API service account needs permission to list pods in each configured namespace. Wildcards are not accepted; at most twenty namespaces can be configured. The recorder only requests pods labeled spark-role=driver and uses the server's existing Kubernetes credentials.

Use one API pod with persistent block storage. Multiple API worker processes in that pod can share one SQLite file: a database lease elects a collector, and a transaction checks its owner, generation and expiry before committing. A stale worker cannot overwrite a newer worker's snapshot. Worker shutdown cancels pending requests and releases the lease. After a crash, another worker can take over once the lease expires.

SQLite WAL requires reliable local filesystem locking. Do not use NFS, SMB or a database file copied independently to multiple replicas. This feature is intended for a small deployment, not distributed HA storage. Back up the database with SQLite's backup facility or during a clean shutdown; copying only the main file while WAL writes are active can omit committed records. Keep the directory private to the API process and back up the database according to your operational needs.

The store initializes schema version 1 transactionally and refuses an unknown future version. A version 1 database without the nullable collection failure-category column gains it on startup; builds that predate the column ignore it. Configuration objects and credential source fields are not collected into the database. A missing/unwritable directory or an invalid configuration prevents recorder startup; the API does not silently fall back to ephemeral storage.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
Each run is keyed by its Kubernetes pod UID. Reusing a pod name or Spark application ID creates a separate record instead of overwriting the old run. Retained fields are:

  • UID, namespace, application ID/name and driver pod name;
  • driver image, Spark version and Kubernetes creation time;
  • first and last observation times, last observed pod phase, and the time the pod was first absent.

Raw pod specifications, annotations, arguments, environment variables, SQL and logs are not selected for storage. Names, image references and other retained identifiers are workload-controlled and can themselves contain sensitive data; the fixed field list is not a content redaction guarantee. The collector selects the designated driver container when a pod also has sidecars.

Disappearance is independent of status. A running pod that disappears remains recorded as last seen Running, with a disappearance time; disappearance does not imply failure or success. Previously observed Succeeded and Failed phases remain terminal. A pod with the same UID that reappears clears its disappearance marker. The recorder cannot recover pods created and deleted entirely between polls, statuses it never observed, or runs that predate its first successful scan.

A namespace snapshot commits only after every Kubernetes page succeeds. Authentication failures, expired/repeated cursors, page limits, malformed metadata, cancellation or timeouts do not mark unseen pods missing and do not publish partial results. Other namespaces can still be collected while time remains in the overall budget. The starting namespace rotates between cycles so one slow namespace cannot continually prevent later namespaces from being collected.

Observation intervals are not execution duration or utilization. Retained status counts include missing runs and are affected by polling and retention; they are not a success-rate denominator, a cost report, lineage completion or a compliance audit trail.

docs.title: Bounds and retention
docs.text:
All settings below are optional environment variables with the SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_ prefix.

Suffix Default Meaning INTERVAL 30 Seconds between collection cycles, 5–3600. TIMEOUT 15 Overall Kubernetes collection budget in seconds, 1–300. REQUEST_TIMEOUT 5 Timeout per Kubernetes request in seconds, 1–30; the overall budget can interrupt it sooner. PAGE_SIZE 200 Pods requested per page, 1–500. MAX_PAGES 20 Maximum pages per namespace, 1–100. RETENTION_DAYS 30 Delete records not observed for this many days, 1–3650. MAX_ROWS 10000 Maximum retained records across namespaces, 1–1000000.

SQLite lock waits are bounded to two seconds per transaction. The lease includes the collection budget, poll interval and a safety margin. No new namespace scan starts after the collection budget expires. Retention is enforced after both successful collections and recorded failures. The oldest records by last observation are removed first when the row limit is exceeded; a small limit can discard useful history, including records for still-present pods. SQLite reuses freed pages, so deleting rows need not shrink the database file immediately. Logical retention is not physical erasure and does not expire independent backups. Define backup access and expiry separately.

Restart API workers to change these settings. Increasing page limits may increase memory use and cluster API traffic; use namespaces and quotas that match the deployment's scale.

docs.title: Read-only HTTP API
docs.text:
GET /runs/v1/config returns enabled namespaces, retention settings and the collection status of each namespace. GET /runs/v1 returns {schema_version: 1, items: [...], next_cursor: string | null}. Each item contains:

{
  "uid": "6fb31548-331f-4c94-bb51-b0af6b8cd263",
  "namespace": "analytics",
  "app_id": "daily-report",
  "name": "Daily report",
  "driver_pod": "daily-report-driver",
  "image": "registry.example.com/jobs/report:approved",
  "spark_version": "4.0.5",
  "status": "Succeeded",
  "created_at": "2026-11-07T12:00:00Z",
  "first_seen": "2026-11-07T12:00:15Z",
  "last_seen": "2026-11-07T12:04:15Z",
  "disappeared_at": "2026-11-07T12:04:45Z"
}

Creation time, image, Spark version and application ID can be null. Disappearance time is null for a present pod. Filters are namespace, status (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown), presence (all, present, missing) and limit (1–200, default 50). Pass next_cursor back as cursor with the same filters. Ordering uses immutable first-observed time and UID, so updating an existing run does not move it between pages. Retention may remove rows between requests. Only currently configured namespaces are exposed, even if the database contains older records from another namespace.

In remote mode, history and metrics use the same operator bearer authorization as other API routes. The recorder does not introduce tenant-specific permissions.

docs.title: Health and Prometheus
docs.text:
/health remains a lightweight liveness probe. GET and HEAD /ready check actual pod-list access in the configured namespaces, with a five-second overall deadline. Without history, readiness checks the API's default namespace and fails when that listing fails.

With history, readiness also requires an initialized, readable recorder database. A namespace is fresh when its last successful snapshot is within the freshness window: twice the poll interval plus the collection timeout and ten seconds (85 seconds with the defaults). Set SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_READINESS to choose how stale namespaces affect readiness:

Mode /ready result degraded (default) 503 when the database is unavailable, pod listing fails in every configured namespace, or no namespace is fresh. Otherwise 200, reporting degraded while any namespace is stale. strict 503 unless pod listing succeeds and collection is fresh in every configured namespace.

In degraded mode, one namespace that the recorder cannot collect, for example because its pod-list permission was removed, the Kubernetes API throttles it, or it exceeds the page limit, no longer removes the API from its Service. Submissions, application views and the other namespaces keep working while the stale namespace is reported in logs, metrics and the console. A pod-list failure in only some namespaces is tolerated until it makes their collection stale. With one configured namespace, both modes behave the same. After startup, readiness is 503 until a snapshot succeeds in at least one namespace (degraded) or in every namespace (strict). Use strict when the API should receive traffic only while history is current for every namespace.

Both probes remain accessible without a bearer in remote mode, so their bodies are limited to {"status":"ready"}, {"status":"degraded"} (both 200) or {"status":"not_ready"} (503). They do not expose namespace, database or credential errors; the authorized configuration endpoint and logs below identify stale namespaces. Failed readiness removes the pod from service traffic; liveness does not restart it merely because Kubernetes is temporarily unavailable.

docs.title: Collection status and logs
docs.text:
GET /runs/v1/config also returns readiness, freshness_seconds and one collection entry for each configured namespace:

{
  "namespace": "batch",
  "fresh": false,
  "last_success": "2026-11-07T12:00:15Z",
  "last_attempt": "2026-11-07T12:09:45Z",
  "last_error": "forbidden"
}

last_success is null before the first successful collection and last_attempt before the first attempt. last_error is null after a successful collection; otherwise it is a fixed category of the latest failure: unauthorized, forbidden, not_found, throttled, server_error, api_error (another Kubernetes status), timeout, connection, pagination (an expired or repeated continuation token), page_limit (more driver pods than PAGE_SIZE × MAX_PAGES), invalid_metadata, store or unexpected. Kubernetes and database error messages are never stored, returned or logged. The console's Recorded runs page shows a notice when the selected namespace is stale. Opened for a namespace that is not recorded, it shows the first recorded namespace instead.

The worker that holds the collection lease logs a warning when a namespace becomes stale, with the age of its last success and its last error category, and an info line when it is fresh again. The category is not_attempted when the collection budget expired before the namespace was reached. Each API worker also logs its own readiness changes with their reason, including the not-ready state it observes before the first snapshot after startup. These lines are written once per transition, not on every probe or collection:

WARNING:  Run-history collection for namespace batch is stale: last success 412s ago; last error: forbidden
WARNING:  API is ready but degraded: run-history collection is stale in batch (last error: forbidden)
INFO:     Run-history collection for namespace batch is fresh again
INFO:     API readiness recovered

spark-on-k8s api start writes these records with the server's log format and --log-level (SPARK_ON_K8S_API_LOG_LEVEL). The warning level omits the recovery lines.

docs.title: Prometheus metrics
docs.text:
Set SPARK_ON_K8S_METRICS_ENABLED=true to expose /metrics in Prometheus text format. It remains protected by the remote operator bearer when remote mode is enabled. Configure the scraper's authorization through its secret mechanism; do not place a token in a scrape URL. The endpoint also serves the API's operation counters. Run-history metrics include:

  • spark_on_k8s_history_enabled;
  • spark_on_k8s_runs_recorded{namespace,status};
  • spark_on_k8s_collection_successes_total{namespace} and spark_on_k8s_collection_failures_total{namespace};
  • spark_on_k8s_collection_age_seconds{namespace} (-1 before any successful collection);
  • spark_on_k8s_collection_stale{namespace} (1 when the namespace has no successful collection within the freshness window, including before its first collection; otherwise 0).

Labels contain only configured namespaces and five bounded status values. No application IDs, pod names, images or exception text appear in metric labels. Counters persist with the SQLite database. For example, alert on spark_on_k8s_collection_stale == 1 to find a stale namespace while the degraded readiness mode keeps the API in service.

docs.title: Helm configuration
docs.text:
The chart uses /health and /ready for liveness and readiness. To enable history, provision an existing ReadWriteOnce block-backed claim and allow the API's filesystem user to write it:

replicaCount: 1
autoscaling:
  enabled: false
namespaces: analytics,batch
runHistory:
  enabled: true
  namespaces: [analytics, batch]
  existingClaim: spark-run-metadata
  intervalSeconds: 30
  retentionDays: 30
  maxRows: 10000
metrics:
  enabled: true

The database is mounted at /var/lib/spark-on-k8s/runs.sqlite3. The chart requires a claim and explicit namespaces, rejects multiple replicas/autoscaling, and uses a Recreate rollout so two API pods do not compete for the claim. Its default fsGroup: 10001 gives the non-root API write access on volume types that support fsGroup; see non-root deployment for a claim written by an earlier root process. Existing environment overrides remain supported. Make sure history namespaces also have the pod-list permissions configured by namespaces or an externally managed service account. To require every history namespace to be fresh for readiness, set the mode through env:

env:
  - name: SPARK_ON_K8S_RUN_HISTORY_READINESS
    value: strict

The separately configured sparkHistory chart section still refers to Spark History Server event logs.

docs.title: Migrate from the Spark Operator
docs.text: Teams running the Kubeflow Spark Operator describe applications as SparkApplication and ScheduledSparkApplication custom resources. Since 0.13.0, spark-on-k8s job assess-operator assesses those manifests offline and drafts equivalent job files for the settings that translate.

docs.title: What changes: who owns the application
docs.text:
Read this before comparing YAML. The operator is a controller: it watches custom resources, submits them, restarts or resubmits them according to their restart policy, runs schedules and deletes finished applications after a time to live. spark-on-k8s is a client. It creates the driver pod, Service and ConfigMaps, then returns or observes the run when asked. Nothing reconciles the application afterwards.

Concern Spark Operator spark-on-k8s Submission Controller runs spark-submit in cluster mode Client creates the driver pod directly; Spark runs in client mode inside it Retries restartPolicy resubmits The caller retries; each retry is a new submission (automation) Schedules ScheduledSparkApplication A Kubernetes CronJob or Airflow Spark UI Operator-created Service or Ingress ui_reverse_proxy: true with the API's Spark UI proxy, or kubectl port-forward Cleanup timeToLiveSeconds apps prune on a schedule you own, or app delete; prune ages count from pod creation, not completion; the driver pod owns executors and client-created objects Driver pod shape Operator webhook or pod template Driver pod templates and job-file fields

Keep the operator for workloads that depend on controller behavior, such as automatic resubmission after node loss. Both can run in the same cluster while you migrate; the assessor never reads or changes cluster resources.

docs.title: Assess a manifest
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s job assess-operator spark-pi.yaml
spark-on-k8s job assess-operator manifests.yaml --output json > assessment.json
spark-on-k8s job assess-operator spark-pi.yaml --draft-dir drafts/

The input can contain several YAML documents. Each sparkoperator.k8s.io/v1beta2 SparkApplication or ScheduledSparkApplication is assessed; other documents, including older API versions, are listed as skipped. Files are limited to 1 MiB, and YAML aliases or duplicate keys are rejected.

Every field in an assessed document receives one status. A finding for an object or list covers the fields nested below it.

Status Meaning mapped The draft carries the setting with the same meaning, or the SparkJob default already behaves the same way. target names the SparkJob setting. approximated The draft carries it, or its intent is covered differently; note states the difference. Review each one. unsupported Not carried into the draft. note says why and alternative recommends what to use instead. Unrecognized fields are always unsupported: nothing is translated by guesswork. ignored Observed state or server-written metadata (status, metadata.uid), unmounted volumes and settings that have no effect in the source either.

An application is migration_ready only when it has no unsupported findings and its draft passes offline validation. A restart policy that resubmits, a schedule, or an operator-only feature such as monitoring therefore always produces migration_ready: false. Readiness is an assessment result, not a guarantee that the job behaves identically: compare a staging run before switching production.

Each application also lists notes for differences that are not tied to one field, such as the lifecycle change above, a missing namespace (job files default to default), a missing driver service account (job files default to spark) or unset memory overhead (job files default to 512 MiB per pod).

docs.title: Output and exit codes
docs.text:
--output json writes one document to stdout:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "operation": "assess_operator",
  "error": null,
  "migration_ready": false,
  "applications": [
    {
      "document": 1,
