      "kind": "SparkApplication",
      "name": "spark-pi",
      "namespace": "spark-jobs",
      "migration_ready": false,
      "counts": {"mapped": 20, "approximated": 6, "unsupported": 1, "ignored": 0},
      "findings": [
        {
          "path": "spec.restartPolicy",
          "status": "unsupported",
          "target": null,
          "note": "spark-on-k8s submits once; no controller resubmits ...",
          "alternative": "Retry from the caller ..."
        }
      ],
      "notes": ["Lifecycle ownership changes: ..."],
      "draft": {"apiVersion": "spark-on-k8s/v1", "kind": "SparkJob", "...": "..."},
      "draft_error": null,
      "draft_file": null
    }
  ],
  "skipped": [{"document": 2, "api_version": "v1", "kind": "ConfigMap", "reason": "..."}]
}

Paths use dots for fields, [N] for list positions and [key] for map keys such as spec.sparkConf[spark.executor.memory]. Consumers should check schema_version, tolerate additional fields and avoid parsing the text report.

Exit code Meaning 0 Every document was read and assessed, including when fields are unsupported or migration_ready is false 1 Unreadable or invalid input (invalid YAML, no Spark Operator application, a document without metadata.name or spec), or a draft file could not be written; the JSON result has an operation_error 2 Invalid CLI arguments, including a missing input file or a --draft-dir that is an existing file

Use migration_ready or the counts to gate a migration in CI; the exit code does not.

docs.title: Drafts
docs.text:
A draft is a spark-on-k8s/v1 SparkJob document containing only the mapped and approximated settings. The command builds it, then validates and plans it in process exactly like spark-on-k8s job validate, without contacting Kubernetes. Only a draft that passes is emitted; otherwise draft is null and draft_error explains the validation failure (for example, no image in the source).

--draft-dir DIRECTORY (created if missing) writes each valid draft to DIRECTORY/NAME.yaml with a header comment marking it as a draft. Existing files are never replaced, and nothing is written when any destination already exists. The JSON output always contains the draft object.

spark-on-k8s job assess-operator spark-pi.yaml --draft-dir drafts/
spark-on-k8s job validate drafts/spark-pi.yaml
spark-on-k8s job plan drafts/spark-pi.yaml --output json

The draft name is the source name, converted to a valid SparkJob name when needed. Generated application IDs add a timestamp suffix, so driver pods are no longer named NAME-driver. A ScheduledSparkApplication produces a draft of its spec.template; schedule it separately.

docs.title: Credentials stay out of reports and drafts
docs.text: Findings never contain source values. A setting that looks like a credential is reported as unsupported and left out of the draft, using the same detection as plan redaction: sensitive key or variable names (password, token, secret.key, access.key and similar), credentials in URLs, signed URL parameters and NAME=secret tokens in arguments or Java options. Move such values to Kubernetes Secrets and reference them, for example with spark.kubernetes.executor.secretKeyRef.NAME for executors and a valueFrom.secretKeyRef entry in the driver pod template. Detection is pattern-based: review drafts before committing them, because positional arguments or unusual names can still contain sensitive data.

docs.title: How fields translate
docs.text:
The report is the authoritative accounting for a given manifest. The main translations are:

Spark Operator field SparkJob setting metadata.name, metadata.namespace metadata.name, spec.namespace metadata.labels driver_labels and executor_labels, except kueue.x-k8s.io/ labels, which the operator does not copy to pods (unsupported) image, driver.image, executor.image image; a different executor image becomes spark.kubernetes.executor.container.image imagePullPolicy, imagePullSecrets image_pull_policy; pull secrets in the driver template and spark.kubernetes.container.image.pullSecrets mainApplicationFile, mainClass, arguments app_path, class_name, app_arguments sparkConf, hadoopConf spark_conf (hadoopConf keys gain the spark.hadoop. prefix) Driver and executor cores, memory, memoryOverhead driver_resources and executor_resources (whole cores, MiB) executor.instances, dynamicAllocation executor_instances deps.packages, deps.jars, deps.files, deps.pyFiles, deps.archives packages; spark.jars, spark.files, spark.submit.pyFiles, spark.archives serviceAccount service_account (driver); spark.kubernetes.authenticate.executor.serviceAccountName (executors) nodeSelector, labels, annotations driver_* and executor_* maps env, envFrom, volumeMounts, configMaps, secrets, tolerations, affinity, security contexts, sidecars, initContainers driver_pod_template and executor_pod_template; executor literals and Secret keys use spark.executorEnv.* and spark.kubernetes.executor.secretKeyRef.*, and executor Secret mounts use spark.kubernetes.executor.secrets.*

Notable approximations and unsupported fields:

  • mode, type, sparkVersion and pythonVersion have no SparkJob field: the image and app_path determine them.
  • The driver's CPU request and limit both equal driver_resources.cpu in whole cores, so driver.coreRequest and driver.coreLimit are approximated. Executor values become spark.kubernetes.executor.request.cores and limit.cores.
  • A driver sidecar that keeps running keeps the driver pod, and any waiting, running. Prefer a native sidecar; see driver pod templates.
  • gpu and hostNetwork are unsupported: add GPU limits or host networking to the pod templates yourself, then verify the running driver and executor pods.
  • Dependencies given as local paths are unsupported: the driver resolves them in its own pod. Bake them into the image and use local://, or use a remote URI.
  • sparkConf keys that shape a cluster-mode driver pod (spark.kubernetes.driver.secrets.*, .volumes.*, .podTemplateFile and similar) are unsupported; driver labels, annotations, node selectors, resources and the driver service account are translated into SparkJob fields instead.
  • restartPolicy other than Never, schedules, timeToLiveSeconds, sparkUIOptions, driverIngressOptions, monitoring, batchScheduler, sparkConfigMap, hadoopConfigMap, proxyUser and operator pod template fields are unsupported. The recipes cover scheduling, batch schedulers, lineage and object storage.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The assessor is not a controller, importer of live resources or parity checker. It reads files only, does not read the cluster or the operator's configuration (for example webhook defaults), and does not compare a draft with pods the operator created. Volumes, sidecars and other pod fields are copied into templates without a complete Kubernetes schema check; the API server still validates them at submission. To trial a migration, submit the validated draft in a staging namespace next to the existing application and compare its output, pod specifications from job plan and resource use before retiring the custom resource.

docs.title: Spark compatibility
docs.text:
The client supports the Apache Spark 3.5 and Spark 4 container entrypoint. It creates a driver Pod and starts spark-submit in client mode inside that Pod; Spark creates the executor Pods. No Spark installation or Java runtime is needed on the machine running the Python client, CLI, or API.

The execution matrix covers the maintained 3.5 line, the first Spark 4 minor line, and the current Spark 4 release:

Spark Apache image tag Scala binary version Runtime Java Upstream Python minimum 3.5.9 apache/spark:3.5.9-scala2.12-java17-python3-ubuntu 2.12 17 3.8 4.0.5 apache/spark:4.0.5-scala2.13-java17-python3-ubuntu 2.13 17 3.9 4.3.0 apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu 2.13 21 3.11

The workflow pins these images by digest. These are selected test combinations, not the complete set of runtimes supported by Apache Spark. See the upstream requirements for 3.5.9, 4.0.5, and 4.3.0. Other Spark releases and custom images need their own validation. Spark Connect, custom schedulers, GPU workloads, and third-party connectors are outside this matrix. Connect has a separate server lifecycle matrix for Spark 4.0.5 and 4.3.0.

docs.title: Client and application runtimes
docs.text:
The spark-on-k8s Python package requires Python 3.11 or newer. That is separate from the Python and Java runtimes in the application image. The driver and its Python workers must use compatible Python versions and the PySpark version that matches the image's Spark distribution. The integration workflow runs the client on Python 3.11 and uses the Python runtime supplied by each Apache image.

When upgrading a Java or Scala application, match the Spark dependencies and Scala artifact suffix to the image. For example, Spark 4 uses spark-sql_2.13, whereas the selected Spark 3.5 image uses spark-sql_2.12. Use Maven's provided scope for Spark dependencies; the image supplies them at runtime. Match third-party connectors, such as Iceberg, to both the Spark minor version and Scala binary version supported by that connector.

Spark 4 also changes SQL behavior, including enabling ANSI mode by default. The client does not disable these checks. Validate application queries against the Spark SQL migration guide when upgrading.

docs.title: Build the examples with Spark 4
docs.text:
The example Dockerfiles default to Spark 3.5.9. From the repository root, build the Python example with Spark 4.3.0:

docker build -t pyspark-job \
  --build-arg SPARK_IMAGE=apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  examples/python

For Java, change the compile-time dependencies as well as the runtime image:

docker build -t java-spark-job \
  --build-arg SPARK_IMAGE=apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  --build-arg SPARK_VERSION=4.3.0 \
  --build-arg SCALA_BINARY_VERSION=2.13 \
  examples/java

The Java builder uses JDK 17, which can compile against both selected Spark 3 and Spark 4 distributions. The resulting application runs on the image's JDK. Load or push the resulting image and submit it using the example instructions. Do not replace the Apache image's entrypoint: the client relies on its driver command and Spark's executor command.

docs.title: Execution tests
docs.text:
The Spark runtime compatibility workflow creates an isolated kind cluster for each of the three versions. It installs the built client wheel, compiles a Java job against the image's exact Spark jars, and submits five small applications through SparkOnK8S:

  • Python worker computation and a DataFrame aggregation, including Secret-backed environment variables in both driver and executor.
  • Multiple SQL statements mounted in a managed ConfigMap, including a quoted semicolon and a checked aggregation.
  • A SQL error that must fail the driver and prevent the next statement from running.
  • A Java class entrypoint that performs and checks a distributed aggregation.
  • An unschedulable driver whose bounded wait must time out while the Pending driver is retained, diagnosed and then cancelled through its receipt.

Successful jobs must create executor Pods owned by the driver. After every job, the test deletes the driver and checks that its Pods, Services, Secrets, and ConfigMaps are garbage collected. The workflow uploads logs, Pod status, events, and the execution result, including on failure. Each job uses one executor, a four-minute application deadline, and a 30-minute overall deadline. At most two matrix jobs run concurrently. The harness accepts only a kind context and creates and deletes its own uniquely named namespace.

Local Spark computation can also be checked without Docker. With JAVA_HOME pointing to JDK 21, run from a checkout:

REPOSITORY="$PWD"
RUNTIME_DIR="$(mktemp -d)"
uv venv --python 3.11 "$RUNTIME_DIR/runtime"
uv pip install --python "$RUNTIME_DIR/runtime/bin/python" 'pyspark==4.3.0'
cd "$RUNTIME_DIR"
"$RUNTIME_DIR/runtime/bin/python" -I "$REPOSITORY/tests/integration/spark/run_local.py" \
  --spark-version 4.3.0 --artifacts "$RUNTIME_DIR/results"

Repeat with PySpark 3.5.9 or 4.0.5 and JDK 17 for the other matrix rows. This executes Python, SQL, SQL failure, and Java workloads with local[2]; it does not validate Kubernetes submission, networking, RBAC, or resource cleanup. The Kubernetes workflow requires a working Docker daemon. Its run results are the evidence for cluster compatibility; local-mode results are separate evidence.

The JVM matrix compiles a Java class against each runtime image's Spark jars. This proves that selected workload, not compatibility of an existing Scala assembly or arbitrary third-party connector. Rebuild and test your actual application with the intended Java, Scala binary version, Spark jars and connector set before upgrading it.

docs.title: Spark Connect companion
docs.text:
Use an existing Spark Connect endpoint from notebooks or Python tools without creating a Kubernetes job for every interactive query. This companion creates independent client sessions. To create a server using the SDK or CLI, see Create a Spark Connect server on Kubernetes. For an end-to-end notebook that provisions a server, runs distributed queries and resumes after a kernel restart, follow Jupyter notebooks on Kubernetes.

Install the optional thin client in a Python 3.11–3.14 environment:

uv pip install 'spark-on-k8s[connect]'

The extra targets Spark 4 clients and keeps pandas below 3, as required for full upstream compatibility. pandas 2 has no Python 3.15 wheels, so this optional extra is limited to Python 3.11–3.14; the base SDK and CLI retain Python 3.15 support. For Spark 3.5 servers, install the base package and a matching pyspark[connect] version instead. Match client and server versions when possible. The base Spark-on-K8s CLI/SDK does not import PySpark or need Java. The Spark 4 thin client also needs no local JVM.

docs.title: Named connection profiles
docs.text:
Create connect.toml with endpoint addresses and references to credentials:

[profiles.production]
endpoint = "sc://spark.example.com:443"
tls = true
token_env = "SPARK_CONNECT_TOKEN"

[profiles.local]
endpoint = "sc://127.0.0.1:15002"
tls = false

Set the referenced token through your normal secret manager or shell environment. Profile files reject embedded credentials, connection-string parameters, duplicate keys, and unknown settings. TLS is enabled by default. Non-loopback plaintext connections require an explicit allow_insecure = true; use this only with a trusted network or an independently protected tunnel. TLS verifies server certificates using the upstream gRPC client. There is no disable-certificate-verification option.

Spark Connect clients always use TLS when a token is configured, except for the hostname localhost, where Spark 4 clients send the token over gRPC local credentials. A profile with token_env and tls = false is therefore rejected unless its endpoint host is exactly localhost; use sc://localhost:PORT rather than 127.0.0.1 for a tunneled token-protected server. PySpark also reads SPARK_CONNECT_AUTHENTICATE_TOKEN from the environment, so unset it when using a plaintext profile without a token.

spark-on-k8s connect check connect.toml --profile production --timeout 15 --output json

The check runs a small remote DataFrame action and reports the server's Spark version and the PySpark client version that ran the query. It runs in a separate process with a total timeout, so an unavailable server cannot leave a stuck CLI. Exit codes are 0 for success, 1 for configuration/connection failure, 2 for CLI usage errors, 5 for timeout and 130 for interruption. Error output omits gRPC details that could contain credentials. A timed-out session may remain until the server's session expiry policy cleans it up; the check never stops the shared server.

With --output json, the command writes one document using the automation contract. namespace is empty because the check does not use Kubernetes. A failure has status: "error", spark_version: null, client_version: null, warnings: [] and error: {code, message} with operation_error, timeout or interrupted:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "operation": "connect_check",
  "namespace": "",
  "error": null,
  "status": "ok",
  "spark_version": "4.3.0",
  "client_version": "4.3.0",
  "warnings": []
}

docs.title: Client and server versions
docs.text:
A Spark Connect client of a different release can pass a tiny query and then fail later with errors unrelated to your code. For example, the Jupyter guide records a 4.3.0 client that passed readiness against a 4.0.5 server and then failed to create a DataFrame from local rows. When the check knows both versions and their major or minor numbers differ (for example a 4.3 client with a 4.0 or 3.5 server), it adds a version_skew warning. Patch releases such as 4.0.5 and 4.0.6 are not compared.

The warning does not change the result: the check still succeeds with exit code 0. Text output prints it on stderr; JSON output lists it in warnings as {"code": "version_skew", "message": "..."}. An unknown client version (client_version: null) or an unparseable version produces no warning, which does not establish compatibility. Install a client matching the server's major.minor version. To make a script fail on any warning, check the field explicitly:

spark-on-k8s connect check connect.toml --profile production --output json > check.json
jq -e '.error == null and (.warnings | length) == 0' check.json

ConnectProfile.probe() returns the same client_version and warnings. In your own sessions, compare the versions with version_warnings():

from pyspark.version import __version__ as client_version
from spark_on_k8s.connect import ConnectProfile, version_warnings

with ConnectProfile.from_file("connect.toml", profile="production").session() as spark:
    for warning in version_warnings(client_version, spark.version):
        print(warning["message"])

docs.title: Notebook and application sessions
docs.text:
from spark_on_k8s.connect import ConnectProfile

profile = ConnectProfile.from_file("connect.toml", profile="production")
with profile.session() as spark:
    assert spark.range(100).count() == 100
    spark.range(5).show()

Every context opens a separate Connect session and attempts to release it on exit, even when user code raises an exception. If both application code and release fail, the original application exception is preserved with a cleanup note. A release-only failure raises ConnectError; server-side session expiry remains the fallback. It does not reuse or stop another notebook session. After the generated-data example works, try your warehouse data (for example spark.read.parquet("s3a://warehouse/events/")) only after verifying the server has the required connector, storage permissions and data. Files and data paths are interpreted on the server. Cluster-wide state and static Spark configuration belong to the server; classic RDD/SparkContext APIs are not available through Connect. Authenticate and authorize the server with your existing gRPC gateway and identity system: profiles do not provide server-side isolation.

For local access to a private Kubernetes service, use your normal kubectl port-forward tunnel and the loopback profile. The helper never reads or changes your kubeconfig. connection_string() is available for advanced integration but can return credentials; do not log it. Profile representations contain only the environment-variable name.

See the upstream Spark Connect overview and client installation guide.

docs.title: Create a Spark Connect server on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Create a private Spark Connect server when you want notebooks or Python tools to share a long-running Spark driver. The server launches real Kubernetes executors using the existing submission machinery. The separate connection profiles guide covers client sessions and existing services. For the complete local notebook workflow, including an isolated kernel, planned restart and cleanup, use Jupyter notebooks on Kubernetes.

This feature creates one driver and its private Services in an existing namespace. It does not restart a failed driver or restore sessions after a driver replacement. Use a new server receipt when replacing a server. Server pools, admission queues, authentication gateways and the Helm chart are outside this lifecycle helper.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Prepare the namespace and driver service account using the existing namespace setup guide. The driver needs permission to create and manage its executors. The caller needs permission to create/read/delete driver pods and Services in that namespace, and to list pods there for connect server list.
  • Use a Spark 4 image containing the Connect server JAR. Specify its exact local:/// path; the helper does not download a guessed Spark/Scala artifact. Kubernetes integration tests cover the pinned Spark 4.0.5 and 4.3.0 images in .github/workflows/spark-connect.yml.
  • Creation, status and deletion use the base package and do not need local Java or PySpark. Install spark-on-k8s[connect] on Python 3.11–3.14 for query readiness checks and interactive sessions. A separately installed compatible Connect client can also be used; see the client installation boundary.

The generated Connect Service is ClusterIP, with no public load balancer or Ingress. It serves plaintext gRPC inside the cluster. Use it only within a trusted network; anyone able to reach it has access to the server's execution environment and data permissions. It is not a tenant-isolation boundary. An external TLS and authentication gateway remains an administrator responsibility. No credentials are stored in the server receipt.

docs.title: Create and connect from the CLI
docs.text:
Create a server and save its identity in a new file:

spark-on-k8s connect server create \
  --image apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  --server-jar local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar \
  --namespace spark --service-account spark \
  --name notebook --executors 1 \
  --driver-memory 1024 --executor-memory 1024 \
  --receipt-file connect-server.json --output json

The result contains the private endpoint and a server handle. Creation means that Kubernetes accepted the resources; query_ready is initially false. The receipt is published atomically without replacing an existing file. Keep it for status, readiness and deletion: it records the driver and Service UIDs, not just their names.

Use --kubeconfig FILE --context NAME on each server command to select an explicit cluster. Otherwise, the project's usual Kubernetes connection settings apply. Server workload settings are taken from the server configuration, rather than inheriting unrelated batch-submission defaults from environment variables.

For a notebook on your machine, keep a separate terminal running a tunnel. Replace SERVICE_NAME with server.service_name from the receipt:

kubectl --namespace spark port-forward service/SERVICE_NAME 15002:15002

Use the same kubeconfig and context as the creation command. The tunnel is managed by you; closing it does not stop the server. Spark can take time to start after creation. If the tunnel exits with a connection-refused error during startup, inspect the driver logs and restart the tunnel once the gRPC listener has started. Create connect.toml:

[profiles.notebook]
endpoint = "sc://127.0.0.1:15002"
tls = false

Then verify this particular server and open a session:

spark-on-k8s connect server wait connect-server.json \
  --profile-file connect.toml --profile notebook --timeout 120 --output json

from spark_on_k8s.connect import ConnectProfile

profile = ConnectProfile.from_file("connect.toml", profile="notebook")
with profile.session() as spark:
    assert spark.range(100).groupBy().sum("id").first()[0] == 4950
    spark.sql("SELECT 'connected' AS status").show()

Readiness checks a real remote action and verifies the remote spark.app.id against the receipt. A successful query against a different server is rejected. Resource identities are checked again before reporting readiness. A Kubernetes Running phase alone does not establish query readiness.

The readiness result reports the spark_version returned by the server, the local client_version that ran the query and warnings. A client and server that differ in major or minor version produce a version_skew warning, as described in client and server versions; readiness still succeeds. connect server wait prints the warning on stderr in text mode and copies it to a top-level warnings array in JSON.

Inside the cluster, use the returned private endpoint in a profile with tls = false and an explicit allow_insecure = true only for your trusted network. Files, connectors and data permissions belong to the server image and service account; your local notebook's filesystem is not automatically available there.

docs.title: Python SDK
docs.text:
from spark_on_k8s.client import ExecutorInstances, PodResources, SparkOnK8S
from spark_on_k8s.connect import ConnectProfile
from spark_on_k8s.connect_server import ConnectServerConfig

client = SparkOnK8S()
server = client.create_connect_server(
    ConnectServerConfig(
        image="apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu",
        server_jar="local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar",
        namespace="spark",
        service_account="spark",
        app_name="notebook",
        driver_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=1024, memory_overhead=512),
        executor_resources=PodResources(cpu=1, memory=1024, memory_overhead=512),
        executor_instances=ExecutorInstances(initial=1),
        spark_conf={"spark.sql.shuffle.partitions": "4"},
    )
)
print(server.endpoint)
print(server.to_dict())  # Persist this identity before waiting.

# After establishing a tunnel to server.service_name:
profile = ConnectProfile(endpoint="sc://127.0.0.1:15002", tls=False)
client.wait_connect_server_ready(server, profile=profile, timeout=120)
with profile.session() as spark:
    assert spark.range(10).count() == 10

ConnectServerHandle.from_dict() restores a saved identity. For the CLI receipt, pass its inner server mapping: the file envelope is {"schema_version": 1, "server": {...}}. Resource options use the same PodResources and ExecutorInstances types as application submission. Additional Spark settings and packages are explicit; settings that would change the managed master, identity, driver networking, Connect port or resource contract are rejected before creating resources. The explicit exception spark.kubernetes.executor.request.cores accepts a positive Kubernetes CPU quantity no greater than the configured executor cores, so fractional scheduling requests are possible while executor cores remain managed by PodResources.

docs.title: Private images, credentials and node placement
docs.text:
A server for real data or ML work often needs an image from a private registry, credentials such as object-storage keys, and nodes from a particular pool, for example GPU nodes. Use the typed settings below instead of Spark properties: spark_conf cannot set spark.kubernetes.* properties, and literal credentials in Spark properties appear in driver arguments and diagnostics.

Purpose CLI option (repeatable) ConnectServerConfig field Value Pull from a private registry --image-pull-secret NAME image_pull_secrets Existing image pull Secret names, used by the driver and executors Credentials as environment variables --driver-env-from-secret NAME=SECRET:KEY, --executor-env-from-secret NAME=SECRET:KEY driver_env_from_secrets, executor_env_from_secrets Variable name mapped to a key of an existing Secret Select nodes --driver-node-selector KEY=VALUE, --executor-node-selector KEY=VALUE driver_node_selector, executor_node_selector Node label keys and values Allow tainted nodes --driver-toleration, --executor-toleration as KEY[=VALUE][:EFFECT] driver_tolerations, executor_tolerations Kubernetes toleration mappings

The helper only references Secrets: it never creates, reads or copies them, and their values never pass through the SDK, CLI, receipts, plans or logs. Kubernetes resolves each SECRET:KEY reference when it starts a container. An administrator creates the Secrets in the server's namespace, for example from files so that values stay out of command lines and shell history:

kubectl --namespace spark create secret generic private-registry \
  --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=./registry-config.json
kubectl --namespace spark create secret generic s3-credentials \
  --from-file=access-key=./access-key.txt --from-file=secret-key=./secret-key.txt

See Kubernetes' guide to pulling an image from a private registry for the registry configuration file.

Every client of a server runs code in its driver and executors, so any client can read these variables, for example with a query. Give a server only credentials that all of its users may hold; a shared server is not a tenant-isolation boundary.

Create a server on labeled, tainted GPU nodes with a private image and storage credentials:

spark-on-k8s connect server create \
  --image registry.example.com/data/spark-connect-ml:4.3.0 \
  --server-jar local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar \
  --namespace spark --service-account spark --name ml-notebook \
  --image-pull-secret private-registry \
  --driver-env-from-secret AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=s3-credentials:access-key \
  --driver-env-from-secret AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=s3-credentials:secret-key \
  --executor-env-from-secret AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=s3-credentials:access-key \
  --executor-env-from-secret AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=s3-credentials:secret-key \
  --executor-node-selector example.com/pool=gpu \
  --executor-toleration nvidia.com/gpu:NoSchedule \
  --receipt-file ml-server.json --output json

In the SDK, the same settings are fields of ConnectServerConfig:

ConnectServerConfig(
    image="registry.example.com/data/spark-connect-ml:4.3.0",
    server_jar="local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    app_name="ml-notebook",
    image_pull_secrets=["private-registry"],
    driver_env_from_secrets={"AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID": "s3-credentials:access-key"},
    executor_env_from_secrets={"AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID": "s3-credentials:access-key"},
    executor_node_selector={"example.com/pool": "gpu"},
    executor_tolerations=[{"key": "nvidia.com/gpu", "operator": "Exists", "effect": "NoSchedule"}],
)

A node selector restricts pods to nodes with every listed label; a toleration only permits scheduling on nodes with a matching taint. To dedicate a pool, use both. In the CLI, KEY=VALUE:EFFECT creates an Equal toleration and KEY:EFFECT an Exists toleration; omitting the effect tolerates every effect. Use the SDK for tolerationSeconds or a key-less toleration. The mapping reuses existing submission mechanisms:

  • The driver gets imagePullSecrets and valueFrom.secretKeyRef variables through a generated driver pod template, and node selectors and tolerations through the submission options of the same name.
  • Executors are created by Spark. They use Spark's spark.kubernetes.container.image.pullSecrets, spark.kubernetes.executor.secretKeyRef.NAME and spark.kubernetes.executor.node.selector.KEY properties. Spark has no property for tolerations, so executor tolerations use an executor pod template, stored in a ConfigMap owned by the driver. Creating it requires your permission to create and patch ConfigMaps in the namespace; Kubernetes deletes it with the driver.

Validation happens before any Kubernetes request: Secret and label syntax, toleration fields and operators, and variable names. Variable names are identifiers ([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*). Names starting with SPARK_ are rejected because Spark and this helper set such variables. An executor variable cannot also be set with spark.executorEnv.NAME in spark_conf. These settings map individual Secret keys; the application option driver_env_vars_from_secrets instead imports every key of a Secret into the driver.

Kubernetes, not this helper, checks that the referenced Secrets, keys, labels and taints exist. A missing pull Secret leaves the driver in ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff; a missing variable Secret or key stops the container from starting (CreateContainerConfigError); unmatched node selectors leave pods Pending as unschedulable. Readiness then times out and keeps the server. Run spark-on-k8s app diagnose --namespace spark --app-id APP_ID for the driver, or inspect executor pod events, then delete the server before creating a corrected one.

docs.title: Preview a server offline
docs.text:
connect server plan accepts the same server options as create, without a receipt or cluster selection. It opens no Kubernetes connection and prints a redacted preview of the driver Pod, both Services and, with executor tolerations, the executor template ConfigMap that creation would request, as YAML or, with --output json, as a versioned document with "operation": "connect_server_plan":

spark-on-k8s connect server plan \
  --image registry.example.com/data/spark-connect-ml:4.3.0 \
  --server-jar local:///opt/spark/jars/spark-connect_2.13-4.3.0.jar \
  --namespace spark --service-account spark --name ml-notebook \
  --image-pull-secret private-registry \
  --executor-env-from-secret AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=s3-credentials:access-key \
  --executor-toleration nvidia.com/gpu:NoSchedule --output json

The document contains plan and pod_settings, which lists the typed settings above: Secret names and keys, never values. Plan redaction hides fields whose names suggest credentials, such as the driver's imagePullSecrets and Spark properties naming Secrets, and the contents of ConfigMaps, so pod_settings is where to review those references. Identifiers in the plan, such as the -preview application ID, are illustrative. The SDK equivalent client.plan_connect_server(config) returns an ApplicationPlan; its raw resources are unredacted, which for these settings still contain only references.

For an image with Python ML libraries and GPU executors, see Build an ML image for Spark Connect.

docs.title: Observe, stop and recover
docs.text:
spark-on-k8s connect server status connect-server.json --output json
spark-on-k8s connect server delete connect-server.json --output json

The SDK equivalents are connect_server_status(server) and delete_connect_server(server). Deletion requests shutdown of the recorded driver and cleanup of its owned Services/executors. It reports a deletion request, not instantaneous completion. Closing a client session or tunnel leaves the server running. Keep the receipt until Kubernetes has removed the resources.

To bound a server that might be forgotten, or whose receipt or client is lost, add --max-runtime SECONDS to create (max_runtime in ConnectServerConfig). Kubernetes stops the driver that long after its pod starts, whether or not anyone deletes it. Choose a value longer than any session you need: open sessions then fail and the server is not restarted. Status reports terminated with driver_reason: "DeadlineExceeded". The stopped driver pod and its Services remain until delete (or apps prune) removes them; see driver lifetime limits.

Status reports observed resource presence, driver phase and the driver pod's Kubernetes driver_reason (or null), including missing or terminating resources. It also reports the driver's created_at time (UTC) and age_seconds, computed with your local clock and never negative; both are null when the driver is missing. Status does not run a query, so it cannot learn the server's Spark version: spark_version is reported only from a spark-version label on the driver pod, which this helper does not set, and is otherwise null. Use connect server wait for the server-reported version and version warnings. Permission errors and unreachable Kubernetes APIs remain errors, not evidence that a server has disappeared. Destructive operations verify all recorded resource identities before issuing UID-conditional deletion requests; a stale receipt cannot delete a same-name replacement.

A readiness timeout exits with code 5 and leaves the server running. Inspect the driver logs or diagnostics, repair connectivity or configuration, and retry the check. Do not create another server simply because a readiness check timed out. Without a compatible local client, the wait fails immediately with exit code 1 and the client installation message instead of polling until its timeout. Creation failures include their phase, available partial identity and cleanup outcome. If creation confirmed ownership of a driver and later setup fails, the helper attempts to remove only that owned driver. An uncertain create response is not permission to adopt or delete a resource by name. Failed or uncertain cleanup requires inspection of the reported resource identity before retrying.

Server CLI commands emit one versioned JSON document with --output json. Runtime failures retain the available server or partial run identity. Exit codes are 0 for an accepted operation, 1 for an operational error, 2 for CLI usage errors, 4 for a Kubernetes not-found error, 5 for a timeout and 130 for interruption. Interruption retains any confirmed partial identity and does not initiate extra cleanup. If it interrupts rollback or deletion already in progress, that request may have reached Kubernetes; inspect the reported cleanup outcome. Status can successfully report missing resources without treating that observation as a transport error.

docs.title: Find forgotten servers
docs.text:
A server keeps its driver and executors running after the notebook, tunnel or script that created it has gone. To find servers in a namespace without a receipt:

spark-on-k8s connect server list --namespace spark

APP ID                                     STATUS   AGE   CREATED               SPARK  IMAGE
notebook-6f0c3b8e2d4a4f1c9e7b5a3d1f2e4c6b  running  3d4h  2026-11-06T08:00:00Z  -      apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu

The command is read-only. It lists driver pods labeled spark-role=driver and spark-on-k8s.io/connect-server=true with an application ID, oldest first. Servers created through the CLI, SDK, notebook example or tools built on them carry these labels. It does not verify receipts, Services or query readiness, and it never deletes anything. Labels are not proof of ownership: anyone able to create pods in the namespace can apply them. The helper records no creator identity, so choose a recognizable --name (name in the list) when creating a server.

With --output json, the versioned document has "operation": "connect_server_list", the namespace and items (null on error). Each item contains app_id, name, namespace, driver_pod, driver_uid, status (starting, running, terminated, deleting or unknown), driver_phase, spark_version (from the optional spark-version label, usually null), the driver image, created_at and age_seconds. Exit codes match the other server commands. The SDK equivalent client.list_connect_servers("spark") returns the same items. Each call inspects one namespace. A cluster administrator can find servers in every namespace with kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -l spark-role=driver,spark-on-k8s.io/connect-server=true.

To stop a server you no longer need:

  1. Prefer its receipt, such as connect-server.json or the notebook example's server-receipt.json: spark-on-k8s connect server delete RECEIPT verifies every recorded identity before requesting deletion.
  2. If the receipt is lost, confirm that nobody still uses the server: deletion ends every session on it. Then delete its driver by the listed application ID: spark-on-k8s app delete --namespace spark --app-id APP_ID. The command looks up that single driver and deletes it with its UID as a precondition. Kubernetes then garbage-collects the Services and executors it owns, asynchronously.
  3. Run connect server list again. The server shows deleting until Kubernetes removes the driver, then disappears from the list. A terminated server has stopped Spark but its resources remain until deleted.

For upstream configuration details, see the Spark Connect server configuration and Kubernetes client-mode requirements.

docs.title: SQL jobs without Airflow
docs.text:
The SQL client submits a local .sql file or inline statements using a PySpark image. Airflow is optional. Install the SQL extra from this source checkout:

uv sync --locked --extra sql

After a release containing this feature is published, install that release with python -m pip install 'spark-on-k8s[sql]'. The current source documentation may include features absent from the latest PyPI release.

Configure Kubernetes access, namespace spark, and service account spark as in Getting Started. Then submit a local file:

uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s sql submit \
  --image apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  --namespace spark --service-account spark --name daily-summary \
  --file queries.sql --logs

Or submit inline SQL:

uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s sql submit \
  --image apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu \
  --namespace spark --service-account spark \
  --sql "SELECT 'quoted;semicolon' AS value; SELECT sum(id) FROM range(100);" \
  --executor-initial-instances 1 --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=2 --wait

Use exactly one of --file and --sql. --logs streams output and waits; --wait waits without streaming. Both return a nonzero CLI exit status when the application fails (exit code 3; timeouts use 5). Add --output json for the shared versioned submission receipt, or --timeout 300 to bound observation after submission. A timeout does not delete or stop the application. Without either waiter flag, submission returns before the job finishes. Use the regular app commands to inspect its status or logs.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
SparkOnK8S.submit_sql accepts the same submission options as submit_app, except app_path, app_arguments, and class_name, which the SQL runner manages:

from spark_on_k8s.client import ExecutorInstances, SparkOnK8S

client = SparkOnK8S()
pod_name = client.submit_sql(
    sql_file="queries.sql",  # Or sql="SELECT 1; SELECT 2;"
    image="apache/spark:4.3.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu",
    namespace="spark",
    service_account="spark",
    executor_instances=ExecutorInstances(initial=1),
    app_waiter="log",
)
print(client.app_manager.app_status(namespace="spark", pod_name=pod_name))

The return value is the driver Pod name, as with submit_app. Set dry_run=True to return an offline ApplicationPlan; its to_dict() preview redacts SQL contents and other ConfigMap data. Generated SQL mounts take precedence over matching mounts in a driver template. Explicit conflicting SDK mounts and nested driver-template mounts that could shadow the SQL files are rejected. SQL runs in a single Spark session and preserves temporary views between statements. The first failed statement stops execution and fails the application. Statements already completed are not rolled back: this is not a multi-statement transaction.

The client splits SQL before submission, preserving quoted semicolons and comments. It mounts the runner and a JSON statement list in a managed ConfigMap at /configmap; do not mount another ConfigMap there. The image needs PySpark, but does not need Airflow, spark-on-k8s, or sqlparse. Deleting the driver Pod removes the managed ConfigMap through Kubernetes ownership. Empty or comment-only SQL is rejected by the SDK and CLI.

SQL is plaintext in the ConfigMap and may appear in application logs. Use Kubernetes Secrets for credentials, and configure storage/catalog credentials through Spark settings or the SDK's secret options. Input and output data must be accessible to the driver and executors; a path on the submitting machine is not automatically uploaded. The SQL file itself is uploaded, subject to the Kubernetes ConfigMap size limit.

For scheduled and templated SQL, the Airflow operator uses the same runner. Jinja templating belongs to Airflow; the standalone SDK and CLI send SQL as provided. Review Spark compatibility before changing runtime images or connector versions.

docs.title: Locate a failed statement
docs.text:
The SQL runner records the local file basename (or <inline>), statement number and original starting line in a companion metadata file. It stops at the first failure and reports that location plus the Spark error condition when available. The runner no longer prints the complete query in its own progress or failure messages. Spark's own logs and displayed result rows can still contain data; apply your normal log-access and retention controls.

Earlier successful statements are not rolled back. For quality gates, run explicit Spark SQL assert_true(...) statements before writes where possible. A successful pod only establishes program completion, not business correctness.

docs.title: Single sign-on gateway
docs.text: The API does not authenticate users. Put an authenticating gateway in front of the console before anyone outside the cluster administrators can reach it. This recipe uses oauth2-proxy with any OpenID Connect provider, in front of the Helm chart's API Service. The manifests are in examples/sso-gateway.

docs.title: What the gateway does and does not provide
docs.text:
The gateway decides who reaches the console: only users who sign in with your provider, have an email address in the allowed domain and belong to the allowed group get a session. That session admits them to every console surface: pages, static assets, JSON routes, Spark UI and History proxies and log streams.

It does not authorize individual actions inside the API. The API never learns who is signed in. Every admitted user can do everything the console offers, with the API's single Kubernetes service account: list applications, read logs, open Spark UIs and, unless that account is read-only (readOnly: true, the chart default), kill or delete drivers. Hiding the console's kill and delete buttons does not remove those routes. Kubernetes audit logs attribute those actions to the API service account; only the gateway's request log records the signed-in user. Use separate releases, service accounts and groups for separate trust boundaries; see operational boundaries. The gateway also does not isolate Spark or History HTML from the console origin; see browser and gateway boundaries.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  browser[Browser] -- HTTPS --> ingress[Ingress]
  browser -. sign-in .-> idp[OIDC provider]
  ingress --> gateway[spark-console-gateway<br/>oauth2-proxy]
  gateway -. code exchange .-> idp
  gateway -- only allowed peer --> api[spark-console-spark-on-k8s<br/>API pods]
  kubelet[Kubelet probes] --> api
File Contents console-values.yaml Chart overlay for release spark-console: ClusterIP Service, chart Ingress disabled, public WebSocket origin gateway.yaml oauth2-proxy ConfigMap, Deployment, Service and Ingress network-policy.yaml Admits only gateway pods to the API pods console-values.yaml 
# spark-on-k8s chart values for a console reached only through the oauth2-proxy
# gateway in this directory. See docs/user-guide/sso-gateway.md.
# Install as release "spark-console": gateway.yaml and network-policy.yaml refer to
# the resulting Service name and pod labels. Combine with your image and access values.
service:
  type: ClusterIP
  port: 8000
# The gateway owns the public route; do not also publish the API Service.
ingress:
  enabled: false
env:
  # The exact browser origin. The gateway terminates TLS, so the API's direct
  # Host/scheme comparison cannot match it and log streams need this list.
  - name: SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WEBSOCKET_ALLOWED_ORIGINS
    value: https://spark.example.com
# Remote submission stays disabled: SSO users do not hold the operator bearer token.
gateway.yaml 
# oauth2-proxy gateway in front of the spark-on-k8s console. See docs/user-guide/sso-gateway.md.
# Apply in the "spark-console" release namespace after creating the spark-console-gateway
# Secret. Replace spark.example.com, the issuer, client ID, email domain and group.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: spark-console-gateway
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: oauth2-proxy
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: spark-console-gateway
data:
  # oauth2-proxy labels this structured format alpha; run --config-test before upgrading.
  alpha-config.yaml: |
    server:
      bindAddress: 0.0.0.0:4180
    upstreamConfig:
      upstreams:
        # One route for pages, /static assets, Spark UI proxies and log WebSocket upgrades.
        - id: spark-console
          path: /
          uri: http://spark-console-spark-on-k8s:8000
          proxyWebSockets: true
    providers:
      - id: oidc
        provider: oidc
        name: Single sign-on
        clientID: spark-console
        clientSecretFile: /etc/oauth2-proxy/client/client-secret
        code_challenge_method: S256
        scope: openid email profile
        # Your identity provider must release this group in the ID token's groups claim.
        allowedGroups:
          - spark-console-users
        oidcConfig:
          # Must equal the "issuer" in the provider's discovery document, character for character.
          issuerURL: https://login.example.com
          emailClaim: email
          groupsClaim: groups
          insecureSkipNonce: false
    # No injectRequestHeaders: the API authorizes nothing per user, so none are sent upstream.
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: spark-console-gateway
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: oauth2-proxy
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: spark-console-gateway
spec:
  # Cookie sessions keep no server-side state; replicas share only the Secret.
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: oauth2-proxy
      app.kubernetes.io/instance: spark-console-gateway
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: oauth2-proxy
        app.kubernetes.io/instance: spark-console-gateway
    spec:
      # The gateway never calls the Kubernetes API.
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 65532
        runAsGroup: 65532
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: oauth2-proxy
          # Pinned by tag for readability; deploy a digest you have verified for this tag.
          image: quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy:v7.15.6
          args:
            - --alpha-config=/etc/oauth2-proxy/alpha-config.yaml
            - --redirect-url=https://spark.example.com/oauth2/callback
            - --email-domain=example.com
            - --skip-provider-button=true
            # Background console requests receive 401 instead of a cross-origin login redirect.
            - --api-route=^/(app|apps|runs/v1|webserver/api|webserver/ws)(/|$)
            # The gateway answers these paths itself, so the API's probes are never proxied.
            - --ping-path=/health
            - --ready-path=/ready
            - --cookie-name=__Host-spark-console
            - --cookie-secure=true
            - --cookie-samesite=lax
            - --cookie-expire=8h
            - --session-cookie-minimal=true
          env:
            - name: OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: spark-console-gateway
                  key: cookie-secret
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 4180
              protocol: TCP
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: http
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              memory: 128Mi
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop:
                - ALL
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/oauth2-proxy/alpha-config.yaml
              subPath: alpha-config.yaml
              readOnly: true
            - name: client
              mountPath: /etc/oauth2-proxy/client
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: spark-console-gateway
        - name: client
          secret:
            secretName: spark-console-gateway
            items:
              - key: client-secret
                path: client-secret
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: spark-console-gateway
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: oauth2-proxy
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: spark-console-gateway
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: oauth2-proxy
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: spark-console-gateway
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
      protocol: TCP
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: spark-console-gateway
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: oauth2-proxy
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: spark-console-gateway
  # Raise your controller's read/idle timeout here if it closes quiet log streams.
spec:
  # Set ingressClassName to your controller; omitting it selects the cluster default class.
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - spark.example.com
      secretName: spark-console-tls
  rules:
    - host: spark.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: spark-console-gateway
                port:
                  name: http
network-policy.yaml 
# Only the gateway pods may open connections to the "spark-console" API pods.
# See docs/user-guide/sso-gateway.md. Kubernetes keeps allowing connections from the
# pod's own node, which carry the kubelet's /health and /ready probes.
# Your network plugin must enforce NetworkPolicy, or this object has no effect.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: spark-console-api-from-gateway
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: spark-on-k8s
      app.kubernetes.io/instance: spark-console
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: oauth2-proxy
              app.kubernetes.io/instance: spark-console-gateway
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: http

oauth2-proxy runs as a separate Deployment, not as a sidecar in the API pod. The chart has no sidecar setting, and its Service and kubelet probes target the API container port directly. A sidecar would have to make the API listen only on loopback, which breaks the chart's HTTP probes, or leave the API port open beside it. A separate Deployment keeps the chart unchanged, rolls out and scales independently, and makes the boundary explicit through the NetworkPolicy. Cookie sessions keep no server-side state, so gateway replicas share only their Secret.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
You need an OIDC client registered as a confidential web application with the redirect URI https://spark.example.com/oauth2/callback, a provider that releases group membership in the ID token's groups claim, an ingress controller with a TLS certificate in the spark-console-tls Secret, and a network plugin that enforces NetworkPolicy. Replace spark.example.com, the issuer, client ID, email domain and group in the example files before applying them.

  1. Install the API release. Add your image and access values as described in chart deployment boundaries; Helm replaces lists, so merge any env entries of your own into one list.

    : "${API_IMAGE_DIGEST:?Set the verified API image digest}"
helm upgrade --install spark-console ./chart --namespace spark-system --create-namespace \
  -f examples/sso-gateway/console-values.yaml \
  --set-string image.digest="$API_IMAGE_DIGEST"

  2. Restrict connections to the API pods:

    kubectl apply --namespace spark-system -f examples/sso-gateway/network-policy.yaml

  3. Create the gateway Secret from your environment. Never commit either value.

    : "${OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET:?Set the client secret issued by your provider}"
kubectl create secret generic spark-console-gateway --namespace spark-system \
  --from-literal=client-secret="$OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET" \
  --from-literal=cookie-secret="$(python3 -c 'import base64, os; print(base64.urlsafe_b64encode(os.urandom(32)).decode())')"

  4. Deploy the gateway and wait for it:

    kubectl apply --namespace spark-system -f examples/sso-gateway/gateway.yaml
kubectl rollout status --namespace spark-system deployment/spark-console-gateway

Open https://spark.example.com/webserver/apps. The example pins quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy:v7.15.6 by tag; deploy a digest you have verified for that tag. oauth2-proxy labels the structured alpha-config.yaml format alpha, so validate it with the new image before upgrading: oauth2-proxy --alpha-config alpha-config.yaml <your flags> --config-test.

docs.title: Settings the console depends on
docs.text:
Setting Where Reason SPARK_ON_K8S_API_WEBSOCKET_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://spark.example.com Chart env The gateway terminates TLS, so the API's direct Host/scheme comparison cannot match the browser origin and would reject log streams. Use the exact origin without a path. See log WebSocket origins. One upstream for / with proxyWebSockets: true alpha-config.yaml Pages, /static assets, /webserver/ui/... proxies, JSON routes and the /webserver/ws/logs/... upgrade all pass through one authenticated route. --redirect-url Gateway args The absolute public callback; it must equal the URI registered with the provider. --ping-path=/health, --ready-path=/ready Gateway args oauth2-proxy answers these paths itself, without authentication, before routing. The API's own probe endpoints are therefore never proxied; the kubelet probes the API pod directly. --api-route for /app, /apps, /runs/v1, /webserver/api and /webserver/ws Gateway args After a session expires, background console requests and log streams receive 401 instead of a login redirect that browsers block across origins. Reload the page to sign in again. --email-domain and allowedGroups Args and provider A user must satisfy both. Add the scope your provider uses to release groups if openid email profile is not enough. code_challenge_method: S256, insecureSkipNonce: false Provider Use PKCE and verify the ID token nonce. __Host- cookie name, --cookie-secure, --cookie-samesite=lax Gateway args The session cookie is host-only, HTTPS-only and HttpOnly (the default). Lax cookies, including oauth2-proxy's sign-in CSRF cookie, are still sent on the top-level return from the provider; Strict breaks that return. Lax withholds the session from cross-site subrequests and form posts. The kill and delete routes use PATCH and DELETE, which another origin can send only after a CORS preflight that the API does not approve. --cookie-expire=8h, --session-cookie-minimal=true Gateway args The cookie holds no provider tokens and is not refreshed. A user removed from the group keeps access until the session expires; shorten the lifetime for faster revocation.

The example leaves --reverse-proxy disabled, so oauth2-proxy does not use client-supplied X-Forwarded-* or X-Real-IP headers for its redirects or client addresses; the absolute redirect URL makes them unnecessary. To log real client addresses, enable it only together with --trusted-proxy-ip set to your ingress controller's address ranges. Raise the ingress controller's read or idle timeout if it closes quiet log streams; that setting is controller-specific.

docs.title: Identity headers are deliberately absent
docs.text:
The example defines no injectRequestHeaders, so oauth2-proxy sends no user, email, group or token headers to the API. The API authorizes nothing per user. A gateway-injected or client-forged X-Forwarded-Email therefore grants nothing, and it cannot be used to add per-user rules later without changing the API.

The API reads one identity header only when SPARK_ON_K8S_AUDIT_IDENTITY_HEADER names it, and then only copies it into audit events as an unverified claim. With this example a client can send that header itself, so leave the variable unset, or have the gateway inject the header with injectRequestHeaders so that it replaces any client-supplied value. An event records no identity when the request carries the header more than once.

oauth2-proxy does not remove arbitrary client-supplied headers. That is acceptable here because the Spark UI and History proxies forward only the documented request header allowlist: cookies, Authorization and identity headers from the browser or gateway never reach Spark UIs. Log streams use the API's Kubernetes client. Do not place a component that trusts identity headers behind this gateway unless oauth2-proxy sets those headers itself, which replaces client-supplied values of the same name.

docs.title: Keep the API reachable only through the gateway
docs.text:
The NetworkPolicy selects the release's API pods with the chart's selector labels and admits connections only from the gateway pods, on the API's http port. The ingress controller and every other pod or namespace cannot connect to the API Service. Kubernetes always allows connections from the pod's own node, which carry the kubelet's /health and /ready probes, and kubectl port-forward remains available to administrators.

The chart's helm test pod is not a gateway pod, so it cannot connect while the policy applies. Other in-cluster callers need their own rule or a separate release: a Prometheus scraper for /metrics, or the Airflow task UI through SPARK_ON_K8S_AIRFLOW_SERVICE_URL. The policy has no effect unless the network plugin enforces NetworkPolicy.

docs.title: Remote submission and automation
docs.text:
Keep remote submission disabled on this release, which is the chart default. Run automation against a separate release with remote submission enabled, its own service account and policy, and its own route that is not behind browser single sign-on. The CLI authenticates there with the operator bearer token; see remote submission.

Enabling remote submission on the SSO release requires the operator token on every request. The gateway would then have to discard each client's Authorization header and inject the server token into every HTTP request and WebSocket upgrade, which makes every admitted user an operator-token holder, and remote CLI clients could no longer pass the gateway. This recipe does not cover that configuration.

docs.title: Serve the console below a path
docs.text:
To publish the console at https://spark.example.com/platform/spark, oauth2-proxy removes the prefix before forwarding; the ingress must not. oauth2-proxy builds its sign-in, callback and return URLs from the path it receives, so stripping the prefix in front of it would send browsers outside the prefix. Change the example as follows and register the new callback with your provider. The WebSocket origin setting does not change: an origin has no path.

# console-values.yaml: add to env
- name: SPARK_ON_K8S_API_ROOT_PATH
  value: /platform/spark

# gateway.yaml, alpha-config.yaml upstream
- id: spark-console
  path: ^/platform/spark/(.*)$
  rewriteTarget: /$1
  uri: http://spark-console-spark-on-k8s:8000
  proxyWebSockets: true

# gateway.yaml, changed and added oauth2-proxy args
- --redirect-url=https://spark.example.com/platform/spark/oauth2/callback
- --proxy-prefix=/platform/spark/oauth2
- --api-route=^/platform/spark/(app|apps|runs/v1|webserver/api|webserver/ws)(/|$)
- --ping-path=/platform/spark/health
- --ready-path=/platform/spark/ready
- --cookie-name=__Secure-spark-console
- --cookie-path=/platform/spark

Also point the gateway container's liveness and readiness probes at /platform/spark/health and /platform/spark/ready, and change the Ingress path to /platform/spark with pathType: Prefix. See mounted paths for how the API uses its root path.

A prefix usually means other applications share the host. Scoping the session cookie to the prefix keeps browsers from sending it to them. A __Host- cookie must use Path=/, so this variant uses the __Secure- name prefix, which still requires HTTPS but no longer prevents a sibling subdomain from setting a cookie with the same name.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
tests/chart/test_sso_gateway_example.py runs with the core test suite. It renders the chart with console-values.yaml and checks that the public origin, callback, Ingress and WebSocket allowlist agree; that the upstream targets the rendered API Service with WebSocket proxying; that the API probe paths are answered by the gateway and no authentication bypass is configured; that the NetworkPolicy selects only the API pods and admits only gateway pods; that no identity headers are injected; and that no credentials are committed.

tests/integration/sso_gateway/check.sh is an opt-in end-to-end check that CI does not run. On a disposable kind cluster named sso-gateway-ci, it deploys the example with a mock OIDC provider, then drives sign-in from a pod that is not a gateway pod, once at the host root and once with the /platform/spark changes above. It checks that the NetworkPolicy blocks that pod and still passes the kubelet probes, that a user outside the group is refused, the session cookie attributes, console pages and assets, 401 responses for anonymous API and log-stream requests, that the API probes are not proxied, that a log-stream upgrade succeeds for the public origin and fails for another origin, and that no credentials or identity headers reach a Spark UI upstream. It does not exercise an ingress controller, TLS, a real identity provider, a browser's cookie enforcement or a running Spark application. Build and load the API image as the chart workflow does, then run it from the repository root:

API_IMAGE=ghcr.io/hussein-awala/spark-on-k8s:chart-ci bash tests/integration/sso_gateway/check.sh

docs.title: Interface stability and 1.0
docs.text: This page classifies the public surfaces of the current source and states what each level promises. The support boundaries define what the project owns and how a documented contract is retired; this page applies that policy surface by surface. Use the documentation for your installed release: some surfaces listed here do not exist in older releases.

docs.title: Stability levels
docs.text:
Level What you can rely on Stable A documented contract you can build automation on. A patch release does not change it incompatibly. An incompatible change in a minor release follows the deprecation process: a release-note notice, normally a usable compatibility path for at least one published release, a deprecation register entry and migration steps. A security or correctness fix can break a contract sooner; its release notes state the reason and the operational consequence prominently. Experimental Available for evaluation while its design settles. It can change or be removed in any release. Release notes record the change, without a deprecation period. Internal An implementation detail, even when it is importable, visible in the browser or reachable over HTTP. It can change in any release without notice.

A surface that is neither documented in a guide nor listed on this page is Internal. Human-readable output is never a contract: progress and error messages, --help text, log formatting and the console's layout can change in any release. Automation uses the versioned JSON results and exit codes instead.

Stable behavior includes the lifecycle rules stated across the guides. An uncertain status is not reported as absence. A submission receipt identifies a run; it does not establish that the workload or its data writes succeeded. An observation timeout does not cancel the application; the Airflow operator's startup timeout is the documented exception that deletes a Pending driver. A shared operator token is not tenant isolation.

docs.title: Versioned documents
docs.text:
Several Stable contracts carry a version marker: schema_version in JSON results and files, apiVersion: spark-on-k8s/v1 in job files and /v1 in HTTP paths. Within one marker, changes are additive, such as a new field in a result. Consumers check the marker, ignore unknown fields and do not depend on key order or messages. A change that existing consumers cannot tolerate, such as removing or renaming a field or changing its type or meaning, uses a new marker and follows the deprecation process.

A release can add optional job-file fields, and existing job files keep working after an upgrade. Job files reject unknown settings, so a file that uses a new field needs a release that knows it.

docs.title: Python package and CLI
docs.text: Surface Level Contract Entry points in the Python reference overview, such as SparkOnK8S, RunHandle, JobSpec, ApplicationPlan, Diagnosis and the Spark Connect profile and server classes Stable Documented methods, arguments and results Module pages under Implementation details, undocumented helpers and names starting with _ Internal Reference pages exist for contributors Full content of generated Kubernetes resources, including ApplicationPlan.resources Internal Naming and identity rules documented in the guides are Stable CLI commands and options Stable Command guides; usage errors exit with code 2 CLI --output json results and exit codes Stable schema_version: 1; contract coverage and exit codes Submission receipt files Stable schema_version: 1; receipts Job files Stable apiVersion: spark-on-k8s/v1, kind: SparkJob; job files Offline plan documents Stable envelope schema_version: 1, run identity and capacity summary; the embedded resources are Internal Diagnostic and doctor reports Stable schema_version: 1 and finding code values; diagnostics Spark Connect profile files Stable Named connection profiles Documented SPARK_ON_K8S_* environment variables Stable The guide that documents each variable

docs.title: API, console and run history
docs.text: Surface Level Contract Remote submission routes /jobs/v1/plan and /jobs/v1/submit Stable Request document, schema_version: 1 results, HTTP status and error codes; HTTP contract Submission policy files Stable schema_version: 1; admission policy Run history routes /runs/v1 and /runs/v1/config Stable schema_version: 1, filters and cursor; read-only HTTP API /health, /ready and the documented /metrics names and labels Stable Health and Prometheus Application routes: GET on /apps/list_apps and /apps/list_apps/{namespace}, and PATCH (stop) and DELETE on /app/{namespace}/{app_id} Stable Paths and methods; REST API Console diagnostics endpoint Stable Console and Airflow task tab Console page and Spark UI proxy URLs, such as /webserver/apps?namespace=... and /webserver/ui/{namespace}/{app_id} Stable REST API Other /webserver/api routes, React components and packaged static assets Internal Transport and rendering for the shared console Run history SQLite database Internal Read records through /runs/v1. The store refuses an unknown future schema version, so an older release cannot open a database upgraded by a newer one

docs.title: Airflow
docs.text: Surface Level Contract SparkOnK8SOperator documented arguments and Kubernetes connection behavior Stable Airflow Native task tab settings and permission model Stable Native task tab Triggers, operator links, XCom records used for adoption and the task tab, plugin routes and other provider modules Internal Documented behavior, not their structure

docs.title: Deployment artifacts and integrations
docs.text: Surface Level Contract Helm chart values in the Helm values reference, validated by values.schema.json Stable Versioned with the chart: an incompatible change needs a new chart minor version and migration steps in the chart guide Rendered chart templates and resource names Internal Upgrade notes describe required migrations API image version tags Stable An exact version tag identifies a release; X.Y and latest move as the release runbook describes. Pin a digest to fix the contents API image contents, base image and file layout Internal Rebuilt for each release dbt-spark-on-k8s adapter: profile fields, commands and Python modules Experimental Separate distribution with its own versions from 0.1.0; any release may change it; managed dbt Examples, starters and test fixtures Internal Copy and adapt them; their assertions describe what was tested

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
The Python package and its API image share one version. The Helm chart and the dbt adapter have independent versions; see packages and release order.

Before 1.0, a patch release (0.Y.Z) contains fixes and does not change a Stable surface incompatibly, apart from the security and correctness exception. A minor release (0.Y.0) adds features and can make an incompatible change to a Stable surface only through the deprecation process.

From 1.0, Stable surfaces follow Semantic Versioning: an incompatible change needs a new major version and a deprecation notice in an earlier minor release, minor releases add compatible features and deprecations, and patch releases contain fixes. The security and correctness exception remains, stated prominently in release notes. Experimental and Internal surfaces keep their levels.

docs.title: Criteria for 1.0
docs.text:
The spark-on-k8s package and API image move to 1.0.0 when every criterion below holds. Each names evidence a reviewer can check. The Helm chart and the dbt adapter decide their own 1.0 separately. 1.0 is a statement about interface stability; it does not add a support period, a response time or a certification.

  1. Classified surfaces. Every public surface appears on this page, each Stable row links to its canonical guide or reference page, and no Stable surface depends on an Experimental one. Experimental surfaces stay outside the 1.0 promise unless they first become Stable. Evidence: this page and a strict documentation build.
  2. Contract tests. Each versioned document and each documented exit code has a regression test for its marker, required fields and codes, so an incompatible change fails CI. Evidence: the test paths, listed in the 1.0 release PR.
  3. Two releases without breaks. Every versioned Stable contract has shipped unchanged, apart from additive changes, in at least two consecutive published minor releases. Evidence: release notes for those releases.
  4. No pending removals. The deprecation register has no entry awaiting removal, so 1.0 starts without scheduled breaking changes. Evidence: the register.
  5. Legacy paths decided. The register or this page records whether each legacy path is retained or retired: the Airflow 2.11 compatibility profile, the text-only app kill, app delete and app logs commands, and the unversioned application routes under /apps and /app. Evidence: the recorded decisions.
  6. Release process exercised. At least two releases were published through the tag-triggered workflow with exact-commit eligibility, a retained release record of package hashes, image digests and chart version, and a GitHub release body extracted from its release-notes file. Evidence: the release records.
  7. Qualified deployment. The 1.0 candidate's API image and matching chart version pass a staging smoke test and are recorded as a cluster-qualified combination. Evidence: the release record.
  8. Named runtime matrix. The installation and compatibility guides name the supported Python, Spark, Airflow and Kubernetes versions for 1.0, and each has a CI job that passes on the release commit. Evidence: the release eligibility record.
  9. Security process. Private vulnerability reporting is enabled, the security policy states which release lines receive fixes, including the previous major line after a later major release, and no accepted advisory for the release line is unresolved. Evidence: the repository's Security tab.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Choose the outcome you need. The API and Airflow are optional: neither is required to submit a job from Python or the CLI. These routes describe the current source; first choose a published release or a source checkout. To compare spark-on-k8s with a Spark operator, a managed Spark service or plain spark-submit, read when to use it first.

If you already have a Spark application image and Kubernetes access, follow Installation, then Getting started. If you want to try the included data example before arranging cluster access, start with the local ETL route below. It runs Spark and Java inside Docker.

Your goal Prerequisites and owner Install/profile First observable success Next guide See a real ETL result locally Application author: source checkout, Docker and capacity for the documented 2 GiB container; no cluster Starter application image; no API/Airflow SPARK_STARTER_OK after Parquet output and replay checks ETL starter Submit an existing Python/JVM application Administrator supplies namespace, scoped service account and cluster access; author supplies a compatible image and reachable data Core package; sql extra for SQL Recorded driver identity, then terminal success and application output Getting started, job files, automation Explore an existing Spark Connect service Platform owner supplies endpoint, trust/credentials and permitted data; author uses a compatible client connect extra on its supported Python versions Bounded check succeeds against that endpoint Spark Connect Explore data from a Jupyter notebook Platform owner prepares namespace, driver permissions and trusted cluster access; author supplies a compatible image Locked notebook group plus connect; optional JupyterLab frontend Distributed query and rendered table, then reconnection to the same server after a planned kernel restart Jupyter guide and notebook Run dbt with temporary Spark compute Platform owner supplies Kubernetes access, shared warehouse and external Hive metastore Separate experimental dbt-spark-on-k8s package dbt completes and owned compute is observed absent Managed dbt Create an interactive Spark Connect server Platform owner prepares a namespace, driver permissions and trusted network access Base package for lifecycle; connect extra for queries Receipt identifies private resources; a real query verifies readiness Server setup Observe jobs in a browser Operator supplies API deployment, scoped Kubernetes access and access-controlled networking api extra or a selected API image/chart Console lists the expected namespace and opens a known run Local console, chart deployment Move Spark Operator applications Application owner supplies sparkoperator.k8s.io/v1beta2 manifests; no cluster access needed to assess Core package An offline report for every field and a draft job file that passes job validate Spark Operator migration Run a scheduled Airflow task Airflow owner supplies a supported installation, connection and worker/triggerer access; author supplies the job image airflow; airflow-ui for native Airflow 3 task tab Task runs an application and reaches its documented outcome Airflow

The Python version used to submit a job is separate from the runtimes inside its application image. Use the Spark compatibility guide for Spark, Java, Scala and application-Python choices; the base client needs no local JVM.

A local ETL check proves computation on its fixture, not cluster networking or storage permissions. For shared clusters, ask the administrator for namespace-scoped permissions before using the namespace setup helper: that helper's cluster-wide grant is intentionally broader.
