Driver and executor data access must both work.

docs.title: When the first attempt fails
docs.text:
What you observe Next inspection What it cannot establish No confirmed driver identity Check the submission error and doctor guidance; an ambiguous response may still have created resources Caller checks do not prove the driver's runtime access or that nothing was created Driver stays Pending Diagnose the known application using diagnostics; inspect scheduling, image and storage evidence An empty or incomplete report does not establish health Driver terminated or logs stopped Inspect its final status and diagnostic evidence; logs ending alone are not success A termination request does not prove a completed graceful drain Process succeeded but data is wrong Check application output assertions and input/replay assumptions; see starters Kubernetes success does not validate business results

Keep the generated run identity. Share only sanitized evidence with the relevant application or cluster owner. For project fit, compatibility and operating limits, read when to use it and support boundaries.

docs.title: ETL and lakehouse starters
docs.text: The source checkout includes two small projects with data, application images, and portable job definitions. Each has real Spark execution checks; they are starting points for batch pipelines, not production storage or catalog installations. Run the following commands from the repository root.

docs.title: Order events to Parquet
docs.text:
examples/starters/etl/ reads JSON events with an explicit schema. It normalizes country codes, quarantines invalid amounts, countries, and timestamps, chooses the latest event per order, and writes three Parquet datasets:

Dataset Fixture result clean_orders 4 orders; o1 keeps its latest amount of 1,250 cents quarantine 4 invalid events with rejection reasons daily_revenue 1 January: France, 2 paid orders, 1,750 cents; 2 January: US, 1 paid order, 2,000 cents

Cancelled orders remain in the clean dataset but are excluded from revenue. Money uses integer cents and dates use UTC. Revenue stays on the original order date even when a newer event arrives on a later day; the fixture checks that case. Equal update timestamps use a deterministic record hash as a tie-break. Replace that rule with an authoritative event sequence if your source provides one. Replays overwrite only the three named datasets under the selected output prefix, so use a dedicated prefix for this job. This Parquet replacement is not an atomic multi-table transaction: do not run concurrent writers against the same output prefix.

Build and check the example without a Kubernetes cluster:

docker build -f examples/starters/etl/Dockerfile -t starter-etl:4.3.0 .
docker run --rm --network none --memory 2g --cpus 2 \
  -e SPARK_LOCAL_IP=127.0.0.1 \
  --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/tests/integration/starters/check.py,target=/opt/spark/work-dir/check.py,readonly" \
  --entrypoint /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit starter-etl:4.3.0 \
  --master 'local[2]' --conf spark.ui.enabled=false --conf spark.driver.host=127.0.0.1 \
  /opt/spark/work-dir/check.py --case etl --project /opt/spark/work-dir/starters \
  --work-dir /tmp/starter-check --spark-version 4.3.0

The check runs the pipeline twice and reads the written Parquet data to assert those results. SPARK_STARTER_OK indicates success; output data in this disposable container is removed when it exits. The ETL check covers Spark 3.5.9, 4.0.5, and 4.3.0 in the runtime workflow. Use the matching SPARK_IMAGE build argument to test another supported image.

docs.title: Replayable Iceberg updates
docs.text:
examples/starters/lakehouse/ bootstraps two fixture orders and merges a batch containing a new order and two versions of an existing order. It deduplicates the incoming batch and updates a stored order only when the incoming timestamp is newer. Equal incoming timestamps use amount and country as deterministic tie-breaks; equal timestamps already stored in the table are not overwritten. The expected final rows are o1=1250, o2=500, and o3=2000 cents. Replaying the batch must leave those values and the row count unchanged.

This example uses Spark 4.0.5, Scala 2.13, and Iceberg 1.12.0. Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 publishes Spark 3.5, 4.0, and 4.1 runtime artifacts; it does not publish a Spark 4.3 runtime artifact. Do not use this jar with Spark 4.3. See the official Iceberg release artifacts.

Download the pinned jar, verify its published checksum, and build the image:

mkdir -p examples/starters/target
ICEBERG_JAR=examples/starters/target/iceberg-spark-runtime-4.0_2.13-1.12.0.jar
curl --fail --location --retry 3 \
  https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2/org/apache/iceberg/iceberg-spark-runtime-4.0_2.13/1.12.0/iceberg-spark-runtime-4.0_2.13-1.12.0.jar \
  -o "$ICEBERG_JAR"
printf '%s  %s\n' \
  '03b923f05fb7c9224dbf36a0a443726915a4b81fd9ff171e7c90395e992220294197918c3725076485f6e72bfdd4838d46599a37416ccdd77abc757330b02aff' \
  "$ICEBERG_JAR" | shasum -a 512 --check
docker build -f examples/starters/lakehouse/Dockerfile -t starter-lakehouse:4.0.5 .

The jar is bundled into the image; Spark does not need to download Maven packages at runtime. Check merges, replay safety, and reading the pre-merge snapshot:

docker run --rm --network none --memory 2g --cpus 2 \
  -e SPARK_LOCAL_IP=127.0.0.1 \
  --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/tests/integration/starters/check.py,target=/opt/spark/work-dir/check.py,readonly" \
  --entrypoint /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit starter-lakehouse:4.0.5 \
  --master 'local[2]' --conf spark.ui.enabled=false --conf spark.driver.host=127.0.0.1 \
  /opt/spark/work-dir/check.py --case iceberg --project /opt/spark/work-dir/starters \
  --work-dir /tmp/starter-check --spark-version 4.0.5

The check verifies both the original snapshot and the current table contents. This is a single-writer demonstration. The bootstrap step is not a concurrent initialization protocol, and snapshot cleanup or retention policies are not configured. Set those policies before growing a real table indefinitely.

docs.title: Submit on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Configure namespace spark and service account spark as described in Getting Started. The job definitions mount the same PVC at /data in both driver and executor templates. This is required: a driver's local filesystem is not shared with executor Pods.

examples/starters/storage.yaml requests ReadWriteMany. Select an RWX-capable StorageClass for your cluster and ensure it grants write access to group 185. The templates set fsGroup: 185, but storage provisioners differ in how they apply ownership. For a single-node demo only, ReadWriteOnce can be used instead.

kubectl apply -f examples/starters/storage.yaml
kubectl -n spark get pvc spark-starter-data

Continue only when the claim is Bound. For a local kind cluster, preload the images; the job files use image_pull_policy: Never:

kind load docker-image starter-etl:4.3.0 starter-lakehouse:4.0.5
uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s job validate examples/starters/etl/job.yaml
uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s job plan examples/starters/etl/job.yaml --output json
uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s job submit examples/starters/etl/job.yaml --timeout 300
uv run --no-sync spark-on-k8s job submit examples/starters/lakehouse/job.yaml --timeout 300

For another cluster, push the images to a registry it can access, then update the job files' image names and use IfNotPresent. Change the input and output paths for your own data. Data paths must be accessible to every Pod; the client does not upload local datasets. The same job files can be loaded with JobSpec and passed to an Airflow operator.

The lakehouse job uses a Hadoop catalog on the shared filesystem at file:///data/lakehouse. It requires a filesystem with appropriate atomic rename semantics. For object storage, configure a suitable catalog (for example REST) and storage connector instead of changing this local path to an S3 URI. Follow Iceberg catalog configuration and keep credentials in Kubernetes Secrets or workload identity.

Deleting a driver does not delete these output datasets or the PVC. The local checks and CI container checks validate Spark computation and data results; shared-storage provisioning and Kubernetes execution of these particular starter jobs still depend on the target cluster. The separate compatibility workflow also exercises actual Kubernetes submission and driver-owned resource cleanup.

docs.title: Adaptation contracts
docs.text:
The ETL example records the first matching rejection reason. When a row violates multiple rules, later reasons are not retained. Keep that precedence in mind when diagnosing upstream input; a production extension should use stable rule IDs and explicitly decide whether multiple reasons or raw records may be retained.

Latest-event deduplication is not point-in-time feature reconstruction. For example, a change received after a prediction timestamp must be excluded from that prediction's training features even when it is the latest update today. Replay determinism does not establish historical feature correctness.

For CDC adaptation, define an authoritative source sequence and deletion policy. Equal event timestamps, backfills and delete-then-reinsert events cannot be ordered safely by timestamp alone. This starter is a batch demonstration, not a database CDC connector contract.

Lakehouse before_snapshot/after_snapshot values are observed table state. They do not independently prove which writer committed a snapshot. Keep the single-writer restriction when interpreting the example as execution evidence.

To adapt an Iceberg example to Delta or Hudi, begin with a complete, reviewed connector configuration. Job profiles recursively merge maps: adding a Delta setting does not remove inherited Iceberg catalog keys. Inspect the effective plan before submission and qualify the chosen Spark/Scala/connector combination. A shared 1Gi demo PVC is a dataset/output mount, not a recommended Spark shuffle layout, production storage capacity baseline or data retention policy.

docs.title: Support and compatibility boundaries
docs.text: Spark-on-k8s submits and observes Spark applications using existing Kubernetes infrastructure. The Python client, CLI and optional integrations share that core. Use Start here to select the smallest installation for your task. This page describes source policy; consult the documentation matching your installed release for its available features and tested versions.

docs.title: What the project owns
docs.text:
Surface Supported contract Outside that contract Python Documented client methods, run handles, configuration types and documented helper imports Every importable private/internal object; thread-safe concurrent use of mutable client convenience properties CLI Documented commands/options and the versioned JSON/exit contracts identified in automation Parsing human progress/error prose or assuming every command returns JSON Job files and plans Documented schema/version and merge behavior in job files A GitOps reconciler, scheduler or proof of cluster admission Experimental dbt Separate managed-command adapter for pinned dbt Core/dbt-spark and Spark 4.3 SQL workloads Stable adapter API, Python models, dbt Fusion/Cloud/v2, automatic cluster/catalog deployment or hard-kill cleanup Airflow Documented operators, connection behavior, provider discovery and supported task UI integration A replacement scheduler, identity system or indefinite support for every Airflow generation API and UI Documented routes/configuration, shared console behavior and the versioned audit event schema User/tenant isolation from a shared operator token, see remote submission; a durable or tamper-evident audit store History Bounded metadata, readiness and recorder metrics as documented in run history Durable Spark logs, audit certification, HA database or submission transaction authority Examples The explicit assertions and runtime combinations attached to each example Certification of every cloud, connector, storage backend or application outcome

Interface stability classifies each of these surfaces as Stable, Experimental or Internal and lists the criteria for a 1.0 release.

Kubernetes administrators own cluster access, admission, workload identities, capacity, storage and network boundaries. Application owners own dependencies, input/output correctness, replay safety and external side effects. A successful pod is not a data-quality certification. Spark Connect profiles support existing endpoints. The optional server lifecycle helper creates and deletes private single-driver servers; administrators retain responsibility for network access, authentication, capacity and replacement after failure.

docs.title: Compatibility and retirement
docs.text:
The installation matrix and Spark runtime matrix name the tested combinations. A dependency range is not evidence that every possible combination has been exercised. Optional integrations must identify their maintained workflow, test cost and review owner; accepting one does not promise every feature on every interface. Airflow 2.11 remains a legacy compatibility path; new deployments should follow the Airflow 3 guidance. Do not remove the legacy path silently.

For a change to a documented contract, state the previous behavior, replacement, affected releases and migration steps in the PR and release notes. Normally retain the old behavior or a usable compatibility path for at least one published release with a deprecation notice before removal. Security or correctness fixes may need an earlier break: explain the reason and operational consequence prominently. Additive JSON fields remain permitted where the existing schema tells consumers to tolerate them. An internal refactor does not need a deprecation notice unless it changes a documented import or observable contract.

Before retiring a Python/Airflow/Spark combination, record upstream support status, actual maintained test coverage, dependency constraints and the proposed replacement. Announce the decision in release notes; do not infer retirement from a failing CI job or silently delete the matrix row to make a build pass. There is no guaranteed support duration, response-time SLA or enterprise certification.

docs.title: Deprecation register
docs.text:
No public API removal or compatibility retirement is scheduled by this change. Airflow 2.11 remains supported by its existing legacy checks; its upstream status alone is not a removal announcement.

When a retirement is accepted, add a row with the affected contract, replacement, first notice release, earliest removal release and decision/migration link. Keep the entry through removal so users can trace the upgrade path. Until then, this register is intentionally empty rather than assigning speculative deadlines.

docs.title: Evaluate and report
docs.text:
For a deployment pilot, record the Python package version, chart version, API image digest and documentation revision separately. Charts and packages have independent release channels. A rendered chart is not evidence of a successful deployment; record what ran in your staging cluster, including one job, diagnostics and the recovery procedure if you enable persistent history. The release runbook defines how future release records should make these distinctions visible.

Use Discussions for usage questions, and issues for reproducible defects. Include sanitized versions and evidence, not credentials or private data. Security reports follow the private reporting policy, which also states which release lines receive security fixes. The deployment security boundary describes gateway, proxy and browser responsibilities.

The project currently has a single maintainer. The governance policy describes roles, how decisions and releases are made, and how contributors become reviewers or area maintainers. Organizations that use the project can list themselves in ADOPTERS.md.

docs.title: When to use spark-on-k8s
docs.text: Use this page to decide whether spark-on-k8s fits your team before planning a pilot. It describes the current source; consult the documentation matching your installed release for its available features. Other products appear here only with their general, long-standing architecture. Check their own documentation for current features, support terms and pricing.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Spark-on-k8s is a Python package that submits Spark applications to a Kubernetes cluster you already operate. The client creates the driver pod, and the resources that belong to it, such as its Service and any Secret or ConfigMaps, directly through the Kubernetes API with the caller's credentials. The Apache Spark image's driver entrypoint runs spark-submit in client mode inside that pod; Spark then creates and owns the executors. The submitting machine needs no Spark or Java.

Nothing is installed in the cluster to submit a job: there is no controller, custom resource definition or admission webhook. The cluster needs a namespace, a driver service account and permission for the submitter to create the application's resources. The other pieces are optional and reuse the same core:

Component What it adds Guide Python client and CLI Submit, wait, stream logs, check status and cancel a recorded run; versioned JSON results, receipts and exit codes; job files with offline plans; SQL jobs; diagnostics Getting started, automation, job files API and web console Application list, driver logs, Spark UI and History Server proxies, and opt-in policy-gated remote submission; deployed with the Helm chart Chart deployment, remote submission Run history Bounded driver metadata that remains after pods disappear, in a single-replica SQLite store Run history Airflow provider Application and SQL operators, deferrable waiting, adoption of a recorded driver on retry, and an Airflow 3 task tab Airflow Spark Connect Profiles for existing endpoints and a lifecycle helper for private single-driver servers Spark Connect, server setup, Jupyter Experimental dbt adapter Temporary Spark compute for one dbt Core command, installed separately Managed dbt

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
These boundaries are deliberate; the support boundaries and operational boundaries describe them in more detail.

  • Not a controller. A SparkJob file is loaded by a client; it is not a Kubernetes custom resource, and nothing reconciles desired state after the client exits. Driver pods use restartPolicy: Never, and a failed driver is not restarted or replaced automatically.
  • Not a scheduler. There is no built-in schedule or queue. Use Airflow, a workflow engine or CI to decide when to submit and whether to retry.
  • Not a multi-tenant service. The API has no built-in user authentication. Remote submission uses a shared operator token and an admission policy, which is not per-user authorization or tenant isolation.
  • Not exactly-once submission. An ambiguous creation response is reported as unknown and never blindly retried. There is no deduplication key, and a receipt identifies a run; it does not make data writes idempotent.
  • Not an infrastructure manager. It does not create clusters, node pools, cloud identities, storage or catalogs, and it does not autoscale nodes. Executors can scale with Spark dynamic allocation within the capacity your cluster provides.
  • Not a log or audit store. Driver logs live with their pods, Spark event logs need a Spark History Server, and run history keeps operational metadata only.
  • Not a managed Spark distribution. You supply the application image. The Spark compatibility matrix lists the tested Apache Spark images. There is no vendor support contract or response-time SLA.

docs.title: Compare the alternatives
docs.text:
Approach What you install and operate Who owns a run's lifecycle Usually the better fit when Spark-on-k8s The Python package wherever you submit; optionally the API chart, Airflow provider or dbt adapter The caller: a script, CI job, notebook or Airflow task submits, then decides whether to wait, retry or cancel You operate Kubernetes and want Python-native submission without cluster-scoped components A Spark operator (SparkApplication resources) A controller, its custom resource definitions and RBAC, and their upgrades The controller, which reconciles each custom resource You want Spark applications declared and managed as Kubernetes objects Airflow KubernetesPodOperator running spark-submit Airflow's Kubernetes provider and an image that can run spark-submit The Airflow task pod; your script and Spark settings define how it relates to the driver Your Airflow deployment standardizes on generic container tasks spark-submit against Kubernetes A Spark distribution and Java on each submitting machine The person or script running spark-submit Spark users who already maintain a local Spark installation Amazon EMR on EKS Amazon EKS plus the EMR service configuration and AWS IAM roles The AWS service, through its job-run API Your organization standardizes on AWS-managed Spark runtimes and support Databricks A Databricks account and workspace; no Spark infrastructure in your Kubernetes cluster The Databricks platform You prefer a managed data platform to operating Spark on Kubernetes

These approaches can coexist. A team can keep a Spark operator or a managed platform for some workloads and use spark-on-k8s where direct submission fits.

docs.title: A Spark operator and SparkApplication resources
docs.text:
Kubernetes operators for Spark, such as the Kubeflow Spark Operator or the Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator, add custom resource definitions to the cluster and run a controller that reconciles them. You declare an application as a custom resource, for example SparkApplication, and the controller submits it and records its state on that resource. Depending on the operator and its version, the controller can also apply restart policies or schedules declared in the resource.

Prefer an operator when you want Spark applications managed with kubectl and GitOps tools like other Kubernetes objects, you need the cluster rather than the caller to own restarts or schedules, or your platform already runs one. Airflow's Kubernetes provider also includes an operator that creates SparkApplication resources; those require a compatible Spark operator in the cluster.

Prefer spark-on-k8s when you cannot or do not want to install cluster-scoped resources, or the submitting process should own each run. It needs namespace permissions rather than custom resource definitions, and it returns a run identity to the caller instead of a resource to reconcile.

Operational cost. An operator adds a controller deployment, CRD upgrades and the cluster-scoped privileges needed to install them. Spark-on-k8s adds nothing to the cluster for submission, but restart and scheduling policy move to whoever submits. If both submit drivers to one namespace, drivers started by the operator can appear in the spark-on-k8s console's application list; use separate namespaces when each tool should show only its own runs.

docs.title: Airflow KubernetesPodOperator running spark-submit
docs.text:
KubernetesPodOperator, from Airflow's Kubernetes provider, runs a container as a pod for each task. Teams often use it to run spark-submit from a Spark image. In client mode the task pod is the driver; in cluster mode it asks Kubernetes to create a separate driver pod.

Prefer KubernetesPodOperator when your Airflow deployment standardizes on generic container tasks, the task does more than submit Spark, or you do not want another Python package in Airflow workers.

Prefer the spark-on-k8s operators when you want the Airflow task to track the Spark driver directly. SparkOnK8SOperator and SparkSqlOnK8SOperator create the driver from the worker without a separate submitter pod, wait for it in the triggerer when deferrable, adopt a recorded Pending or Running driver on retry while its task XCom record remains, and apply documented finish, kill and startup-timeout actions. See the lifecycle table.

Operational cost. Both approaches use an Airflow Kubernetes connection. The spark-on-k8s provider must be installed in the Airflow components that run your DAGs, including triggerers for deferrable tasks. The optional task tab also needs a separately deployed spark-on-k8s API. With KubernetesPodOperator, retry and kill behavior for the Spark driver depends on your wrapper script and spark-submit configuration.

docs.title: spark-submit against Kubernetes
docs.text:
Apache Spark's spark-submit supports a Kubernetes master. In cluster mode, it creates the driver pod from a machine that has a Spark distribution and Java. Spark-on-k8s still runs spark-submit, but inside the driver pod; it replaces the submitting side.

Prefer spark-submit when your users already maintain a Spark installation and rely on Spark's own submission options, such as uploading local dependencies at submission time. Spark-on-k8s expects the application and its dependencies to be available to the driver, normally inside the image; it does not upload files from the submitting machine.

Prefer spark-on-k8s when submitters, CI jobs or services should not need a JVM, or you want run receipts, JSON results with stable exit codes, cancellation by recorded identity, portable job files and diagnostics.

docs.title: Amazon EMR on EKS
docs.text:
Amazon EMR on EKS is an AWS-managed service. You register a namespace in an Amazon EKS cluster as an EMR virtual cluster and submit job runs through AWS APIs. Jobs use Amazon EMR release images, access is governed by AWS IAM, and the service has its own AWS pricing in addition to the underlying cluster and compute.

Prefer EMR on EKS when your organization runs on Amazon EKS and wants AWS-built Spark runtimes, job runs managed through AWS APIs and IAM, and support through AWS.

Prefer spark-on-k8s when you need the same tool on any conformant Kubernetes cluster, including local, on-premises or other clouds, or you want to run Apache Spark images or images you build yourself. It is open-source software under the Apache License 2.0; your costs are your own cluster and its operation.

Operational cost. With EMR on EKS, AWS provides the job submission service and runtime images. With spark-on-k8s, you own image builds, Spark upgrades, cloud identity setup, log and history retention, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Databricks
docs.text:
Databricks is a managed data and AI platform. It provisions and operates Spark compute outside your Kubernetes cluster, and provides its own workspace, notebooks, job scheduling, access controls and pricing.

Prefer Databricks when you want a managed platform rather than operating Spark: managed compute and autoscaling, collaborative notebooks, built-in scheduling, workspace user and permission management, and vendor support.

Prefer spark-on-k8s when Spark must run inside Kubernetes clusters you already operate, for example to reuse their capacity, namespaces and network policies, and your team is prepared to own the images, storage access and operations.

Operational cost. Spark-on-k8s has no platform subscription, but you take on the work a managed platform otherwise performs: capacity, autoscaling, security boundaries, catalog and storage integration, upgrades and support.

docs.title: Do not use spark-on-k8s if
docs.text:
• You need a controller to reconcile declared Spark resources, or to restart failed drivers automatically, including those of long-running streaming jobs.
  • You need per-user or per-tenant authorization inside the tool. Local SDK and CLI users act with their own Kubernetes credentials, but the API acts as one service account. Use separate deployments and namespaces for separate trust boundaries.
  • You need exactly-once submission or a deduplication guarantee across retries.
  • You need the tool to provision or autoscale clusters, node pools, storage, catalogs or cloud identities.
  • You need a durable audit trail, retained driver logs or a highly available metadata service from the tool itself.
  • You need a pool of shared, warm SQL or Spark Connect servers. The Connect helper creates private single-driver servers without authentication gateways.
  • You need a vendor support contract, response-time SLA or certified runtime.
  • You do not have, or do not want to operate, a Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: Moving from another approach
docs.text:
Only Spark Operator manifests have an offline assessor. Spark-on-k8s does not read spark-submit scripts or managed-service job definitions, and it never reads or changes live SparkApplication resources. Plan a side-by-side trial in a staging namespace in every case:

  • From a Spark operator: run the migration assessor on your SparkApplication manifests. It drafts job files for the settings that translate and reports lifecycle features without an equivalent, such as restart policies, schedules and cleanup handled by the controller. Decide who will own them, or keep those workloads on the operator. Read lifecycle ownership first, and record every field you cannot map instead of dropping it; see qualifying an integration.
  • From KubernetesPodOperator and spark-submit: move the submission to SparkOnK8SOperator, keep the application in its image, and compare your current retry and kill handling with the Airflow lifecycle table. Grant the worker and triggerer connections only the permissions in the Airflow permission table.
  • From spark-submit: map its arguments to spark-on-k8s app submit options, which accept Spark properties as repeated --conf key=value, or to a job file's spark_conf. Use the automation contract instead of parsing log output.
  • From EMR on EKS or Databricks: the repository has no migration guidance. Evaluate runtime differences between the vendor's Spark build and the Apache Spark images you would use, connector and catalog availability, how cloud identity maps to Kubernetes service accounts, where scheduling will live, and how logs and history will be retained.

For any pilot, record the versions and staging evidence described in Evaluate and report: at least one real job and its diagnostics, plus the recovery procedure if you enable persistent history. Include a controlled failure so that you observe how each tool reports it.
